nations: Southern Ute;Ute Mountain Ute;Ute Indian Tribe of Utah;Kiowa;Comanche;Apache of Oklahoma;Eastern Shoshone;Northern Cheyenne;Northern Arapaho;Cheyenne and Arapaho of Oklahoma
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834, Art. 1 (as cited for congressional title)
summary: TREC selected nations using three legal criteria: aboriginal (original/Indian) title from initial and continuous use; congressional (reserved) title, where Congress legislated the land as Indian Country, citing the 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act Art. 1; and treaty title, for tribes that signed treaties with the US about land now in Colorado.
verbatim_quote: Congressional title, or reserved title, indicates that Congress has enacted legislation acknowledging the title of the land as Indian Country, as seen in the Indian Trade and non-Intercourse Act of 1834, Article 1.
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler record only treaty cessions. TREC adds aboriginal and congressional title as separate layers of legal interest that existed before and alongside any cession.
map_implication: Model three title layers per nation (aboriginal, congressional/Indian Country under 1834 Act, treaty) rather than a single ceded/not ceded polygon state.
notes: This is TREC's framework, not a disputed fact. The 1834 Act is the Act of June 30, 1834, 4 Stat. 729 (cite added by reader, not in source).

instrument: Royce, Indian Land Cessions (Royce maps)
summary: TREC itself used the Royce maps to identify nations involved in cessions, and reproduces a 'Royce Map showing ceded Indian Lands in Colorado 1896'. It states that historical documents, especially treaties, carry pervasive bias and that firsthand American Indian accounts are scarce.

instrument: Indian Claims Commission claims of the ten nations
summary: TREC reviewed ICC reports for every nation. It states land was central in every claim but not one acre was returned, and argues this departs from other land disputes where possession was typically restored.
verbatim_quote: Despite land being a central issue in every claim, not a single acre was returned to the possession of Tribal Nations.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC reports (dockets not named in this chunk)
federal_account_contrast: The federal framing treats ICC awards as settling title. TREC frames them as money paid in place of land, a discriminatory remedy.
map_implication: Where an ICC docket 'extinguished' title by payment, mark the polygon as 'title extinguished by ICC payment; no land returned' rather than 'ceded by treaty'. Pull docket numbers from the tribal chapters.
notes: The claim that possession is 'typically restored' in non-Indian land disputes is a general legal assertion without citation here.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
instrument: Indian Claims Commission Act (1946)
summary: Executive summary says critics argue the ICC was unfair, returned no land, and paid no compounding interest on awards. TREC recommends Congress correct the ICC's construction, discriminatory processes and implementation.
verbatim_quote: Critics argue that the ICC lacked fairness in its process and failed to return any land to the Indian Nations. The lack of compounding interest on awards also raises legal questions.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account presents ICC as final settlement. TREC flags no land return and no interest as structural defects.
map_implication: For ICC-adjudicated areas, show award amount and valuation date with a note that awards carried no interest and no land.
notes: Recommendation p25: 'correct the vast issues involved in the construction, discriminatory processes, and implementation of the Indian Claims Commission.' Act is 60 Stat. 1049 (reader addition).

summary: CSU received Morrill Act grants funded by illegal or coerced dispossession, still owns much of its original parcels (managed by the State Land Board) and earns revenue from mineral and grazing leases. source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes (intro + exec summary)
nations: Tribal Nations that ceded land in Colorado
instrument: Treaties ceding Colorado land
summary: TREC says treaties did not address water rights, so unless Congress expressly excluded them, nations retain them as inherent reserved rights. Recommends Congress and Interior calculate water rights taken without permission.
verbatim_quote: Water rights were not explicitly addressed in the treaties, meaning that unless Congress specifically stated that they were not included, it is within the inherent powers of Indian Nations to have reserved them without notice.
federal_account_contrast: Cession framing implies water went with land; TREC argues it was reserved.
map_implication: Add a 'water rights not addressed in instrument' attribute to cessions.
notes: Legal theory, close to the reserved-rights doctrine (Winters v. US, 1908) but extended to ceded lands, which is not settled law. Source cites no case.

The book says the nations understood a wagon-wheel-width road, but trails grew up to two miles wide, destroying timber and game, and the 1858 Colorado gold rush made the treaty unenforceable.
verbatim_quote: The Indian Nations understood they were consenting to a road or highway no wider than the width of a wagon-wheel track. Instead, the road was sometimes up to two miles wide
federal_account_contrast: Federal text reads as a general right-of-way grant; Native understanding was far narrower.
map_implication: Add Santa Fe Trail corridor note: right-of-way consent understood as narrow track; damage beyond consent.
notes: Author openly labels comments 'biased criticisms and witticisms' (p.46).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, preamble and Article 4
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: The treaty itself describes the nations as 'inhabiting the said territory south of the Arkansas River' and repeatedly refers to 'their said territories', an implicit US acknowledgment of their territory. No land was ceded.
verbatim_quote: the Camanche [sic], and Kiowa, and Apache tribes or nations of Indians, inhabiting the said territory south of the Arkansas River.
federal_account_contrast: Royce lists no cession for 1853; the recognition of territory is not drawn.
map_implication: Draw 1853 Fort Atkinson 'territories inhabited' (south of Arkansas River) as recognized occupancy, not a cession; includes SE Colorado south of the Arkansas.
notes: No boundaries beyond 'south of the Arkansas River'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, Articles 6, 7, 9, 10
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: Article 6 promised $18,000 a year for ten years (plus five more at the President's discretion) in goods; Article 7 promised US protection and compensation for depredations by US citizens. The author found no compensation for treaty violations in the annual Indian appropriations acts of those years.
verbatim_quote: I could not find any evidence in the annual Indian Appropriations Acts during these years where there was compensation for losses from treaty violations.
sources_cited_by_source: Author's review of annual Indian Appropriations Acts (not individually cited)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows the promise; non-performance of Article 7 is not catalogued.
map_implication: Record Fort Atkinson Art.7 protection/compensation promise as unperformed (per PSL); Art.6 delivery to be verified.
notes: Book does not say whether the $18,000 annuities themselves were delivered. Art.6 commentary calls 'by these presents' a bribe; that is a misreading of a standard legal phrase and should not be repeated as evidence.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, Article 8
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: Article 8 let the US withhold all or part of the annuities from a whole tribe until offenders were surrendered, i.e. collective punishment through food and goods. Later the US threatened to end treaty payments when Kiowa defended their land (p.40).
verbatim_quote: then the United States may withhold the whole part or a part of the annuities mentioned in the sixth article of this treaty, from the tribe so offending
federal_account_contrast: Treated in the federal record as a routine enforcement clause.
map_implication: Tag annuity-withholding clauses as a structural coercion lever.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27; Fort Laramie Treaty 1851
summary: The author suggests that, as at Fort Laramie 1851, Fitzpatrick likely picked the 'chiefs and headmen' rather than letting bands select them, noting he forced the Lakota to name one leader over 22 tiyospayes.
verbatim_quote: we could assume that the “chiefs and leaders” were not selected by their bands but followed the practice perfected by Thomas Fitzpatrick during the negotiations of the Fort Laramie Treaty.
federal_account_contrast: Federal text says signers were chiefs and headmen of the nations.
map_implication: Do not flag Fort Atkinson as illegitimate on this basis alone; record as an inference.
notes: Explicitly an assumption by analogy; no Fort Atkinson evidence offered.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Pike's Peak region, Colorado; Kiowa territory
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27 (violated)
summary: The 1858 Pike's Peak gold rush sent thousands through Kiowa land and settlements were built illegally; the US did not stop these violations but threatened to cut treaty payments and send troops when the Kiowa resisted.
verbatim_quote: Settlements were quickly being built illegally on tribal lands, and the United States did not attempt to stop treaty violations made by the Euro-Americans.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Federal record dates loss of these lands to later treaties, not to earlier unauthorized occupation.
map_implication: Mark settler occupation of Colorado lands south of the Arkansas as preceding any Kiowa/Comanche cession.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Sand Creek, near Fort Lyon, Colorado Territory
summary: Governor John Evans began a policy of extermination; about 500 Cheyenne and Arapaho camped under promised protection with a US flag were attacked by Chivington's Colorado militia, killing more than 130, mostly women and children. The book says news of it convinced Plains nations the US could not be trusted, shaping 1865 and 1867 talks.
verbatim_quote: More than 130 Indians were killed, primarily women and children. News of the Sand Creek Massacre spread across the plains, proving that the United States could not be trusted.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Atlas already covers Sand Creek; book links it to Kiowa/Comanche treaty context.
map_implication: Link Sand Creek to Little Arkansas 1865 and Medicine Lodge 1867 as context for consent under threat.
notes: Kiowa-chapter mention; covered in depth elsewhere in the book.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Kit Carson's troops attacked Kiowa and Comanche winter camps; one camp of 176 tipis was burned with all food and supplies, leaving many without shelter or food. Carson was a US commissioner at Little Arkansas less than a year later.
verbatim_quote: A total of 176 tipis were destroyed, along with all food and supplies. Many people were left without shelter, clothing, or food that winter.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text lists Kit Carson as a commissioner with no reference to his attack.
map_implication: Add a point event (likely First Battle of Adobe Walls, Nov 1864) and note Carson's role as 1865 treaty commissioner.
notes: Book says 'around 1864' and does not name Adobe Walls; identification is mine.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Council ground on the Little Arkansas River, eight miles from its mouth, near present Wichita, Kansas
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, preamble and Article 6
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Some Comanche bands were absent; Article 6 made the signers promise to bring in absentees, whose mere receipt of annuities would bind them. The preamble nonetheless declares signers 'duly authorized', and the book comments that many leaders of both nations did not sign.
verbatim_quote: made binding on all parties whenever such absentees shall have participated in the beneficial provisions of this treaty. Comment: Many of the two Nations’ leaders did not sign this treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced (endnote 4); Kansapedia for p.31
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the treaty as binding both nations from signing.
map_implication: Flag 1865 cession as signed without several Comanche bands; consent of absentees was deemed from accepting goods.
notes: Contradiction: p.41 says 'all the leading chiefs eventually signed it'; p.54 says many leaders did not sign. Royce areas from atlas crosswalk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: NE corner of New Mexico; SE corner of New Mexico; Red River at mouth of North Fork; 98th meridian; Cimarron River; southern boundary of Kansas
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Article 2
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Article 2 set apart a reservation 'for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation' of the tribes, bounded from the NE corner of New Mexico south to its SE corner, NE to the Red River opposite the North Fork mouth, down the Red to the 98th meridian, north to the Cimarron, up it to the Kansas line, west along Kansas to its SW corner, then west to the start. The book says it held over 39 million acres; within two years it was cut back at Medicine Lodge.
verbatim_quote: shall be and is hereby set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the tribes who are parties to this treaty
federal_account_contrast: Royce 478/511 shows it as a reservation; the federal record rarely marks it as a guarantee broken within two years.
map_implication: Draw the 1865 Little Arkansas reservation exactly from Art.2 calls (includes Texas panhandle and Oklahoma panhandle) as 'promised 1865, taken 1867'.
notes: Clause 'or such portion... as may hereafter... be designated by the President' made the guarantee conditional; the author calls the vagueness unacceptable. Most of the area lay in Texas, which held its public lands, so the US could not deliver it (my note; not in book).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Country north of the Cimarron River and west of the eastern boundary of New Mexico (includes SE Colorado and SW Kansas)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Article 2 relinquishment clause
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Article 2 had the signers relinquish all claims outside the reservation, 'more especially' north of the Cimarron and west of New Mexico's eastern boundary. This is the clause that extinguished Kiowa and Comanche claims in southeastern Colorado, signed while some Comanche bands were absent.
verbatim_quote: relinquish all claims or rights in and to any portion of the United States or territories, except such as is embraced within the limits aforesaid
federal_account_contrast: Royce draws this as a cession; the book frames the whole article as 'suspect'.
map_implication: For Colorado polygons ceded by Kiowa/Comanche in 1865, add caveat: absent bands, Article 2 judged suspect, reservation promised in return was cut two years later.
notes: Clause text literally reads 'north of the Cimarone River and west of the eastern boundary of New Mexico'; the Royce cession number for this relinquishment should be checked.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Unsettled country south of the Arkansas River
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Article 3
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Until removal, the tribes were 'expressly permitted to reside upon and range at pleasure' over unsettled land south of the Arkansas that they claimed as originally theirs. This is a US admission of their original claim south of the Arkansas, including Colorado.
verbatim_quote: expressly permitted to reside upon and range at pleasure throughout the unsettled portions of that part of the country they claim as originally theirs, which lies south of the Arkansas River
federal_account_contrast: Interim occupancy right is not shown in Royce.
map_implication: Add 1865 interim occupancy/hunting right south of the Arkansas River (incl. SE Colorado) as a reserved right.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
nations: Kiowa; Comanche; Kiowa Apache; Cheyenne; Arapaho
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18
summary: The Kansapedia-derived narrative says the tribes agreed to settle in western Kansas but Kansas lobbied against the treaty and they were forced elsewhere; it also says Dohasan protested but all leading chiefs eventually signed.
verbatim_quote: The tribes agreed to settle in western Kansas. The State of Kansas lobbied against the Treaty, and tribes were forced to settle elsewhere.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text (p.51) places the Kiowa-Comanche reservation south of Kansas, not in western Kansas.
map_implication: Do not map a western Kansas reservation from this; needs verification. Kansas lobbying may relate to the Cheyenne-Arapaho 1865 treaty.
notes: Conflicts with Art.2 boundary and with p.31 ('agreed to live in Indian Territory').

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Articles 4 and 5
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Article 4 promised compensation for injury from roads and posts; Article 5 promised $10 per capita (rising to $15 after removal) annually for 40 years, on a base of 4,000 people. The author found little or no evidence of compensation and notes the treaty lasted only about two years before replacement.
verbatim_quote: There is little or no evidence that an invader was ever charged with violating this treaty or that anyone among the Tribes received compensation.
federal_account_contrast: 40-year annuity was superseded by Medicine Lodge; federal record does not net what was owed vs paid.
map_implication: Record 1865 40-year per-capita promise and its early supersession; check payments in appropriations acts.
notes: Author also says the treaty had 'scarcely been ratified for a few weeks' before a new standard; ratification date not given in book.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Act of March 29, 1867 (sec. 6 repealing treaty-making authority); Act of July 20, 1867 (Peace Commission); N.G. Taylor report of July 12, 1867
summary: Quoting ICC Docket 257, the book shows Congress repealed treaty-making authority in March 1867, then Commissioner Taylor urged its repeal and a large removal territory south of Kansas including the Texas staked plains. The book reads this as proof the Peace Commission was designed for removal, not negotiation.
verbatim_quote: recommend that a large territory be set apart south of the southern line of Kansas and west of Arkansas, including the present Indian Territory and the country known as the staked plains of Texas
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Docket 257, Opinion on Motion for Summary Judgment of Recognized Title, Aug 9, 1971; Kuykendall dissent pp.123-131; Congressional Globe (endnotes 5-11)
federal_account_contrast: Federal narrative frames Medicine Lodge as a peace negotiation; this shows a predetermined removal plan.
map_implication: Link Medicine Lodge to the 1867 removal policy; cite ICC Docket 257.
notes: Book's 'conspired to illegally construct a plan' is the author's conclusion. Book is unclear whether quoted material is from majority or Kuykendall dissent.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: ICC Docket 257, Kiowa, Comanche and Apache Tribes v. United States
summary: The ICC heard a KCA motion for summary judgment of recognized title; the book says there were favorable findings for the tribes, opposed by Chairman Kuykendall in dissent, followed by an appeal to the Court of Claims.
verbatim_quote: This information is taken directly from Commissioner Jerome K. Kuykendall, Chairman of the Indian Claims Commission, dissent pp. 123-131, to have the favorable findings on behalf of the Tribes dismissed.
federal_account_contrast: Shows ICC split on recognized title for KCA lands.
map_implication: Add ICC Docket 257 to KCA polygons; details promised later in the book.
notes: Book says 'U.S. Claims Commission Court', presumably the US Court of Claims. Outcome not in this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
nations: Kiowa; Comanche; Kiowa Apache; Cheyenne; Arapaho
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: The book states the tribes were coerced by threats of starvation and military intimidation into accepting a shared reservation between the Canadian and Red Rivers and allowing railroads.
verbatim_quote: The tribes were forcibly coerced to agree by threats of starvation and military intimidation to share a reservation between the Canadian and Red Rivers in present-day southwestern Oklahoma.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/NARA present Medicine Lodge as a negotiated peace treaty.
map_implication: Flag Royce 510/511 (1867 Kiowa-Comanche cession) as signed under duress (starvation and military threat).
notes: No specific threat is documented in this chunk; Sand Creek (1864) and Carson's 1864 raid provide context.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: Gui-pago (Lone Wolf) was the only Kiowa leader who did not sign Medicine Lodge. With Dohasan dead (1866), Kiowa leadership was divided between Kicking Bird (peace) and Lone Wolf and Satanta (resistance).
verbatim_quote: Gui-pago was the only Kiowa leader who did not sign the Medicine Lodge Treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Federal text says signers were 'duly authorized and empowered to act for the body of the people'.
map_implication: Note Lone Wolf (the elder) did not sign Medicine Lodge.
notes: Do not confuse with Lone Wolf the younger of Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Washita River at 98th meridian; 30 river-miles west of Fort Cobb; North Fork of Red River / 100th meridian; main Red River
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21, Article 2
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: Article 2 set apart a reservation from where the Washita crosses the 98th meridian, up the Washita to 30 river-miles west of Fort Cobb, due west to the North Fork of the Red (or to the 100th meridian then south to it), down the North Fork to the Red, down the Red to the 98th meridian, then north to the start. The US 'solemnly' promised no one unauthorized would ever pass over, settle or reside there.
verbatim_quote: the United States now solemnly agrees that no persons except those herein authorized so to do... shall ever be permitted to pass over, settle upon, or reside in the territory described in this article
federal_account_contrast: The 'ever' guarantee was broken by the Jerome Agreement/1900 Act (outside this chunk).
map_implication: Draw the 1867 KCA reservation from Art.2 calls as 'guaranteed forever 1867'; link to 1892/1900 taking.
notes: Narrative on p.41 describes it as between the Red, North Fork and Washita; and earlier as between Canadian and Red (the combined Medicine Lodge area incl. Cheyenne-Arapaho).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21, Article 2 pencil additions
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: A Department of State note says words in brackets were written in pencil in the original, the rest in ink; the pencil additions include the boundary lead-in and the phrase 'with the consent of the United States' limiting whom the tribes could admit. The author says leaders rejected the boundaries and location, yet they were inserted in a pre-drafted document.
verbatim_quote: The leaders of Kiowa and Comanche rejected these boundaries and the location, yet they were inserted in the document. This is a perfect example of a document that had been previously constructed
sources_cited_by_source: Department of State note on original treaty; Peace Commission proceedings
federal_account_contrast: Ratified text shows no indication the boundaries were disputed or that consent language was added in pencil.
map_implication: Flag Medicine Lodge Art.2 text as containing pencil insertions of unknown timing; check NARA original.
notes: Book does not say who wrote the pencil words or when; do not call it forgery without archival check. Pencil markers appear in the text as '[addition in pencil*]' and '[phrase addition A underlined made in pencil*]'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21
instrument_cite: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867-68 (endnotes 12-14)
summary: Ten Bear (Comanche) said the proposed land was too small and that Texans had taken the best country; Satanta (Kiowa) said he did not want to settle on a reservation. The book argues the commissioners ignored what the leaders said and the result was preordained.
verbatim_quote: that which you now say we must live on is too small. The Texans have taken away the places where the grass grew the thickest and the timber was the best.
sources_cited_by_source: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867-68
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text records assent; recorded speeches show refusal of the land offered.
map_implication: Attach Ten Bear and Satanta statements to the Medicine Lodge record as stated objection to the reservation.
notes: Satanta refers to a reservation 'near the Mountains' (Wichita Mountains).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Medicine Lodge Creek, Kansas; Red River and Wichita Mountains
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21 (hunting concession)
instrument_cite: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission (endnote 14)
summary: Senator Henderson told the council the Kiowa and Comanche could hunt 'up the river' while warning that the buffalo would vanish, a remark the transcript records with laughter. The narrative calls the hunting right a last-minute concession over former lands in Kansas (p.31) or Kansas and Texas (p.41).
verbatim_quote: When that day comes, the Indian must leave his father’s road, or suffer and probably die.(Laughter.)
sources_cited_by_source: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission (endnote 14)
federal_account_contrast: Hunting right appears in the treaty (Art.11, not in this chunk) as a neutral clause; the transcript shows the US expected it to lapse with the buffalo.
map_implication: Map the off-reservation hunting right south of the Arkansas as reserved; note US expectation of its extinction.
notes: Inconsistency: p.31 says Kansas; p.41 says Kansas and Texas.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21 (rations/annuities)
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: After a failed hunt, the Kiowa asked the agent for promised provisions but got none because Congress had not yet acted on the treaty; by 1871 none of the promised rations had been delivered.
verbatim_quote: They requested provisions that were promised in the treaty from the Indian agent. Congress had yet to approve the treaty. Thus, no provisions were granted.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Atlas seed gives Medicine Lodge proclamation 1868-07-25; book indicates obligations went unmet in practice.
map_implication: Add Medicine Lodge non-delivery of rations 1868-1871 to violations catalog.
notes: 'None... by 1871' may overstate; verify against agency reports.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Sherman ordered Satanta, Setangya and Big Tree arrested and sent to Texas for trial; Setangya was killed en route; the others were sentenced to hang, commuted to life with forced railroad labor, released 1873; Satanta was re-imprisoned in 1874 and died by suicide.
verbatim_quote: The three leaders were seized, handcuffed, and transported by armed guards to Texas.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Shows a state court prosecuting treaty-nation leaders for acts of war.
map_implication: Add imprisonment of Kiowa treaty signers by Texas to the violence/state-action layer.
notes: Includes Setangya's Koitsenko death song (p.42).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Quaker (Peace) Policy, 1869
summary: Agent Lawrie Tatum withheld rations to force cultural change; later the government lowered rations to starvation levels to press assimilation while settlers pushed to open the reservation.
verbatim_quote: The government increased the pressure on the Kiowa to assimilate, lowering food rations to levels that caused starvation.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Ration policy is not in treaty records; shows starvation used as a policy tool on a treaty reservation.
map_implication: Add 'sign or starve' context to later KCA land loss (Jerome Agreement era).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Texas panhandle (Palo Duro Canyon, unnamed in book)
summary: Mackenzie's troops destroyed a Kiowa, Comanche and Cheyenne village, its food, shelter and horses, forcing the people back to Fort Sill; all surrendered by April 1875.
verbatim_quote: All the food, clothing, supplies, and shelter were destroyed, and the horses were slaughtered.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
map_implication: Add Palo Duro 1874 event; book writes 'Ronald Mackenzie' (actually Ranald S. Mackenzie).
notes: Identification as Palo Duro is mine.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: After Texas Rangers killed a Kiowa in 1879, the book says Congress made it illegal for any Kiowa to leave the reservation; in the 1880s ranchers illegally used tribal land; the Kiowa refused leasing though some Comanche leased.
verbatim_quote: Some ranchers illegally used tribal land, and others tried to lease it. The Kiowa continually refused to lease any of their land
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
map_implication: Note illegal grazing and Kiowa/Comanche split over leasing on the 1867 reservation.
notes: The claim that 'Congress' barred Kiowa from leaving is unsourced and probably an administrative order; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Kiowa reservation and off-reservation boarding schools
summary: Kiowa children were forced or captured into boarding schools that banned language and religion; three beaten boys froze to death after escaping in 1891 and a 1892 measles outbreak killed more than 220 children. Agent E.E. White banned the Sun Dance in 1888.
verbatim_quote: Some children were captured and placed in boarding schools far from the reservation.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
map_implication: Add boarding school harms to KCA record; Sun Dance ban 1888.
notes: 'More than 220 children' figure unsourced; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: KCA treaties generally
summary: The author asserts that Indian agents produced compliant signers who bound whole nations, and that some government interpreters maliciously distorted treaty contents to benefit themselves.
verbatim_quote: In many cases, the Indian agents produced Indians who were compliant and agreeable to every demand of those agents and became the signers.
federal_account_contrast: Federal texts recite signers as duly authorized.
map_implication: Use only as framing; requires instrument-specific evidence before flagging.
notes: General claim; no specific interpreter named in this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Source caveat: the book states that most of the Comanche and Kiowa history before Part 2 (pp.29-45) was copied directly from Kansapedia with permission, so those pages are a secondary encyclopedia source, not Native-authored analysis. Part 2 commentary (pp.45-60) is the TREC author's own, self-described as including 'biased criticisms and witticisms'.
verbatim_quote: Most of the preceding sections of this report detailing the history of the Comanche and Kiowa Tribes were copied directly from articles online in Kansapedia
map_implication: When citing pp.29-45, cite Kansapedia as the underlying source.
notes: Affects evidence level of all p.29-45 findings.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21
summary: The author annotates Medicine Lodge articles 6-10, 11 (railroad, emigrant and military-post clauses), 13, 14 and 16 against the council transcripts and says these terms were never discussed with tribal leaders. He calls the treaty contents fabrications of the commissioners and their staff.
verbatim_quote: The contents of this treaty are all fabrications by the US commissioners and their staff. None of this is in the treaty transcripts.
sources_cited_by_source: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867-68 (DeMallie & Deloria 1975) cited for the transcripts (endnotes 12-14, earlier chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Kappler prints the articles as the agreed text. PSL says only the hunting right (Art. 11) was actually discussed, so most of the text was not consented to.
map_implication: Flag the 1867 KCA treaty record: 'articles largely absent from council transcripts per PSL'; do not imply informed consent to allotment, school, railroad or military-post clauses.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Lands south of the Arkansas River; old Little Arkansas reservation
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21 Art. 11 and 16
summary: Article 11 kept the right to hunt on any lands south of the Arkansas River 'so long as the buffalo may range thereon', and barred white settlement on the old 1865 reservation for three years. PSL says this was hollow because the military was killing buffalo at the same time to force the tribes onto reservations.
verbatim_quote: This was a hollow promise as the military at this time was killing buffalo to force the Indians onto reservations.
federal_account_contrast: The federal record treats the hunting right as a reserved right that simply lapsed. PSL frames its ending as deliberate destruction of the resource.
map_implication: Map the Art. 11 reserved hunting area (lands south of the Arkansas, incl. SE Colorado) as a reserved-use right, not plain ceded land; note the old 1865 reservation's 3-year no-settlement clause.
notes: The text notes that part of Art. 11 appears in pencil in the original, and gives transcription notes (asterisks) on the original treaty.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21 Art. 15
summary: Article 15 gave $750 for a house for Comanche chief Tosh-e-wa (Silver Brooch) and $500 a year in presents to the ten best farmers. PSL says this should be treated as an illegal bribe.
verbatim_quote: Without question, this needs to be considered illegal and a bribe.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler frames this as an incentive provision.
map_implication: Annotate the 1867 treaty with the Art. 15 payment to an individual chief as an alleged inducement.
notes: The characterization as bribery is the author's opinion; the payment itself is in the treaty text.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek with Kiowa and Comanche, 1867-10-21 Art. 12
summary: Article 12 made any cession of the common reservation invalid unless signed by at least three-fourths of the adult male Indians occupying it. PSL says the government was never able to get three-fourths of adult males to sign a change.
verbatim_quote: unless executed and signed by at least three-fourths of all the adult male Indians occupying the same
federal_account_contrast: This is the treaty's own consent rule. The later 1892/1900 cession did not meet it, according to PSL and Clark.
map_implication: Store the Art. 12 three-fourths consent rule as a property of the 1867 KCA reservation; any later cession record should be tested against it.
notes: Note the treaty text cross-references 'Article III [VI]' for individual selections.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome Agreement as modified by Act of June 6, 1900
summary: Quoting C. Blue Clark (Encyclopedia of the Great Plains), the report says Congress in 1900 approved a modified agreement that lacked enough signatures even counting forgeries.
verbatim_quote: In 1900 Congress had approved a modified 1892 allotment agreement that did not contain sufficient signatures, even with forgeries
sources_cited_by_source: Blue Clark, C., 2011, 'Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock', Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, egp.law.027 (endnote 17)
federal_account_contrast: Statutes at Large present the 1900 act as ratifying a tribal agreement. Clark says the signatures were insufficient and included forgeries.
map_implication: Mark the 1900 KCA cession as 'ratified despite insufficient signatures incl. forgeries (Clark)'; do not render as consensual cession.
notes: Clark's count claim conflicts with the 456/562 figure on p.66; both appear in the source. Verification: verify-plains s.6: forgery alleged by secondary sources only; no court ruled on it.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome Agreement (pending ratification)
summary: During the eight years before ratification, thousands of settlers illegally rushed onto Kiowa lands, took stone, timber and minerals, and set up farms. Towns grew as the Rock Island Railroad was built through the north of the reservation.
verbatim_quote: During that time, thousands of Euro-American settlers illegally rushed into Kiowa lands. These settlers robbed the reservation's stone, timber, and minerals while establishing farms.
federal_account_contrast: Adds illegal pre-ratification occupation that the cession record does not show.
map_implication: Note pre-1900 illegal settlement and resource theft on the KCA reservation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome Agreement vs Medicine Lodge Art. 6
summary: The commission offered 160-acre allotments although Medicine Lodge had provided up to 320 acres per head of family if the land were divided.
verbatim_quote: The commission proposed that the land be divided into 160-acre plots, but the Medicine Lodge Treaty of 1867 called for 320-acre plots
federal_account_contrast: Shows the allotment terms cut the treaty's individual land guarantee in half.
map_implication: Note the reduction from 320-acre treaty selections to 160-acre allotments.
notes: Art. 6 actually says 'not exceeding' 320 acres for a head of family and 80 for single adults over 18.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903)
summary: Lone Wolf sued Interior Secretary Ethan A. Hitchcock to stop allotment. The Supreme Court ruled in 1903 that Congress has plenary power and can abrogate treaty rights, and that its motives cannot be reviewed. The Art. 12 three-fourths condition was sidestepped. The surplus was quickly opened to settlers.
verbatim_quote: Kiowa claims, including the condition of article 12 of the Medicine Lodge Treaty (1867) forbidding cession of Indian land unless approved by three-fourths of the tribe's male members, were sidestepped in the Court's opinion.
sources_cited_by_source: Blue Clark 2011 (endnote 17); Echo-Hawk 2013, In the Light of Justice, 178 (endnote 18); Kansapedia
federal_account_contrast: The federal legal record treats the cession as valid under plenary power. The source frames the case as legalizing a treaty breach.
map_implication: Link the KCA surplus land opening (1901) to Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock as 'cession upheld without valid tribal consent'.
notes: The source gives no U.S. Reports cite (187 U.S. 553 is the standard cite; not in source). Day not stated in the source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: General Allotment Act 1887; Jerome Agreement
summary: More than 50,000 settlers took the tribal land. Allotment ran 1906-1936. Over 65 percent of individual Kiowa holdings and about 93 percent of tribal pasture lands were lost. Oil and gas leases from 1914 paid little and were controlled by the government.
verbatim_quote: Over 65 percent of individual tribal land holdings were lost to Euro-American settlers, and roughly 93 percent of tribal-owned pasture lands were lost.
federal_account_contrast: Adds what happened after cession to the land that was reserved.
map_implication: Annotate the KCA reservation with the post-allotment loss figures (65% individual, 93% pasture).
notes: The text says 'southeastern Oklahoma'; the KCA reservation was in southwestern Oklahoma, so this is likely a slip in the source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC proceedings on Jerome Agreement
summary: The government argued that any award for the Jerome Agreement should be offset by $1.5 million in depredation damages charged to the tribe. The ICC rejected depredation offsets as contrary to the purpose of the proceedings. Kansapedia says the Kiowa were awarded nearly $2 million in 1960 after 11 years.
verbatim_quote: The Indian Claims Commission resolved that offsets for depredations were contrary to the purpose of the proceedings.
federal_account_contrast: Shows the government tried to charge the tribe for 'depredations' against the award.
map_implication: In ICC data, record the proposed $1.5M depredation offset (rejected).
notes: The 'nearly $2 million in 1960' figure does not match the Docket 32 dates below (Amended Final Award 1957-03-29, $2,067,166). Needs checking.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC Docket No. 32 (Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache Tribes v. United States)
instrument_cite: ICC Docket 32; 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505; Act of June 6, 1900, 31 Stat. 677
summary: The tribes claimed $16,268,664. The ICC found the land 'unconscionably' acquired (1951-04-09). Additional Findings (1955-12-13) set the ceded area at 2,033,583 acres worth $4,067,166 ($2.00 per acre) as of 1900-06-06, minus the $2,000,000 already paid. The final award was $2,067,166. The government appealed and lost; the Amended Final Award came on 1957-03-29, with no 5% compound interest and no land returned.
verbatim_quote: concluded that the ceded area consisted of 2,033,583 acres, with a fair market value of $4,067,166 as of June 6, 1900
sources_cited_by_source: ICC 1951a/b Docket 32, 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 505, Findings of Fact and Opinion; Additional Findings of Fact 1955-12-13 (endnotes 28-29)
federal_account_contrast: Royce and Kappler show a cession. The ICC itself found it unconscionable and paid $2/acre, and nearby land was selling at up to $11/acre.
map_implication: For the 1900 KCA cession polygon: claimed $16,268,664; award $2,067,166 net (gross $4,067,166 less $2,000,000 offset); 2,033,583 acres; valued at $2.00/acre; no land returned.
notes: The source says the government appeal went to the 'Court of Federal Claims' (then the Court of Claims). The 1955 date sits in endnote 28's citation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Indian Claims Commission Act 1946, Section 22
summary: Section 22 makes payment a full discharge of all claims and bars any further claim. PSL says the government could appeal awards (and did) while the tribes' reservation of appeal rights was automatically barred, which it calls discriminatory.
verbatim_quote: payment of any claim, after a determination under the Act, shall be a full discharge of the United States of all claims and demands touching any of the matters involved
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Act Sec. 22 (endnote 35, text missing in chunk); TREC rec. endnote 8
federal_account_contrast: The federal framing is that ICC payment extinguishes title. PSL treats it as payment-as-extinguishment without consent.
map_implication: For every KCA polygon resolved through the ICC, label 'extinguished by ICC payment (Sec. 22), not by land return'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: NW Texas, W Kansas, SE Colorado, (Oklahoma panhandle area)
instrument: ICC Dockets 257 and 259-A; Treaty of Little Arkansas with Kiowa and Comanche 1865-10-18
instrument_cite: ICC Docket 257, 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101 (1971-08-09); Docket 259-A; RIT 343, 14 Stat. 717
summary: The ICC granted summary judgment that the tribes held 'recognized title' under the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty to about 39,680,000 acres (Royce areas 510 and 511, map 57) in NW Texas, W Kansas and SE Colorado. After a commissioner's dissent and a Court of Claims referral back, the final judgment awarded $35,060,000, fully approved 1974-04-17. PSL calls it the largest ICC award ever.
verbatim_quote: This tract of land contained approximately 39,680,000 acres located in the northwestern part of the present state of Texas, the western portion of Kansas, the southeastern corner of Colorado
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Docket 257, 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 101, 123-131 (endnote 5); RIT 343, 14 Stat. 717 (endnote 4); endnotes 37-42 missing from chunk
federal_account_contrast: Royce 510/511 appear as ceded by the 1867 treaty. The ICC found recognized title, so money, not land, closed the claim.
map_implication: Royce 510 and 511: tag 'recognized title (ICC Dockets 257/259-A); taken via 1867 treaty; compensated $35,060,000 in 1974 with no land returned'. Treat the SE Colorado portion as KCA treaty-recognized land.
notes: The 'largest ever ICC award' claim needs checking. The government's res judicata argument was rejected. PSL calls the 1867 commission a 'war and relocation commission'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC Dockets 32, 257, 259-A
summary: PSL argues the awards were negligible: no land returned, no 5% compound interest (which PSL says would make $35M worth over $12 billion), no accounting for buffalo loss (put at $48 billion), and no trespass damages under the 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act's $1,000 fine. It says the tribes got $1.00 per acre while nearby land sold for $11.00.
verbatim_quote: the settlement was negligible when juxtaposed against the value of other land in the area being sold for $11.00 per acre while the tribes received $1.00 an acre
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 43-44 (missing from chunk); 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act
federal_account_contrast: This is a critique of ICC valuation methods.
map_implication: In ICC tooltips, show the per-acre award next to contemporary market value where it is known.
notes: Internal inconsistencies: $1.00/acre here vs $2.00/acre for Docket 32 (p.72); buffalo value $48B (p.74) vs $46B (p.92 endnote 11). $35,060,000 / 39,680,000 acres is about $0.88/acre. The $12B interest figure is not shown with any working.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of Fort Atkinson with Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, 1853-07-27
summary: The Fort Atkinson treaty allowed US forts and protected emigrant trails in exchange for $18,000 per year to the signing tribes. Plains Apache headmen Poor Wolf, Poor Bear, Prairie Wolf and Cigar signed.
verbatim_quote: the sum of eighteen thousand dollars per annum
sources_cited_by_source: Avalon Project text of Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, July 27, 1853 (endnote 9)
federal_account_contrast: Names Plains Apache signers who are often merged with the Kiowa.
map_implication: List the Plains Apache signers on the 1853 Fort Atkinson treaty record.
notes: The text says 'By 1850 and 1855' and 'ratified on July 27, 1853'; July 27, 1853 is the signing date. Category ANNUITY_THEFT is not established for this treaty in the chunk; it is used only for the annuity promise. Reviewer may prefer OTHER.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Rocky Mountains; Front Range; SE Colorado; Arkansas Valley
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge 1867 (Apache adhesion)
summary: PSL says the Kiowa Apache have historical ties to the Rocky Mountains, the Front Range and SE Colorado, and share in the Medicine Lodge annuities and in the acknowledgment of territorial claims with the Kiowa and Comanche. It warns that their history risks being erased by merging it into other nations' histories.
verbatim_quote: In terms of the territorial claims in Colorado, the Kiowa Apache have historical ties to the Rocky Mountains, the Front Range, and the southeastern part of the state.
sources_cited_by_source: No specific cite for this sentence
federal_account_contrast: Royce and Kappler usually fold the Apache into the KCA or Cheyenne-Arapaho entries.
map_implication: Show the Apache Tribe of Oklahoma as a distinct nation linked to SE Colorado, Front Range and Arkansas Valley areas, not only as part of 'Kiowa'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: First Battle of Adobe Walls, northern Texas panhandle
summary: Kit Carson's troops attacked a Kiowa and Comanche village. The Kiowa Apache suffered heavy losses defending themselves. PSL says the aim was to force the tribes to terms and onto a reservation. Afterward the Kiowa Apache broke with the Kiowa and allied with the Cheyenne and Arapaho.
verbatim_quote: Kit Carson's brutal attack was an attempt to diminish the fighting capacity of the Kiowa and Comanche, forcing them to come to terms with the United States
sources_cited_by_source: Pafford 2017, Kit Carson's Last Fight, unpublished dissertation, 184 (endnote 11)
federal_account_contrast: Federal histories call it a battle. PSL frames it as coercion leading up to the 1865 and 1867 treaties.
map_implication: Add Adobe Walls 1864 as violence preceding the Little Arkansas (1865) and Medicine Lodge (1867) KCA treaties.
notes: The source calls it a battle and an 'attack', not a massacre; the category is the closest fit. Coordinates not given in the source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas with Cheyenne, Arapaho and Apache 1865
summary: Apache chiefs Iron Shirt, Poor Bear, Old Fool Man, The Crow, The Wolf Sleeve and The Chief signed. The treaty dissolved the Apache confederation with the Kiowa-Comanche and joined them 'on an equal footing' with the Cheyenne-Arapaho. It promised Sand Creek reparations, 320-acre grants to band leaders and 160-acre grants to widows and orphans. PSL says it was never ratified, that $39,050 appropriated in 1866 was not delivered as promised, and that part was returned to the Treasury as 'surplus'.
verbatim_quote: the Interior Department gave some of the money to the tribes and, according to a modern legal assessment, 'returned the rest' to the Treasury as 'surplus.'
sources_cited_by_source: Colorado Encyclopedia, 'Little Arkansas Treaty' (endnotes 14-15, 18); treaty text (endnotes 16-17)
federal_account_contrast: Adds the Apache's distinct status, and the diversion of the reparation funds, to the treaty record.
map_implication: Record the 1865 Apache-Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty with its Sand Creek reparation lands as promised land that was never delivered, and the $39,050 diversion.
notes: CONTESTED: PSL says the Little Arkansas Treaty was 'never ratified'. The Cheyenne-Arapaho(-Apache) Little Arkansas treaty is generally recorded as ratified with Senate amendments (14 Stat. 703) that removed the reservation; the KC one is cited here as RIT 343, 14 Stat. 717. Check whether PSL means the reservation was never established. Page 86 wrongly says the 'Medicine Lodge Treaty of 1866' allocated the $39,050. Verification: verify-plains s.5 OVERRIDES the UNRATIFIED tag (p. 84 'never ratified' is wrong for 14 Stat. 703).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Arkansas Valley between SE Colorado and Kansas
instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas 1865
summary: PSL infers that from 1865 to 1867 the Kiowa Apache lived with the Cheyenne and Arapaho in the Arkansas Valley between SE Colorado and Kansas, where the treaty gave them hunting rights.
verbatim_quote: It thus can be inferred that the Kiowa Apache were with the Cheyenne and Arapaho in the Arkansas Valley between southeastern Colorado and Kansas
federal_account_contrast: Places the Apache in Colorado in the treaty era.
map_implication: Optional: Kiowa Apache presence/hunting layer in the Arkansas Valley, 1865-67, marked as inferred.
notes: The source says this is an inference.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge, Apache adhesion 1867
summary: Seven languages were spoken at the council. The Plains Apache had no proficient interpreter of their own; their speeches went through Arapaho by an Apache-speaking member of Little Raven's band. PSL questions how much the Apache headmen understood. Sherman ordered 50,000 rations for the council.
verbatim_quote: said Apache speeches were translated into Arapaho by an Apache-speaking member of Little Raven's tribe
sources_cited_by_source: Jones 1966, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge, 45, 104-108 (endnotes 22, 25-27)
federal_account_contrast: Kappler shows the Apache signing. PSL questions whether they gave informed consent.
map_implication: Flag the Apache adhesion to Medicine Lodge: 'no Apache-language interpreter; double translation via Arapaho'.
notes: The 50,000 rations is evidence of using rations as an inducement only by inference; PSL does not claim starvation duress. PSL gives the Apache signing date as 1867-10-25; the Apache adhesion is usually dated 1867-10-21 (15 Stat. 589). Needs checking.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Between Fort Cobb and Fort Sill, Indian Territory
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge 1867
summary: PSL says the treaty marked the 'unwilling loss, under duress' of the Apache nomadic life. The Apache settled between Fort Cobb and Fort Sill under Head Chief Pacer, and 'the tribes never received any of the annuities promised.' The population was about 325 by 1891.
verbatim_quote: the treaty marked the unwilling loss, under duress, of their traditional nomadic lifeways
sources_cited_by_source: McAllister & Anderson, Handbook of Texas (endnote 28) for the population
federal_account_contrast: Kappler implies the annuities were delivered under the treaty; PSL says none were received.
map_implication: Tag the Apache adhesion to Medicine Lodge as duress plus non-payment of annuities (single-source claim).
notes: The 'never received any' annuity claim is sweeping and has no cite; it needs verification.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome Agreement 1892
summary: The Jerome Commission offered $2 million for about 2.5 million acres of 'surplus' land and 160 acres per person. The agent noted that the $210,000 biannual grass-lease payments from Texas cattlemen (1886) exceeded the 5% interest on $2 million. PSL says 160 acres could not sustain farming or ranching on the dry land.
verbatim_quote: offered $2 million for approximately 2.5 million acres of surplus land
sources_cited_by_source: Kracht, 'Kiowa-Comanche-Apache Opening', Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (endnote 29)
federal_account_contrast: Shows the tribes were paid less than the land's lease income.
map_implication: Record the 1892 price of under $1/acre ($2M for about 2.5M acres) against $210K per 6 months in grass leases.
notes: The agent is named 'James F. Ranflett' (probably Randlett). 2.5M acres here vs 2,033,583 acres ceded in ICC Docket 32: the ICC figure is the ceded area; the reason for the gap is not explained.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: PSL TREC recommendations for KCA
summary: There are eleven recommendations to Colorado: (1) compensation for pain and suffering from illegal trespass; (2) compensation for water rights; (3) full compensation for the state's role in forced removal; (4) restoring unrestricted cultural use, hunting, fishing and plant gathering on all public lands; (5) payment for railway land, and return of abandoned rail lands; (6) GOCO funding access and sacred-site protection; (7) no property tax on enrolled members living in Colorado; (8) support for reopening the ICC settlement on appeal; (9) tuition waivers plus room and board; (10) a real-estate transaction fee for a permanent fund; (11) buffalo restoration.
verbatim_quote: It is recommended that the State of Colorado support the Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache Tribes of Oklahoma Nation in its efforts to have the Indian Claims Commission settlement opened for appeal.
federal_account_contrast: These are reparative proposals that go beyond the federal settlement.
map_implication: Optional 'TREC recommendations' panel on the KCA nation page.
notes: These are policy recommendations, not historical claims.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act 1834
summary: Recommendation endnote 1 says the KCA lands were within the 1834 Act's Indian Country, so settlers were illegal intruders, and no agency corrected the occupation even when it knew it was illegal.
verbatim_quote: This violation was not corrected by any agency even when they knew the occupation was illegal.
federal_account_contrast: Treats settlement before cession as illegal trespass rather than a frontier.
map_implication: Consider a 'pre-cession illegal settlement' layer for SE Colorado KCA lands.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Recommendation endnote 3 calls the forced removal an act of genocide and says Territorial Governor John Evans failed in his duties as Superintendent of Indian Affairs. It argues the state should be held liable and calls for a full investigation.
verbatim_quote: The forced removal was an act of genocide. Territorial Governor Evans failed in his duties as the Superintendent of Indian Affairs, and the state should be held liable for his actions.
federal_account_contrast: Assigns responsibility to the territorial government, not only the federal one.
map_implication: Link Governor Evans's role to KCA removal from Colorado in the violations catalog.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Pacific Railroad Acts; Colorado School Fund grants
summary: Recommendation endnotes 5 and 9 say Colorado's economy grew from railroad land grants that gave KCA nothing, and that the School Fund received 4 million acres of Colorado land from which KCA students have not benefited.
verbatim_quote: The School Fund received 4 million acres of land in Colorado to support schools
federal_account_contrast: Ties state trust land and railroad grants to Native land.
map_implication: Consider overlaying Colorado state school trust lands and railroad grant lands on KCA treaty areas.
notes: The 4 million acres figure needs checking against Colorado State Land Board records.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Recommendation endnote 6 says Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO) rules bar tribal nations from its funds, and that per the US Forest Service there are over 200 unprotected sacred sites.
verbatim_quote: According to the US Forest Service there are over 200 sacred sites that are not currently protected.
notes: The 200-site figure has no specific source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: PSL says the KCA homeland held the southern buffalo herd of about five million animals, the tribes' primary food source, worth about $46 billion today. It recommends buffalo restoration.
verbatim_quote: There were approximately five million buffalo in the southern herd. The value at today's price is calculated to be roughly 46,000,000,000 dollars.
sources_cited_by_source: None given (p.74 endnote 43 missing from chunk)
map_implication: Possibly note buffalo extermination as a resource taking enabling KCA cessions.
notes: This conflicts with the $48 billion figure on p.74.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Indian Citizenship Act 1924
summary: Recommendation endnote 7 argues KCA members living in Colorado have a reserved right not to pay state property tax because they still live in their homelands, and cites a 'protectorate clause' of the 1924 Citizenship Act.
verbatim_quote: have a reserved right not to pay state property taxes as they are still living within their homelands
notes: This is a legal theory that needs verification; the 1924 Act has no clause commonly known as a 'protectorate clause'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Indian Reorganization Act 1934; Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act 1936
summary: Kiowa leaders opposed the IRA after meeting Collier on 1934-03-20, but Congress extended it to Oklahoma as the OIWA in 1936, which ended allotment. In the 1950s the Kiowa avoided termination by refusing to cooperate.
verbatim_quote: The Kiowa eventually avoided termination by refusing to cooperate with the federal government.
notes: Context only. Also on pp.69-70: the Native American Church was incorporated in 1918 and the Kiowa Six enrolled at OU in 1928 (cultural context, no land implication).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
nations: Eastern Shoshone (Washakie's Band); Comanche; Ute; Navajo
place: Northwest Colorado: Browns Park / Brown's Hole on the Green River; Yampa River; North Park; Front Range north of present Rocky Mountain National Park
summary: The report assembles scholarly and explorer evidence that Shoshone occupied northern Colorado from about AD 1300, and that before 1800 Shoshone country included all land north of the Yampa River, North Park, and the mountains to the Front Range north of Rocky Mountain NP. Lander (1859) put the Eastern Shoshone southern range at Brown's Hole.
verbatim_quote: Shoshone country included all the land north of the Yampa River, North Park, and the mountains to the Front Range north of what is now Rocky Mountain National Park.
sources_cited_by_source: Peter Faris article (Shoshone medicine wheel, Browns Park), quoting Marcia Tate, Donald Grayson, Sydney Lamb, J. Donald Hughes (endnotes 3-8); William T. Hamilton memoir (n.9-10); F.W. Lander 1859 summary (n.12); Wyoming PBS video 'Who Are the Eastern Shoshone?' 2017 (n.1-2)
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler framing of Colorado centers Ute, Cheyenne and Arapaho; Shoshone presence in NW and north-central Colorado is largely invisible on cession maps.
map_implication: Add an Eastern Shoshone aboriginal-use layer in Colorado: north of the Yampa River, North Park, Front Range north of RMNP, Browns Park/Green River. Note overlap with Ute use.
notes: Hughes quote is secondary (via Faris). Browns Park area also Ute; area was a multi-tribe trade and wintering ground per Hamilton.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River (lat 43 deg 30 min N); South Pass; headwaters of North Platte; Bear River near mouth of Smith's Fork; Brown's Hole on Green River
summary: Explorer F.W. Lander's 1859 description of Eastern Shoshone range gives mappable limits: north to Wind River waters (lat 43 30), east from South Pass to North Platte headwaters, west to Bear River near Smith's Fork, south to Brown's Hole.
verbatim_quote: range from the waters of Wind river [sic] or latitude 43 30' on the north and from the South Pass to the headwaters of the North Platte on the east, and to Bear river [sic] near the mouth of Smith's Fork on the west.
federal_account_contrast: A federal-agent-era territorial description predating any Shoshone treaty; useful baseline for pre-treaty Shoshone territory.
map_implication: Use as a second boundary sketch for pre-1863 Eastern Shoshone territory alongside 1863 Art. 4; south limit reaches into Colorado (Browns Park, approx 40.8N 108.9W).
notes: Report paraphrases Lander with partial quotation; check original Lander report (likely in Commissioner of Indian Affairs annual report 1859-60).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter | Twain's Geography 'The Horse Creek Treaty of 1851' https://twainsgeography.com/chapter/horse-creek-treaty-1851; Wikipedia 'Washakie' (via search)
nations: Eastern Shoshone (Washakie's Band); Sioux; Cheyenne; Arapaho; Crow
place: Horse Creek treaty grounds near Fort Laramie (approx 41.9N 104.0W, near Morrill NE; coordinates not from source)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), Sept 17, 1851
instrument_cite: 11 Stat. 749; Kappler II p. 594 (cite not given in source chunk)
summary: About 80 Shoshone men with families, led by Washakie and accompanied by Jim Bridger, came to the 1851 council though not invited. The Superintendent ruled them outside his instructions, so they were not parties to the treaty; they received presents and went home.
verbatim_quote: These Indians (Shoshone) were not considered by the Superintendent [of Indian Affairs] as embraced by his instructions, and were consequently not parties to the treaty negotiated with the other tribes.
