notes: Report also cites Cheyenne attack en route killing two Shoshone, resolved by 'covering the bodies' ceremony. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-ARA-006 (PSL pp. 170), WEB-DUR-048.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Shoshone territory crossed by emigrant trails (Oregon/California/Mormon trails, South Pass, Fort Bridger)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Arts. 2 and 5
summary: Because the Shoshone were not party to the 1851 treaty, the report argues Article 2 (roads and military posts), Article 5 (boundaries) and free-passage provisions never applied to them, so trails and rights-of-way through Shoshone land had no treaty basis until 1863.
verbatim_quote: the Treaty of 1851 was not made with the Eastern Shoshone; thus they had neither agreed to nor were they bound to Article 2, which allowed the federal government to create roads and military posts
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats 1851 right-of-way provisions as covering the overland routes generally.
map_implication: For 1851-1863 trail corridors through Shoshone country (South Pass to Fort Bridger), mark as used without any treaty consent.
notes: Legal argument by report author; well-grounded in the exclusion fact.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
summary: The report asserts that land in present-day Colorado still belongs to the Shoshone, and (p.124) that the 1868 treaty removed Colorado from the Shoshone lands described in 1863.
verbatim_quote: Furthermore, land in present-day Colorado still belongs to the Shoshone.
sources_cited_by_source: None at this point; later reliance on Royce 520 overlay by Dr. Joseph Robertson
federal_account_contrast: Royce maps show Shoshone 1868 cession as complete extinguishment; report claims a residual Shoshone title in Colorado.
map_implication: Do not color the Colorado part of 1863 Shoshone country as plainly ceded; add note that Eastern Shoshone (per PSL) assert unextinguished title there.
notes: Strong legal claim without citation in this chunk. Compare ICC outcomes for Shoshone (Docket 63 and others) before mapping as never ceded. Note 1868 Art. II general relinquishment clause. Verification: verify-ute-shoshone s.7: the 1868 Fort Bridger treaty Art. 2 relinquished other territory (Royce 520); the claim is the Shoshone/TREC position.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Fort Bridger; Great Salt Lake Valley; Bridger Pass; Cheyenne Pass; Sevier River/Lake
instrument: Stansbury Expedition 1849-50; Pacific Railroad Surveys under Army Appropriation Act of March 1853; House Resolution of Feb 14, 1855
instrument_cite: Stansbury, Exploration and Survey of the Valley of the Great Salt Lake (Senate print 1852); Reports of Explorations and Surveys (12 vols., 1854-61), Vol. II (Beckwith/Gunnison, 1855)
summary: Federal survey expeditions mapped routes, including the future railroad route, through Shoshone and Ute lands without permission or treaty, over ten years before 1863. Congress printed 10,000 copies of the survey reports, which the report says spurred settler and miner rushes.
verbatim_quote: The path for the railroad was determined through Shoshone and other tribal lands without permission or a treaty, and over ten years before the Treaty of 1863.
sources_cited_by_source: Stansbury 1852 report (n.24-27); Reports of Explorations and Surveys Vol. II (n.31-32, 34); House resolution Feb 14 1855 (n.33)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats surveys as neutral exploration, not as use of Indian land.
map_implication: Add a pre-treaty intrusion layer: Stansbury route and Gunnison/Beckwith 38th-39th parallel route; northern route via Cheyenne Pass and Bridger Pass through Shoshone land.
notes: Report calls this 'illegal mapping'; that is the author's legal characterization. Report text says 'Treaty of 1968' (p.102), a typo for 1868. Gunnison killed by Pahvant Ute Oct 26 1853 (report calls it a massacre).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Transcontinental telegraph across Shoshone territory; joined at Fort Bridger Oct 17, 1861 (per source timeline)
instrument: Pacific Telegraph Act of June 16, 1860
summary: The transcontinental telegraph was built across Shoshone territory July-October 1861 under the Pacific Telegraph Act, which granted a quarter-section of 'public land' per 15 miles of line, with no Shoshone consent or treaty. The 1863 treaty later approved it retroactively.
verbatim_quote: there was no Treaty signed by the Eastern Shoshone for the construction of this transcontinental telegraph line across their land.
sources_cited_by_source: Timeline sources n.35-39; Kenneth Alford 2012 'Indian Relations in Utah during the Civil War' quoting Supt. Dyman S. Wood 1861 (n.40)
federal_account_contrast: Statute treats the line's land as 'public land' though title had not been extinguished.
map_implication: Mark 1861 telegraph corridor through Shoshone land as built pre-consent; link to 1863 Fort Bridger Art. 3 as retroactive approval.
notes: Report gives approval date June 15 and signing June 16, 1860.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Appropriation of July 5, 1862 ($20,000) for Shoshone treaty; commission instructions
instrument_cite: Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335 (1945) (quoted)
summary: Per the Supreme Court's account, the 1862 treaty commission was told the treaty should not extinguish Indian title but only secure safe travel routes and fix boundaries, set as far as practicable from the routes.
verbatim_quote: it was not expected that the proposed treaty would extinguish Indian title to the lands, but only secure freedom from molestation for the routes of travel
federal_account_contrast: Supports reading the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty as a right-of-way/peace treaty, not a land cession; Royce maps sometimes frame 1863 areas as cessions.
map_implication: Classify 1863 Fort Bridger (Eastern Shoshone) as recognition of territory plus right-of-way, not a cession; title remained Shoshone until 1868.
notes: Report says case argued Nov 1944, decided Dec 1945. The decision is generally dated March 1945 (324 U.S. 335); verify. That case concerned the Northwestern Bands' 1863 Box Elder treaty, and the Court held the treaties did not recognize title.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Pacific Railway Act 1862; Homestead Act 1862; Morrill Land-Grant Act 1862
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 489; 12 Stat. 392; 12 Stat. 503 (cites not in source)
summary: The report ties the 1862 railway, homestead and land-grant acts to Native land, arguing these laws relied on land to be obtained from tribes by treaty, cession or seizure, making the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty necessary to finance western expansion.
verbatim_quote: Thus, the Fort Bridger Treaty of 1863 was necessary to fund the U.S. Government's expansion west and within the territory of the Shoshone Sovereign Nation.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents these as public-land statutes.
map_implication: Possible cross-link to Land-Grab Universities (Morrill) data for parcels in Shoshone territory.
notes: Report says the Pacific Railway Act designated the 32nd parallel as the route; that appears wrong (the 1862 act chartered the central route, roughly 41-42 N). Flag for correction.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Fort Bridger Treaty of July 2, 1863
summary: The report argues Doty, Lincoln, Connor and Brigham Young worked to take Shoshone land through corruption, massacre and a forced 1863 treaty signing. Shoshone historian Darren Parry says they conspired to force the 1863 signing and that Bear River and Sand Creek pushed Washakie toward treaties.
verbatim_quote: Doty, Lincoln, Young and Connor were all instrumental and I feel conspired together to force the 1863 signing of the treaty at Fort Bridger with all of the Shoshone bands.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows a peace treaty concluded five months after the Bear River Massacre, with no note of coercion.
map_implication: Flag 1863 Fort Bridger treaty: signed about five months after the Bear River Massacre; Native-authored account of coerced signing.
notes: Report itself hedges ('may demonstrate'). Parry is Northwestern Band, an Indigenous account. Report's claim 'Doty obviously wanted the Shoshone moved to Minnesota in 1841' is unsupported and likely wrong (Doty 1841 treaty concerned Dakota/Sioux land); exclude from map.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Bear River / Cache Valley; Washakie, Utah
summary: The report says Brigham Young took control of Shoshone land through the massacre, not a treaty, and over 100 Mormon families moved in. Survivors who settled at Washakie, Utah were later forced off when the LDS Church sold the land.
verbatim_quote: Brigham Young took control of Shoshone land, not with a treaty but through a massacre, and over 100 Mormon families moved into the area.
federal_account_contrast: No treaty cession preceded settlement of Cache Valley / Bear River valley.
map_implication: Mark Cache Valley ('House of the Great Spirit') and Bear River valley settlement as taken before treaty; note Washakie, Utah eviction.
notes: Cache Valley Mormon settlement from 1857-58 preceded any treaty. Killing of 'Chief Pagunapin Smithfield' by settlers (p.105) needs verification of name.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Salt Lake City; Union Pacific grade from Wyoming border to Great Salt Lake
instrument: Union Pacific grading contract, Brigham Young (School of Prophets) and Samuel Reed
summary: About two months before the 1868 treaty, Brigham Young contracted with Union Pacific for about $2,125,000 to build railroad grade from near the Wyoming border to the Great Salt Lake, with his sons and attorney as subcontractors.
verbatim_quote: On May 21, 1868 (nearly two months before the Eastern Shoshone signed the 1868 Treaty) a contract was signed by Brigham Young
federal_account_contrast: Railroad construction is usually framed as authorized by the 1863 and 1868 treaties.
map_implication: Note on UP corridor: commercial contracts let before 1868 treaty signing.
notes: Article 3 of the 1863 treaty did consent to a railway, so 'before treaty' applies to 1868 only.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger with Eastern Shoshone, July 2, 1863
instrument_cite: 18 Stat. 685; Kappler II p. 848 (cite not given in source chunk)
summary: Art. 4 recognizes Shoshone country as described by the nation: north, mountains north of the Snake River valley; east, Wind River Mountains, Peenahpah River, North Fork of the Platte (Koo-chin-agah), and North Park (Buffalo House); south, Yampa River and Uinta Mountains; west undefined, but present bands claimed to Salt Lake. This includes Colorado land.
verbatim_quote: on the east, by the Wind River mountains, Peenahpah river, the north fork of Platte or Koo-chin-agah, and the north Park or Buffalo House; and on the south, by Yampah river and the Uintah mountains.
federal_account_contrast: Royce maps this as area 520; the report argues the boundaries (and Doty's map) understate Shoshone land in Colorado.
map_implication: Draw 1863 Shoshone country as recognized territory (not cession): N = mountains north of Snake River valley; E = Wind River Mts, Peenahpah (Sweetwater? verify), North Platte, North Park CO; S = Yampa River and Uinta Mts; W = Great Salt Lake (claimed). Include North Park and land north of Yampa in Colorado.
notes: Identification of 'Peenahpah river' uncertain. Report states Art. 4 and Doty's map 'have been proven to be inaccurate' without detail.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Shoshone country (routes, telegraph, stage lines, railway corridor)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1863, Arts. 2-3
summary: Articles 2-3 opened routes, military posts, settlements, ferries, and retroactively accepted telegraph and stage lines already built, plus a future railway, through 'any portion of the country claimed by them'. The report reads this as a cover for prior unconsented use.
verbatim_quote: The telegraph and overland stage lines having been established and operated through a part of the Shoshonee country, it is expressly agreed that the same may be continued
federal_account_contrast: Treaty language itself admits the lines preceded consent.
map_implication: Annotate 1863 treaty: Art. 3 retroactive consent for telegraph and stage lines; no compensation for prior use.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1863, Arts. 5-6
summary: The treaty promised $10,000 a year for 20 years in goods as compensation for lost game and $6,000 in presents. The report says Congress often failed to appropriate and deliveries were delayed, causing hardship 1863-1868, and it found no evidence 1863 annuities continued after 1868 or that presents were itemized.
verbatim_quote: Congress often failed to appropriate the money for the Indian supplies and difficulties with transportation delayed distribution.
sources_cited_by_source: None specific; author suggests National Archives search
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows treaty obligations, not shortfalls.
map_implication: Flag 1863 annuities as possibly unpaid or partly paid; needs archival check.
notes: Author notes compensation covers loss of game only, not minerals, timber or other resources.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1863, Art. 7 (Senate amendment re Mexican title)
summary: The treaty text as reproduced includes Article 7, limiting Shoshone title to what existed under Mexican law, under the heading 'Amendment ending Mexican agreements'. This appears to be a Senate-added article.
verbatim_quote: Nothing herein contained shall be construed or taken to admit any other or greater title or interest in the lands embraced within the territories described in said Treaty
federal_account_contrast: Senate amendment narrowed recognized title after signing.
map_implication: Check whether Eastern Shoshone assented to the Art. 7 amendment and when; if not, flag as Senate-amended without consent.
notes: The source does not discuss consent to the amendment. My understanding (not from source) is the Senate added it in 1864 and the treaty was proclaimed 1875 after assent; verify in Kappler.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1863, Art. 4
summary: Three maps of 1863 Shoshone country disagree: Doty's map presented to the Senate (made 1859, likely from War Department mapping of 1850), O. Stewart's 1957 map, and Dr. Joseph Robertson's 2023 Royce 520 overlay. Later maps show more Colorado land than Doty's.
verbatim_quote: Some identified more land in Colorado than that identified by Doty's map.
sources_cited_by_source: Doty map 1859 (Univ. of Utah Marriott Library, ark:/87278/s63z134h, n.75); O. Stewart 1957 map (Marriott Library id 358831, n.76); Robertson 2023 overlay
federal_account_contrast: Royce 520 follows one reading; the atlas likely inherits a polygon smaller than the treaty text supports in Colorado.
map_implication: Compare Royce 520 polygon to treaty text (Yampa River south line, North Park east line) and to Stewart 1957; consider showing a range or uncertainty band in Colorado.
notes: Map images not in text chunk; obtain from Marriott Library links.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Crowheart Butte, Wind River Valley, Wyoming (approx 43.27N 109.20W, not from source)
instrument: Fort Laramie 1851 vs Fort Bridger 1863
summary: The 1851 treaty assigned the Wind River hunting grounds to the Crow and the 1863 treaty to the Shoshone and Bannock. The conflict was settled by a battle and a duel between Washakie and Crow chief Big Robber; Crowheart Butte is now sacred and closed to non-Native climbers.
verbatim_quote: The 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty gave the land to the Crow Indians. Twelve years later, the 1863 Fort Bridger Treaty granted the land to the Shoshone and Bannocks.
sources_cited_by_source: John Elliott, Clio website (n.77-79); oral memory of duel location
federal_account_contrast: Federal treaties assigned the same land to two nations without reconciling them.
map_implication: Flag overlap of 1851 Crow area and 1863 Shoshone country in the Wind River basin; add Crowheart Butte as sacred site.
notes: Duel details are tradition; exact location undocumented per source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Instructions of Commissioner William P. Dole to Supt. O.H. Irish, March 1865
summary: Commissioner Dole told Supt. Irish that because the government had never accepted Indian title to any land in Utah, new treaties should have Indians relinquish 'the right of occupancy' and remove to reservations.
verbatim_quote: [relinquished] the right of occupancy
federal_account_contrast: Shows federal policy of denying Indian title in Utah, relevant to the 1863 treaties.
map_implication: Note in Utah treaty records: federal policy refused to recognize title, framing cessions as occupancy relinquishment.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Fort Bridger, Utah Territory; Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868 (ratified Feb 16, 1869; proclaimed Feb 24, 1869)
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 673; Kappler II p. 1020 (cite not given in source chunk)
summary: Art. II set apart the Shoshone reservation 'for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation' of the Shoshone, with a mappable boundary, and the Shoshone relinquished all other territory. Bannock reservation to be in Port Neuf and Kansas Prairie country.
verbatim_quote: commencing at the mouth of Owl creek and running due south to the crest of the divide between the Sweetwater and Papo Agie rivers; thence along the crest of said divide and summit of Wind River mountains
federal_account_contrast: Federal maps show the reservation; report stresses it was promised as absolute and undisturbed but cut in 1874 and 1897.
map_implication: Draw 1868 Shoshone reservation: mouth of Owl Creek, due south to Sweetwater/Popo Agie divide, along divide and Wind River Mts summit to longitude of North Fork Wind River, due north to its mouth, up channel 20 miles, straight line to Owl Creek headwaters, down Owl Creek to start. Label 'promised absolute and undisturbed'.
notes: Report heading calls it a 'Medicine Lodge Treaties' item, which is loose; it is a Peace Commission treaty. Report says 1868 Art. IV off-reservation hunting rights are still being sought and violated by Wyoming. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-SHO-B-011 (PSL pp. 135;137).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Shoshone 1863 country outside Wind River reservation, incl. Colorado
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1868
summary: The report says over 40 million acres were taken from the Eastern Shoshone in 1868 without adequate compensation, and that no compensation was ever provided for telegraph, stations, railroads and roads built earlier. It also says the 1868 treaty removed Colorado from Shoshone lands.
verbatim_quote: the over 40 million acres of ground taken from the Eastern Shoshone was not adequately compensated for in the 1868 Treaty.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account treats 1868 as a lawful cession for treaty consideration.
map_implication: Flag 1868 Shoshone cession (outside reservation) as inadequately compensated; note unpaid pre-treaty rights-of-way.
notes: Author's valuation (40M acres x $0.25 = $10M; today $200M at $5/acre) is rough and arithmetic for 'today' is not inflation-based. Do not reproduce figures without check.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1868, Arts. III, V, VII, IX, X, XII
instrument_cite: Court of Claims No. H-129 (decided Dec 2, 1938)
summary: Author finds many promised buildings, personnel, farming prizes and goods not delivered or delayed; school funds paid to churches and Carlisle; one agent removed for taking bribes to assign better lands to non-Indians in 1910 allotment period.
verbatim_quote: At least one agent on the Wind River Reservation was removed for taking bribes to assign better lands to non-Indians during the allotment sale and distribution period in 1910.
sources_cited_by_source: Court of Claims H-129 (1938); otherwise author observation
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows treaty promises; not their nonperformance.
map_implication: Add implementation-failure notes to 1868 treaty record; flag 1910 agent bribery (needs name and source).
notes: Mostly author impressions ('I feel'). Winnemucca quote (p.120-121) is from Life Among the Piutes (1883, report says 1863) and concerns Western Shoshone at Battle Mountain, NV, not Eastern Shoshone.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Treaty of Fort Bridger 1868, Art. XI
summary: Article XI requires any future cession of the reservation to be signed by a majority of adult male Indians occupying or interested in it. The author notes neither 1863 nor 1868 treaty itself had that requirement, and the Northern Arapaho were later included in the 1870s.
verbatim_quote: No treaty for the cession of any portion of the reservations herein described which may be held in common shall be of any force or validity as against the said Indians, unless executed and signed by at least a majority
federal_account_contrast: Provides test for later cessions (1872 Brunot, 1896/1897, 1904/1905 acts).
map_implication: Check signature counts on Brunot 1872 and 1896 agreements against Art. XI majority rule; Arapaho placement without Shoshone treaty consent is a known grievance.
notes: 1863 treaty had about 11 signers by mark; 1868 had 8 Shoshone and 6 Bannock signers.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Southern Wind River Reservation, Popo Agie / Little Popo Agie / Sweetwater mining area (Lander region), Wyoming
instrument: Brunot Cession Agreement Sept 26, 1872; Act of Dec 15, 1874
instrument_cite: 18 Stat. 291 (cite not in source); ICC Docket No. 63 (Aug 20, 1954)
summary: The agreement ceded nearly a third of the 1868 reservation after miners and settlers had already moved in. The ICC found the land worth $0.80/acre ($560,513.60) and the $27,500 paid unconscionable.
verbatim_quote: the consideration of $27,500 paid by the defendant to petitioner for the Brunot lands worth $560,513.60 constituted an unconscionable consideration
sources_cited_by_source: Jackson Hole Historical Society & Museum (n.89); Act text (n.90); ICC Docket 63 decision (n.91)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows a ratified cession for consideration; ICC later found it unconscionable but paid money, not land.
map_implication: Draw Brunot cession: south of a line from eastern boundary due east of Little Popo Agie mouth, west to that mouth, up Popo Agie to North Fork, up North Fork to canyon mouth, then west to reservation boundary. Label 'intrusion preceded cession; ICC: unconscionable price'.
notes: Treaty preamble admits mines discovered and citizens made improvements within the reservation before and after 1868, i.e., US did not keep the 'no persons shall pass over, settle upon' promise. Agreement claims majority of adult males consented. Includes $500/yr salary to Washakie. Verification: verify-ute-shoshone s.9: Docket 63 figures consistent ($0.80 x 700,642 acres) but found only in PSL.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: General Allotment (Dawes) Act 1887
summary: Allotment carved the reservation into individual parcels and opened unassigned land to non-Native homesteaders; 245,058 acres were allotted 1907-1919. Washakie's reaction to forced farming: 'God damn a potato!'
verbatim_quote: God damn a potato!
sources_cited_by_source: Paul Olson, The Struggle for the Land (n.92); n.93-94
map_implication: Note allotment-era losses on the Wind River reservation.
notes: Report says unassigned land was 'sold to the government' under Dawes; Wind River surplus opening was by the 1905 act (not in this chunk). Verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Big Horn Hot Springs (Thermopolis), NE corner of Shoshone Reservation at Owl Creek / Big Horn River
instrument: McLaughlin Agreement of April 21, 1896 (Big Horn Hot Springs cession), ratified as amended by Congress
instrument_cite: 30 Stat. 93 (Act of June 7, 1897; cite not in source, verify)
summary: Shoshone and Arapaho ceded a 10-by-10-mile tract including the Big Horn Hot Springs and its water rights. Congress accepted it only as amended, binding when the tribes agreed to the amendment.
verbatim_quote: Beginning at the northeastern corner of the said reservation, where Owl Creek empties into the Big Horn River; thence south ten miles, following the eastern boundary of the reservation, then due west 10 miles
federal_account_contrast: A Congress-amended agreement; tribal consent to the amendment must be checked.
map_implication: Draw 10x10 mile Hot Springs cession at Owl Creek/Big Horn confluence; flag as congressionally amended pending tribal assent.
notes: Chunk ends mid-agreement (continues p.129).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River (Shoshone) Reservation, Shoshone Agency / Fort Washakie, Wyoming
instrument: Fort Bridger Treaty of July 3, 1868 (exclusive-use guarantee) vs. Indian Bureau placement of Northern Arapaho, 1878
summary: The Indian Bureau settled the Northern Arapaho permanently at the Shoshone Agency in 1878. Shoshone attorney George Tunison argued this was done without Shoshone approval, and that from then on the government treated both tribes as equal beneficiaries, sharing Shoshone cession payments and allotments.
verbatim_quote: without Shoshone approval, the Indian Bureau had allowed the Arapaho to settle permanently at the Shoshone Agency in 1878
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/Royce treat Wind River as a single reservation created by the 1868 treaty; the federal record does not mark that half of it was effectively transferred to another nation in 1878 without a treaty or cession by the Shoshone.
map_implication: Annotate the 1868 Wind River reservation polygon: exclusive Shoshone guarantee breached 1878; one-half interest (1,171,770 acres) taken for Arapaho by administrative action, later paid for (1937-1939), not consented.
notes: CONTRADICTION inside the source: p.132 quotes Stamm that the Arapahos were moved in 1878 'only with the consent of the Shoshones', while p.135 (Tunison/Fowler) says without Shoshone approval, and the Supreme Court later ruled for the Shoshone. Both are quoted without reconciliation. Shoshone oral accounts reportedly describe a temporary invitation by Washakie, not permanent settlement; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Agreement with the Shoshone and Arapahoe Tribes, April 21, 1896 (ratified Act of June 7, 1897)
summary: Per Hank Stamm, the 'most important feature' of the 1896 Hot Springs agreement was that the government made the Arapaho equal partners with the Shoshone in rights to the reservation, a change the Shoshone had not previously accepted. The Shoshone later were compensated in the 1930s for lands 'in essence, given to the Arapahos.'
verbatim_quote: the government made the Arapahos equal partners to the Shoshones in the rights to claim the reservation
sources_cited_by_source: Stamm, Land Cession of 1896 Commentary, Jackson Hole Historical Society (endnote 96); record of negotiations at National Archives
federal_account_contrast: The 1896 agreement appears in federal record as a routine joint cession; it actually functioned as a federal device to convert Arapaho presence into co-ownership.
map_implication: Tag the 1896 instrument as a joint-signatory cession in which the federal government treated Arapaho as co-owners of Shoshone treaty land.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Big Horn Hot Springs (Thermopolis), northeast corner of Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Agreement of April 21, 1896 (McLaughlin), ratified Act of June 7, 1897
summary: The tribes ceded about 100 square miles around the Big Horn Hot Springs for $60,000 ($10,000 per capita/cattle; $50,000 in five annual installments for 'civilization' and rations at the Secretary's discretion). Signed by Washakie, Sharp Nose and 271 others (273). Tribes conceded partly because the Big Horn Basin buffalo grounds had been destroyed by cattle and sheep ranches from 1879.
verbatim_quote: the sum of sixty thousand dollars, to be expended for the benefit of said Indians in the manner hereinafter described
sources_cited_by_source: Agreement text reproduced via Jackson Hole Historical Society; Stamm commentary (endnotes 95-96)
federal_account_contrast: Royce-style cession framing records price and area only; context (destruction of hunting grounds, money controlled by Secretary) is absent.
map_implication: Draw 1896 Thermopolis cession (approx. 10 x 10 miles at NE corner); note $60,000 for ~64,000 acres, mostly spent at federal discretion.
notes: Royce area number for 1896 cession not given in source; determine from Royce schedule (Wyoming).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
instrument: Agreement of April 21, 1896, signature certifications
summary: The interpreter certified that some signature names were duplicates but represented different individuals, and the acting agent (an Army captain) certified the 273 signers were a majority of adult males of both tribes combined. Majority was counted across both tribes, not per tribe. The source reproduces this without comment.
verbatim_quote: I certify that the foregoing names, though in some cases duplicates, in every instance represents different individuals.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents the agreement as valid majority consent; the combined-tribe majority and duplicate-name certification are signals worth scrutiny.
map_implication: Flag 1896 cession: consent measured as combined Shoshone+Arapaho majority; duplicate names certified.
notes: Interpretation (combined majority as a legitimacy issue) is this reader's, not the source's; the source only reproduces the text.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: One mile square around principal hot spring, Thermopolis, Wyoming
instrument: Act of June 7, 1897 ratifying 1896 agreement 'herein amended'
summary: Congress ratified the 1896 agreement as amended, granting one mile square around the main hot spring to the State of Wyoming and declaring the rest public land open only under homestead and town-site laws. The chunk gives no evidence the tribes consented to the amendment.
verbatim_quote: one mile square at and about the principal hot spring thereon contained, is hereby ceded, granted, relinquished, and conveyed unto the State of Wyoming
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows a cession to the US; the land actually passed in part directly to a state via a congressional amendment to a negotiated agreement.
map_implication: Mark the 1 sq mi Hot Springs State Park parcel as transferred to Wyoming by congressional amendment; boundary given in Act (start 1/4 mile E of main spring, 1/2 N, 1 W, 1 S, 1 E, 1/2 N).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

instrument: Wyoming v. EPA (10th Cir. 2017), cert. denied June 25, 2018 (Northern Arapaho Tribe v. Wyoming; Eastern Shoshone Tribe v. Wyoming)

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

summary: A Southern Arapaho delegation in Washington, under pressure, signed an agreement relinquishing title to the Medicine Lodge reservation; no Cheyennes attended. Source says the Medicine Lodge reservation had never been formally ceded.
verbatim_quote: No Cheyennes attended these meetings.
federal_account_contrast: A joint reservation relinquished by one of two nations.
map_implication: Flag 1872 relinquishment of Medicine Lodge reservation as Arapaho-only, Cheyenne excluded.
notes: Source later (p.225) says the tribes never ceded the Outlet land until 1890; reconcile (1872 agreement likely unratified).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Grazing licenses approved by Interior, 1883
summary: Cattlemen paid key tribal members, agency staff and traders to secure signatures granting grazing on about 2.4 million acres at two cents per acre; tribes were restricted to 426,202 of 4,294,412 acres. Agent Miles held monopolies and later skimmed surplus-land payments. Cleveland expelled the cattlemen in 1885.
verbatim_quote: the Cheyennes and Arapahoes [being] restricted to a mere 426,202 acres of their 4,294,412-acre reservation
federal_account_contrast: Leasing is invisible in cession maps.
map_implication: Optional layer: 1883-85 grazing leases covering ~2.4 million acres.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Attorney contract (10% fee) with tribal chiefs
summary: Former agent Miles and frontier attorneys supposedly representing the tribes held a vague contract, signed deceptively with a tiny group of chiefs, for 10 percent of any settlement; they held secret communications with the commissioners. $67,000 of tribal money went to the attorneys.
verbatim_quote: It was often difficult to determine whose side the attorneys were on.
federal_account_contrast: Tribal counsel had a financial stake in the cession.
map_implication: Annotate 1890 agreement: tribal attorneys conflicted, $67,000 fee.
notes: Source prints 'May 1869 in Oklahoma City'; almost certainly a typo for 1889 (Oklahoma City founded 1889).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome (Cherokee) Commission agreement with Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1890
instrument_cite: Ratified Act of March 3 1891 (source gives date only; reader: 26 Stat. 1022, verify)
summary: Jerome threatened that the Dawes Act would be forced on them, that Medicine Lodge annuities would lapse, and that the Indian 'will starve'. Beef rations had been cut in half the prior year. Hagan judges it highly likely that attorney money bought the signatures of a handful who recruited others.
verbatim_quote: If you don’t do what the President wants you to do, the law of Congress will be put in force
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows a ratified agreement; source documents coercion and probable bribery.
map_implication: Flag 1890-91 Cheyenne-Arapaho cession as obtained by threats, ration cuts and probable bribery.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome Commission agreement 1890; Medicine Lodge Treaty three-fourths clause (Art. 12)
summary: Secretary Noble told Jerome to get three-fourths of adult males as Medicine Lodge required, 'but close with a majority if you cannot get more'. Agent Ashley claimed only 618 adult males so 464 signatures sufficed; Berthrong finds this not credible and thinks 680 were needed but not available. Most Cheyennes boycotted; a January 1891 protest by seven Cheyenne chiefs was ignored.
verbatim_quote: but close with a majority if you cannot get more
federal_account_contrast: Treaty-required consent threshold likely not met; signature count manipulated.
map_implication: Mark 1891 cession as likely failing Medicine Lodge three-fourths requirement (Lone Wolf-type issue).
notes: Article number not given by source (Art. 12 is reader's knowledge). Protesters: Old Crow, Young Whirlwind, Little Big Jake, White Horse, White Shield, Red Moon, Wolf Face.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Medicine Lodge 1867; Jerome agreement 1890
summary: Major parts of the Cherokee Outlet were promised to the Cheyenne and Arapaho at Medicine Lodge though already designated for the Cherokees. Noble told Jerome not to 'pay twice' for the Outlet; Jerome had the tribes sell 'any rights they might have' in either reservation, causing confusion about what was sold.
verbatim_quote: Jerome stated that the tribes were selling “any rights they might have” in either.
federal_account_contrast: Overlapping US promises to two nations.
map_implication: Show Medicine Lodge reservation overlapping Cherokee Outlet; note double promise.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Jerome agreement ratified March 3 1891; allotment
summary: Price held at 50 cents per acre (about $55 per person). Allotting agents chose allotments for families who refused. Of 4,294,415 acres the tribes retained 529,692 (12 percent); 231,828 school land, 32,343 military, about 3.5 million opened in the April 19 1892 land run of 25,000-30,000 settlers.
verbatim_quote: Of the 4,294,415 acres of the reservation the Cheyennes and Arapahoes retained 529,692 acres
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows a cession; source shows forced allotment at a fraction of statutory $1.25/acre.
map_implication: Attach acreage breakdown to 1891 cession; color retained allotments separately.
notes: Category should arguably be BRIBERY_FRAUD_FORGERY or TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT; ICC_OUTCOME used loosely. Note source later says $1.5M for 4,608,878 acres (p.230), inconsistent with 4.29M acre total.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Source says Boulder Chautauqua sits on land used by Left Hand's Arapahos as winter residence, 'stolen property' never compensated; Boulder was platted in 1858 and incorporated 1871 on unceded Arapaho and Cheyenne land.
verbatim_quote: the stately old buildings sit on stolen property, for which the Arapaho never received compensation
federal_account_contrast: Local land titles derive from settlement before any cession.
map_implication: Add Boulder/Chautauqua as site settled on unceded land in defiance of the 1851 treaty.
notes: Source says 'In 1851 fifty-three Anglo-American squatters platted lots' at Boulder; this is surely 1858/1859 (Boulder City Town Co. 1859). Flag as error. Also 'never compensated' conflicts with ICC award; source means no compensation specific to the site. Verification: verify-plains s.3: attribute 'unceded' to the tribe/TREC.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC Dockets 329/348 compromise settlement
summary: Government offered $15,000,000 to settle all Southern claims, including the claim that $1,500,000 paid for the 1891 taking of 4,608,878 acres was unconscionable. Accepted 338 to 2 at Watonga after notice to 1,542 members. Source argues it was below even the inflation-adjusted 1865 half share ($22.7M) and excluded loss of life and property.
verbatim_quote: The Indian Claims Commission only considered land claims.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account: final settlement; source: inadequate, low turnout vote, no compensation for life or suffering.
map_implication: Mark C-A lands as 'extinguished by ICC payment, 1965 compromise $15M' rather than 'ceded'.
notes: Turnout ~22 percent of notified members.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC Dockets 329, 348, 329-A, 329-B
summary: Tribe's TREC recommendations say the ICC valuations were biased, issues of the 1851 treaty and the illegal taking within Fort Wise 1861 boundaries were unresolved, and the tribes' petition to reserve appeal rights was barred by ICC rules, while the government could appeal. They seek to reopen the settlement.
verbatim_quote: when the Tribes inserted a petition to reserve the rights for appeal, they were automatically barred
federal_account_contrast: Tribe disputes finality of the ICC settlement.
map_implication: Note on ICC layer: tribe contests settlement finality and seeks appeal.
notes: Tribal position paper; legal characterization not independently verified.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Denver and ~20 Colorado towns founded before 1861
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18 1861, Senate removal of Art. 11
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 1163; Kappler II 807 (not given by source; verify)
summary: Tribe says the Senate's removal of Article 11 of Fort Wise and the amendment needed to ratify are suspicious: the amended document has erasures, possible date changes and misrepresented signatures. They say this bears directly on Denver and about 20 cities founded before 1861.
verbatim_quote: several places in the amended document contain erasures, possible date changes, and outright misrepresentation of signatures
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats Fort Wise as ratified with amendment assented to; tribe alleges forgery.
map_implication: Flag Fort Wise 1861 cession (Royce area to be determined) as contested: alleged altered amendment and signatures.
notes: Source does not say what Art. 11 provided. Reader's understanding: the original Art. 11 concerned recognition of land grants/claims to individuals (possibly town sites); verify against Kappler. Fort Wise itself is covered in other PSL chunks. Verification: verify-plains s.2: tribe's allegation; untested.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Front Range to Continental Divide; Colorado
summary: Tribe says the Front Range up to the Continental Divide was legally titled to them, 100,000 trespassers mined gold in 1859, and they were never compensated for minerals or water. Also claims railroad grants, state school land (4 million acres) and CSU land (19,000 acres still held) came from their land.
verbatim_quote: The Front Range and up to the continental divide were all legally titled to the Cheyenne and Arapaho
federal_account_contrast: ICC valued only surface land; minerals extracted before cession not compensated.
map_implication: Add layer for gold-rush mining on 1851 treaty land before 1861 cession; mark CSU and state school lands derived from C-A treaty land.
notes: Tribal recommendations; figures not independently sourced. Verification: verify-plains s.3: attribute to the tribe/TREC.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Indian Country west of the Mississippi (incl. Colorado plains and Front Range)
instrument: Trade and Intercourse Act of 1834
instrument_cite: 23rd Cong., Sess. I, Ch. 161, June 30, 1834 (as cited by source; 4 Stat. 729)
summary: The source argues the 1834 Act recognized Cheyenne title and required removal and fines of trespassers, but the US failed to enforce it for 39 years, and this non-enforcement was a major cause of Sand Creek. It says the Act was rescinded in 1873 after Homestead, Morrill and Pacific Railroad Acts of 1862 had dispersed Cheyenne land.
verbatim_quote: The federal government failed to deal with the illegal occupation, which lasted for 39 years, and the inaction caused measurable harm to the Cheyenne.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 1: 1834 Act text, Statute I, June 30, 1834
federal_account_contrast: Federal cession framing treats settlement as following lawful cession; source frames 1858-1861 Colorado settlement as illegal trespass under federal law the US itself refused to enforce.
map_implication: Add a layer/annotation: Colorado Front Range settlement 1858-1861 occurred on land that was Indian Country under the 1834 Act, before any cession.
notes: Claim that the Act was 'rescinded in 1873' is the author's and is not cited; verify. The 4 Stat. cite is reader-supplied.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Plains treaty councils generally (Fort Laramie 1851, 1868)
summary: The source says 'treaty negotiations are a myth': commissioners arrived with prepared texts, read articles aloud, heard objections, and sent the unchanged text to the Senate, while Native leaders believed their spoken input was incorporated. Lakota speak of the 'Chicago Re-write' for 1868.
verbatim_quote: In every treaty we evaluated, the process was the same. Treaty commissioners represented the United States government; most often, these were military representatives who came with a prepared treaty in hand
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 3-5: DeMallie, Proceedings of the Great Peace Council 1867-68 (1975); Gary Roberts unpublished dissertation; Jefferson Davis quote
federal_account_contrast: Kappler presents treaty text as the negotiated agreement; the source says spoken terms the nations relied on were never written.
map_implication: In treaty detail panels, add a note that written text may not reflect what was agreed orally; link oral-term evidence where available.
notes: Generalization by the author across treaties evaluated.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Cheyenne governance: Council of Forty-Four Chiefs
summary: Cheyenne national decisions, especially war and peace and treaties, belonged to the Council of 44 (ten-year terms, equal band representation, consensus), with military societies (incl. Dog Men / Dog Soldiers) subordinate. This is the standard against which the source judges every treaty signature: individual chiefs acting without Council approval lacked authority.
verbatim_quote: The Council of Forty-Four Chiefs was a self-perpetuating body of tribal trustees; each member was selected by a predecessor
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 6-12: Sheldon Spotted Elk, 'Northern Cheyenne Tribe: Traditional Law and Constitutional Reform,' Tribal Law Journal 12 (2012); Leo Killsback, A Sacred People (2020) pp.27-28, 189; Grinnell, The Fighting Cheyennes pp.6-7
federal_account_contrast: Federal treaty records treat whoever marked a paper as authorized 'chiefs and headmen'; Cheyenne law required Council of 44 consent.
map_implication: Add a signatory-authority field to Cheyenne treaties: whether Council of 44 approval is documented.
notes: Lists ten bands incl. Hevhaitanio (Dog Men or Dog Soldiers) as a band and Hotametaneo'o (Dog Men) as a society. Source says bands may have last gathered as one around 1849, splitting North/South by 1857; others say they kept meeting incl. on Fort Laramie 1851 and Fort Wise 1861.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Confluence of Cheyenne River and Missouri River
instrument: Treaty with the Cheyenne, 1825
instrument_cite: Not given in source (Kappler 2:232; 7 Stat. 255, July 6, 1825; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: First Cheyenne treaty. A Cheyenne representative took the proposal back to the Council of 44, which approved it; it allowed immigrants to cross Cheyenne territory undisturbed. With no Cheyenne interpreter, a Lakota gave the signers' names in Lakota, so the recorded names are Lakota renderings.
verbatim_quote: This treaty's unusual feature is that the Cheyenne names appear as Lakota names.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 13: author's own review of treaties
federal_account_contrast: Kappler lists names as if Cheyenne; source notes they are Lakota translations, a record-quality issue. Also a positive example where Council of 44 approval did occur.
map_implication: Note on the 1825 treaty: Council of 44 approval reported; signatory names are Lakota renderings.
notes: No land cession. Kappler/Stat. cite reader-supplied.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: From about 1845, and sharply after the 1849 California gold rush, emigrant trespass destroyed buffalo herds; this pressure produced the 1851 Fort Laramie council.
verbatim_quote: By 1849, the rush of illegal immigrants was destroying the buffalo herds.
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats emigrant trails as lawful passage; source calls emigrants illegal trespassers under the 1834 Act.
map_implication: Optional: show Platte emigrant route as pre-treaty trespass corridor.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Laramie / Horse Creek council grounds (approx. 42.20 N, -104.56 W for Fort Laramie)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851
instrument_cite: Not given in source (11 Stat. 749; Kappler 2:594; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: Commissioner D.D. Mitchell told the council the US did not want their land and that the boundaries were not intended to take land or limit hunting and passage; he promised compensation for 50 years, mainly for right of free passage on emigrant trails.
verbatim_quote: We do not come to you as traders ... We do not want your land, horses, robes, nor anything you have
federal_account_contrast: Later federal use of 1851 boundaries as the base for cessions and ICC claims contradicts the oral assurance that boundaries took no land.
map_implication: Render 1851 territory as a recognized homeland (not a cession), with Mitchell's assurance quoted.
notes: Mitchell also asked each tribe to designate a single chief.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 6 (head chiefs)
summary: Mitchell and Fitzpatrick wrongly believed the Cheyenne Medicine Chief could represent all Cheyenne; Article 6 bound nations to sustain US-selected 'head-chiefs'. The source says this subverted Council of 44 governance and set a precedent of holding whole tribes responsible for the acts of a few and of accepting signers who did not speak for the tribe.
verbatim_quote: Mitchell and Fitzpatrick made a serious error when they believed that the Medicine Chief of the Cheyenne could represent all of the Cheyenne in the treaty process.
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text presents chosen head chiefs as national authority.
map_implication: Flag 1851 Cheyenne signatures as not representing the Council of 44.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851
summary: The source lists possible Cheyenne signers (Stone Forehead of the Heviqsnipahis, chosen spokesman; Whiteface Bull, Oivimana; White Antelope, Isiometannui; Bear Feather, Wutapiu) and says all were Southerners representing only four of ten bands; no Northern band chief signed.
verbatim_quote: all the Chiefs who signed were Southerners, representing only four Manhao (what the Cheyenne called themselves) out of ten.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 27: Gary Roberts unpublished dissertation p.64
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats Cheyenne as a single party bound by these marks.
map_implication: Flag Northern Cheyenne as non-signatory to 1851 for any polygon derived from it.
notes: Source hedges: 'may have signed'; and Northern bands 'may have agreed'. Elsewhere (p.250) says six original Cheyenne signatures existed, four reappear on the amendment. Inconsistency between four and six signers.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Between the North Platte and Arkansas rivers (Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 5
summary: The US recognized the land between the North Platte and Arkansas as Cheyenne and Arapaho country. The source says assigning two sovereign nations one undivided tract violated their sovereignty and created later confusion; no Cheyenne-Arapaho line was drawn. Article 5 also preserved claims to other lands and hunting, fishing and passage rights.
verbatim_quote: the United States government recognized the land between the North Platte and Arkansas as the country of the Cheyenne and Arapaho.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty Article 5; endnote 16 (author note: 'Possible map showing the 1851 boundaries?')
federal_account_contrast: Atlas/Royce treat 1851 land as a starting tract later ceded; source stresses nothing was ceded in 1851.
map_implication: Draw 1851 Fort Laramie Cheyenne-Arapaho territory (North Platte to Arkansas, mountains to roughly the forks of the Republican/Smoky Hill per treaty text) as promised/recognized land, not ceded; note the treaty reserved rights to other lands.
notes: Source gives only North Platte-Arkansas; full metes and bounds are in treaty Article 5 (not reproduced in this chunk).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 5 final clause
summary: The source argues the reserved hunting, fishing and passage rights still exist unless a later treaty abrogated them, especially for Northern Cheyenne, many of whom say they never signed a treaty.
verbatim_quote: they do not surrender the privilege of hunting, fishing, or passing over any of the tracts of country heretofore described.
federal_account_contrast: Atlas cession polygons do not represent reserved usufructuary rights.
map_implication: Add 'reserved hunting/fishing/passage rights (claimed extant)' attribute to the 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho tract.
notes: Legal survival of rights is the author's argument.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Articles 3 and 4
summary: Article 3 bound the US to protect the nations against depredations by US citizens, but set no enforcement method; the 1834 Act's removal and $500-$1,000 fines were never enforced. Article 4's phrase 'lawfully residing' conflicts with the 1834 Act, under which no settler could lawfully reside.
verbatim_quote: Such significant treaty violations were not enforced (or went unenforced), and this caused major economic harm for the Cheyenne.
federal_account_contrast: Adds treaty-protection violations not in a cession-only record.
map_implication: Record Article 3 non-enforcement as a violation of the 1851 treaty.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 8
summary: Article 8 let the President withhold annuities from a whole nation for violations by any member, with no due process; the source calls it collective punishment and says the government did later manipulate annuities.
verbatim_quote: The government could manipulate annuities, and they did.
map_implication: Note annuity-withholding clause in 1851 treaty record.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
nations: Cheyenne; Arapaho; Lakota; Crow; Plains nations
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 7 (annuities)
instrument_cite: Prucha, American Indian Treaties pp.440-442; Kappler vol. IV p.1078-1080 (as cited)
summary: The Senate unilaterally cut annuities from 50 years to 10 (plus 5 at the President's discretion). Only three nations' assent was obtained; an Indian Office endorsement says the Indians 'never got together for the purpose'. Only four of six original Cheyenne signers and two of three Arapaho appear on the amendment. The treaty was omitted from Statutes at Large in 1867 and never proclaimed.
verbatim_quote: This [amendment] was to be submitted to the Indians, but they never got together for the purpose.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 18-23: Prucha pp.440-442; Luke Lea to A.H.H. Stuart May 29, 1852 (Kappler IV:1078); Harry Anderson, Nebraska History 37 (1956); Kappler IV:1080
federal_account_contrast: Kappler 1904 printed the treaty as amended and accepted; Kappler later (1929) admitted the error. Royce 1899 p.786 footnote says the treaty was never ratified.
map_implication: Mark Fort Laramie 1851 as Senate-amended without full consent and never proclaimed; show that Kappler vol. II text is misleading on assent.
notes: Source contains date errors: says Senate 'ratified' Sept 17, 1851 (actually the signing date) and that the treaty went to Fillmore Feb 17, 1852 and he refused to sign; Senate struck 50-year term May 24 (1852). Verify against Prucha. Verification: verify-plains s.1: Kappler footnote says all nations except the Crow assented; PSL's 'only three nations' is not confirmed.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Commissioner Luke Lea to Secretary A.H.H. Stuart, May 29, 1852
summary: The Commissioner of Indian Affairs himself wrote that a treaty amended without Indian consent is a 'mockery' of contract. A federal official's own admission useful for the atlas.
verbatim_quote: how such a proceeding in view of the legal principles involved, can be considered anything but a mockery of the highest and most solemn form of contract it is difficult to perceive.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 2 and 19: Kappler IV:1078; Prucha p.440
federal_account_contrast: Primary federal source contradicting unilateral amendment practice.
map_implication: Quote in the 'Senate amended without consent' category explainer.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Roy v. United States and Oglala and Cheyenne Indians (Ct. Cl. 1910); Moore v. United States and the Sioux and Cheyenne (1897)
instrument_cite: Cited via Prucha p.442 n.; also New York Indians v. US, 170 U.S. 1 (source prints '170, U.S. 23')
summary: The Court of Claims held presidential proclamation unnecessary and treated the 1851 treaty as valid, reasoning from a 'wards' fiduciary theory and claiming the Sioux agreed to the amendment. The source disputes the factual premise and the diminished-sovereignty reasoning. In the 1920s Secretary of State Kellogg refused to have the President proclaim it.
verbatim_quote: The Indians were our wards, and we thus occupied a fiduciary relationship to them.
federal_account_contrast: Shows federal branches disagreed on whether the 1851 treaty was ever in force.
map_implication: Ratification-status field for 1851 should read 'contested: never proclaimed; Court of Claims treated as valid'.
notes: Source names 'Francis Kellogg' (Frank B. Kellogg). New York Indians cite as printed appears wrong; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Indian Claims Commission Cheyenne-Arapaho claim
instrument_cite: ICC Docket 329 (cited elsewhere in chunk, endnote 46, decided Dec. 1961)
summary: The source says the ICC erred by stipulating the unratified 1851 treaty as the basis for the Cheyenne-Arapaho land claim.
verbatim_quote: the Indian Claims Commission ("ICC"), established by Congress in 1946, erred by stipulating the 1851 Treaty was the grounds for the claim, as the Treaty was never ratified
federal_account_contrast: ICC framing treated the 1851 boundary as the legal title baseline.
map_implication: Note on ICC outcome: valuation was premised on a treaty whose ratification is contested.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: Cheyenne warriors killed and scalped a Shoshone father and son traveling to the council; the Cheyenne chiefs then held a 'scalp peace', returning undanced scalps with gifts. The Missouri Republican also describes the military societies as able to act without chiefs' consent.

sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 28: Missouri Republican 1851 (A.B. Chambers, B. Gratz Brown)

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)

instrument: Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: Grattan fired on Brule Sioux in the 1854 'Mormon cow' affair, killing Conquering Bear, whom the source says was coerced into signing the 1851 treaty as Lakota representative. Afterward the US military struck a Cheyenne camp and killed ten people; Cheyenne retaliation killed 18 whites.
verbatim_quote: the United States military struck the Cheyenne camp and killed ten people.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 29: Nadeau, Fort Laramie and the Sioux Indians pp.90-91; Hafen and Young, Fort Laramie and the Pageant of the West pp.221-245

map_implication: Add 1856 attack on Cheyenne camp (10 killed) as violence event near Platte route; location not specified.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: War Department ordered a punitive expedition against the Cheyenne eight days after agent Twiss concluded a peace, for acts already 'settled and forgiven by treaty'. Col. Sumner's 1857 campaign defeated the Cheyenne; Northern bands withdrew to the Powder River and Southern bands were left in the path of expansion.

sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 31-32: Chalfant, Cheyennes and Horse Soldiers pp.59-61; Grinnell, The Fighting Cheyenne pp.112-123

map_implication: Add Solomon's Fork 1857 as violence event preceding the gold rush and Fort Wise.

map_implication: Mark the 1868 Northern Cheyenne cession as conditional on a reservation never provided; show the Northern Cheyenne reservation as executive-order land, not a treaty reservation.
notes: Legal conclusion is the author's.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1868 (NC & NA), Article 8; Agreement of 1876 ratified Feb 28, 1877
instrument_cite: Act of Feb 28, 1877, ch. 72 (44th Cong., 2d Sess.) (19 Stat. 254, reader-supplied)
summary: Article 8 required any cession to be signed by a majority of adult males. The source says the 1876-77 Manypenny agreement, which ceded Black Hills land and all outside the reduced Sioux reservation incl. hunting rights, could not have been signed by Cheyenne already removed to Oklahoma and lacked majority assent.
verbatim_quote: No treaty for the cession ... shall be of any force or validity as against the said Indians unless executed and signed by at least a majority of all the adult male Indians
federal_account_contrast: Act states the Northern Arapaho and Cheyenne were 'duly authorized' parties.
map_implication: Flag 1877 Black Hills cession as lacking Article 8 majority for Northern Cheyenne.
notes: Source's chronology is wrong: it dates the agreement September 1877 (text says Spotted Tail Agency, September 28, 1877), but the agreement was signed Sept-Oct 1876 and ratified Feb 28, 1877, before the May 1877 removal. The 'could not have signed' argument needs re-checking; the majority-consent argument stands independently. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-CHY-B-008 (PSL pp. 302).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
nations: Sioux bands; Northern Arapaho; Northern Cheyenne
place: Great Sioux Reservation western boundary: 103rd meridian, South and North Forks Cheyenne River, Cannon Ball River
instrument: Agreement of 1876 (Manypenny Commission), ratified Act of Feb 28, 1877, Articles 1-5

Article 4 pushed removal to Indian Territory; Article 5 tied rations to school attendance.
verbatim_quote: the said Indians do hereby relinquish and cede to the United States all the territory lying outside the said reservation, as herein modified and described, including all privileges of hunting
federal_account_contrast: Rations-for-cession ('sign or starve') context is not in the source here.
map_implication: Ensure Northern Cheyenne are listed as parties affected by the 1877 Black Hills taking polygon; boundary description usable for mapping.
notes: Commissioners included A.G. Boone of Fort Wise.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Red Fork of the Powder River (Willow Creek), about 20 miles west of Kaycee, Wyoming
summary: US troops found and burned the 173-lodge Northern Cheyenne village, destroying winter supplies; the source says it affected the Cheyenne more than Little Bighorn. Starvation forced surrenders in spring 1877.
verbatim_quote: U.S. troops found them and burned their village.
federal_account_contrast: Usually framed as a battle (Dull Knife Fight).
map_implication: Add Dull Knife Fight (Red Fork Powder River) as violence event leading to surrender and removal.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: Cheyenne accounts of the Little Bighorn were discounted because they used different cardinal directions; Richard Fox's 1984-85 archaeology found the Cheyenne accounts most accurate. Rosebud is the battle 'where the girl saved her brother' (Buffalo Calf Road Woman). Context: 1874 refusal to sell the Black Hills.
verbatim_quote: when the correct cardinal directions as used by the Cheyenne were applied to the battlefield site, the Cheyenne stories were the most accurate.
federal_account_contrast: Validates Cheyenne oral history over military accounts.
map_implication: Context only.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Red Cloud Agency, Nebraska; Spotted Tail Agency, Nebraska
instrument: Agreement with the Sioux (and Northern Cheyenne/Arapaho), Sept 26, 1876 (Black Hills / Manypenny agreement)
summary: The report reprints the 1876 agreement text, including Article 6 promising a house for each principal chief if the Indians removed to Indian Territory. The author's endnote calls this an unlawful use of bribery in Indian politics.
verbatim_quote: the Government shall erect for each of the principal chiefs a good and comfortable dwelling-house.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/federal record presents the agreement as a consensual cession; source frames the chief-house clause as a bribe tied to removal.
map_implication: Tag the 1876/1877 agreement (Black Hills cession) with a 'bribery inducement alleged' note for Cheyenne signers.
notes: Ratified by Act of Feb 28, 1877 (19 Stat. 254) per general knowledge, not cited in this chunk. Royce area for 1877 Black Hills cession not given by source; verify (likely Royce 1, 2 area for Sioux, Royce schedule 1877).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Red Cloud Agency and Spotted Tail Agency, Nebraska
instrument: Agreement of Sept 26, 1876; Cheyenne signatures dated Spotted Tail Agency Sept 28, 1877
summary: The signature block shows Cheyenne marks (Living Bear, Spotted Elk, Black Bear, Turkey Legs, Calfskin Shirt) appended at Spotted Tail Agency on Sept 28, 1877, a year after the commissioners signed. Elsewhere the author states no Northern Cheyenne leader legally signed the 1877 agreement.
verbatim_quote: Dated and signed at Spotted Tail Agency, Nebraska, September 28, 1877.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty signature block reprinted; p. 321 narrative
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the agreement as binding on the Northern Cheyenne; the source says Cheyenne signers were few and lacked authority, and signed after Congress had already enacted it.
