notes: Text extraction puts Little Wolf under 'Arapahos'; layout may be garbled. Calfskin Shirt is the father of Bear Bow (see p. 328 finding).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
nations: Northern Cheyenne; Northern Arapaho; Southern Cheyenne; Southern Arapaho
place: Medicine Lodge reservation (Indian Territory); Great Sioux Reservation
instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868 (Fort Laramie)
summary: Author argues that because the U.S. never located the Northern Cheyenne on either of the two reservations the 1868 treaty named (Medicine Lodge lands, which were disputed and too small, or the Sioux reservation), their forfeiture of 'territory outside of the two reservations' is void and they retain a legitimate land claim.
verbatim_quote: The failure to fulfill locating the Northern Cheyenne within the agreed upon locations vacates the forfeiture of their "territory outside of the two reservations mentioned above."
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats the 1868 relinquishment as an effective cession; source asserts it is void for U.S. non-performance.
map_implication: Flag the 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho relinquishment as 'conditional cession, condition unfulfilled' in Indigenous view.
notes: Legal argument by the author, not a court holding.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868
summary: Author says the U.S. lacked authority to assign the Northern Cheyenne land inside the existing Sioux reservation, since the 1868 Sioux treaty reserved no such right.
verbatim_quote: the U.S. government did not have the authority to assign land within the boundaries of an existing reservation.
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats the option to join the Sioux as a valid treaty term.
map_implication: Note that the 1868 'attach to Sioux reservation' option conflicted with Sioux treaty rights.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, 1868, Article 2
summary: Author says ambiguous Article 2 language left the Northern Cheyenne without a permanent reservation until 1884, effectively exiled in their homeland for twenty years.
verbatim_quote: Essentially the Northern Cheyenne were exiled in their homeland for twenty years.
federal_account_contrast: Adds the human cost of the 16-year gap between 1868 and the 1884 executive order.
map_implication: Timeline: mark 1868-1884 as a period with no secure Northern Cheyenne land base.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, 1868
summary: Author states the 1868 treaty was made by a limited number of people, none with authority to bind the whole people, and that handwritten council transcripts show the farming provisions were rejected.
verbatim_quote: Many people today have concluded that the Treaty of 1868 was made by a limited number of People, and none of those had the authority to bind all the People to this treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 34, 35 (references handwritten transcripts, not cited specifically)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record lists the signers as representative chiefs.
map_implication: Flag 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty: signer authority contested.
notes: Transcripts referenced but not cited; verify against the 1868 council proceedings.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, 1868 (article on Army officer attesting delivery of goods)
instrument_cite: H.R. Rep. No. 98, 42nd Cong., 3rd Sess. (1872), Investigation of Indian Frauds
summary: The treaty clause requiring an Army officer to attest annuity deliveries is called a failure because of widespread fraud in Indian Country, citing the 1872 House frauds investigation.
verbatim_quote: This was an absolute miserable failure because of the fraud that happened during this time in Indian Country.
federal_account_contrast: Adds that annuity terms the map may treat as compensation were not delivered as promised.
map_implication: Attach annuity-fraud note to 1868 treaty record; cite H.R. Rep. 98, 42-3.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: 1876-77 Agreement
summary: Author notes several 1877 agreement provisions (allotment selection, on-reservation obligations) could never be performed by the Cheyenne because most had already been moved to Oklahoma, which commissioners must have known.
verbatim_quote: This would have been nearly impossible for the Cheyenne since the majority of them had already been moved to Oklahoma.
federal_account_contrast: Shows agreement terms were drafted around a removal already under way.
map_implication: Link 1877 agreement to Northern Cheyenne removal to Indian Territory.
notes: Chronology: removal south was summer 1877; Cheyenne signatures Sept 1877. Worth checking.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 | PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Powder River Country, Montana, to Indian Territory (Darlington / Fort Reno agency area; source says Fort Sill)
instrument: Forced relocation after 1877 surrender
summary: After surrendering in 1877, the Northern Cheyenne were force-relocated by the Army to Indian Territory, where as many as one-third died of disease (dysentery, influenza, malaria). Grinnell: nearly two-thirds of 999 were sick within two months; 41 died the first winter, and Cheyenne sources put deaths much higher.
verbatim_quote: as many as one-third of the interned Cheyenne died of disease
sources_cited_by_source: Sandoz 1964, 27-28; Grinnell 1956, 400; Little Chief testimony to Congressional committee 1878 (Grinnell 401)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record frames 1877 as consolidation with Southern kin under treaty; source frames it as forced internment with mass death.
map_implication: Draw removal route Powder River to Indian Territory 1877; add mortality note.
notes: Source repeatedly says 'Fort Sill'; the Northern Cheyenne were held at the Cheyenne-Arapaho (Darlington) agency near Fort Reno. Likely a source error. Mortality figures differ (one-third vs 41 deaths). Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-CHY-A-055 (PSL pp. 293-294).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Source summarizes that warfare marked by the slaughter of perhaps half the Cheyenne at Sand Creek, the Washita, and Sappa Creek preceded the 1877 surrender.
verbatim_quote: in warfare marked by the slaughter of perhaps half their number at places such as Sand Creek, the Washita, and Sappa Creek
federal_account_contrast: Sappa Creek (1875) is rarely in federal treaty-based records.
map_implication: Ensure Sappa Creek (Kansas, April 1875) is included in massacre layer alongside Sand Creek and Washita.
notes: 'Half their number' is a broad estimate.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: On Sept 9, 1878, about 350 Northern Cheyenne (92 fighting-age men, 261 women, children, elderly) under Dull Knife and Little Wolf left Indian Territory for the north, eluding up to 13,000 troops over 1,000 miles.
verbatim_quote: it was far better to die trying to return home than to stay and resign themselves to a tragic death from disease or starvation.
sources_cited_by_source: Gerry Robinson (Northern Cheyenne), WYOHistory.org; Sandoz 1964, 147; Andrist 1964, 321
federal_account_contrast: Federal record calls this an outbreak; source frames it as a flight home from deadly internment.
map_implication: Draw 1878 Northern Cheyenne exodus route as a story line.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Dull Knife's band of 149 (46 men, 61 women, 42 children) was captured Oct 23, 1878, disarmed, horses impounded, and interned in a barracks at Camp Robinson. Officials secretly arranged a second forced relocation south and the Kansas governor's demand for trial of leaders.
verbatim_quote: We are back on our own ground, and have stopped fighting. We have found the place we started to come to.
sources_cited_by_source: Powell 1969, 217-225; Grinnell 1956, 417; Military Division of the Missouri Briefs 9079, 9421, 9983, 10209, 10315
federal_account_contrast: Adds archival military correspondence showing the return south was decided without the prisoners' knowledge.
map_implication: Mark Fort Robinson as internment site of Dull Knife's band 1878-79.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: After the Cheyenne refused to return south, Capt. Henry W. Wessells cut off food and firewood on Jan 4 and water on Jan 8, 1879, in subzero weather, and put Wild Hog in irons on Jan 9, to force consent to removal.
verbatim_quote: Wessells immediately began attempting to "change their minds" by cutting off their food and firewood, escalating on January 8 to cutting off their water.
sources_cited_by_source: War Dept. 1879 Board of Officers 'Proceedings', RG 98 NARA, Wessells testimony 75-79; Powell 1969, 231-232; Grinnell 1956, 425-426
federal_account_contrast: A textbook case of starvation used to compel a removal; the Army's own court of inquiry documents it.
map_implication: Tag Fort Robinson 1879 with DURESS_STARVATION (food, fuel, water withheld) and HOSTAGE (leaders in irons).
notes: Some Cheyenne say water and fuel were cut off for the full eight days (endnote 31).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Camp Robinson, White River, and Pine Ridge escarpment, Nebraska; final washout ~35 mi NNW of Camp Robinson on Warbonnet/Antelope Creek
summary: On the night of Jan 9, 1879, about 130 starving prisoners broke out; troops rode people down in the snow and civilians executed wounded and mutilated women. Pursuit ended Jan 22 when troops fired volleys into a washout, killing all the men. Army count: 64 Cheyenne dead, 78 captured, 7 unaccounted.
verbatim_quote: the troops simply rode people down, shooting them and leaving them to freeze where they fell
sources_cited_by_source: War Dept. 1879 'Proceedings' (testimony of Cummings, Baxter, Pettys, Simpson); Powell 1969; Sandoz 1964; Grinnell 1956; Bronson 1908; Ricker Tablets
federal_account_contrast: Federal sources call it the 'Fort Robinson outbreak'; the report calls it the Fort Robinson Massacre (p. 337).
map_implication: Add Fort Robinson Massacre (Jan 9-22, 1879) to massacre layer with points at Fort Robinson and the final washout.
notes: Casualty counts vary: Wessells 'about 30' first night vs burial detail 'about fifty' (Grinnell 423); Cummings 39 men and 22 women and children.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: White River near Camp Robinson, Nebraska
summary: Army officers testified that civilians (trader J.W. Dear, Henry Clifford) followed troops killing wounded Cheyenne and mutilating bodies, including sexual violation of dead women. Wounded children included infants who died of gunshot wounds.
verbatim_quote: As there were no soldiers there, I was convinced that these civilians were killing wounded Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: 'Proceedings' 1879, Cummings testimony 167-169; List of Indians Wounded 139-140; Ricker Tablets vol. 2, 289
federal_account_contrast: Civilian atrocities absent from treaty-based records.
map_implication: Include civilian participation and child casualties in the Fort Robinson massacre record.
notes: Clifford denied the charges (Proceedings 161-165).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Fort Leavenworth / Kansas; back to Indian Territory
summary: Seven surviving men (Wild Hog, Tangle Hair, Left Hand, Old Crow, Porcupine, Blacksmith, Noisy Walker) were shipped to Kansas for trial demanded by the Kansas governor, acquitted for lack of evidence, then sent back to Indian Territory. Wild Hog and his wife tried to stab themselves rather than go south.
verbatim_quote: All were ultimately acquitted of any criminal actions, but they were then returned to Fort Sill, Oklahoma.
sources_cited_by_source: 18th Biennial Report, Kansas State Historical Society 1910-12; Powell 1969, 273-274; Sandoz 1964, 270
federal_account_contrast: State prosecution as an arm of removal.
map_implication: Note Kansas state role in prosecuting Northern Cheyenne exodus leaders.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Pine Ridge; Fort Keogh (Miles City, MT); Tongue River
summary: Survivors (about 58 women, children and elders) were sent to Pine Ridge on Jan 31, 1879; Dull Knife reached Pine Ridge separately; Little Wolf's band of 112 surrendered March 25, 1879 to Lt. W.P. Clark and was allowed to stay. The report says the breakouts forced creation of a Montana reservation.
verbatim_quote: The breakouts of 1878-79 had achieved one accomplishment: they had forced the U.S. Congress to establish a reservation in Montana.
federal_account_contrast: The source credits Cheyenne resistance, not federal grant, for the reservation.
map_implication: Link Northern Cheyenne Reservation origin to the 1878-79 exodus.
notes: The reservation was created by executive order (1884), not Congress; the source wording is loose.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Executive Order of Nov 26, 1884 creating Tongue River (Northern Cheyenne) Reservation
summary: The reservation (371,200 acres, 680 sq mi) was made by executive order, which the author calls legally questionable because the 1865, 1868 treaties and 1877 agreement confirmed a northern reservation on land the Cheyenne legally possessed. Boundaries excluded Cheyenne families homesteading near the Tongue River.
verbatim_quote: Did the Cheyenne honestly give up their rights to land in the north?
federal_account_contrast: Atlas likely shows EO reservation as a grant; source says it shrank land the Cheyenne never ceded.
map_implication: Draw the 1884 EO boundary (371,200 acres) and mark surrounding Powder River/Tongue River lands as never-validly-ceded per source.
notes: p. 322 quote gives 'Executive Order on 16 November 1884' vs 26 November elsewhere; the commonly cited date is Nov 26, 1884.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: West bank / east of Tongue River, Montana
instrument: Executive Order of March 19, 1900 (McKinley) extending reservation
summary: The 1900 extension to the Tongue River raised the reservation to 444,157 acres, but Cheyenne who had homesteaded east of the river were relocated west of it; whites had already homesteaded most of the area.
verbatim_quote: Those who had homesteaded east of the Tongue River were relocated to the west of the river.
federal_account_contrast: Adds a small internal removal hidden inside a boundary 'expansion'.
map_implication: Draw 1900 extension boundary to Tongue River; note Cheyenne homesteaders east of river displaced.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Northern Cheyenne Reservation; St. Labre Mission, Ashland, MT
instrument: Courts of Indian Offenses (Commissioner Hiram Price, 1883); Cheyenne Court of Indian Offenses 1889; Sun Dance ban 1880
summary: The BIA and Catholic and Mennonite missions suppressed Cheyenne religion: Courts of Indian Offenses (1883; Cheyenne court 1889) punished dances and medicine men, the Sun Dance was banned around 1880 for about 50 years, and the Council of 44 lost authority to the agent.
verbatim_quote: The suppression of the Sun Dance continued for approximately 50 years.
sources_cited_by_source: Prucha 1984; Pahr 1997; Stands in Timber & Liberty 1967; Weist 1977; Moore 1974
federal_account_contrast: Cultural suppression not part of land records but tied to reservation confinement.
map_implication: Optional: add reservation-era religious suppression context to the Northern Cheyenne reservation entry.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Near present Chief Dull Knife College, Lame Deer, Northern Cheyenne Reservation, MT
summary: Head Chief and 13-year-old Young Mule were killed by about 90 First Cavalry troops after Head Chief killed a white man who was illegally on the reservation grazing cattle; the agent rejected the tribal offer of 30 horses as compensation.
verbatim_quote: The man was illegally on the reservation, and his cows were grazing illegally on Cheyenne land.
federal_account_contrast: Shows ongoing trespass on the reservation and military enforcement.
map_implication: Optional point: Head Chief and Young Mule, 1890.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: White River, Pine Ridge Reservation, SD; Busby, MT
summary: The White River Cheyenne, living at Pine Ridge since 1879, were allowed to join the Northern Cheyenne Reservation in 1890-91 over BIA opposition; some stayed with Oglala kin.
verbatim_quote: General Miles had suggested this recommendation, but the Bureau of Indian Affairs opposed it.
federal_account_contrast: Oral source for a relocation not in treaty records.
map_implication: Note White River Cheyenne relocation Pine Ridge to Busby 1890-91.
notes: Text says 1890 in narrative and 1891 in band addendum.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Red Cloud Agency area; Black Hills; El Reno, OK (affidavit)
instrument: 1876 Black Hills agreement
summary: In a sworn 1918 statement, Bear Bow, son of signer Calf Skin Shirt, said his father understood the 1876 agreement as allowing whites to mine Black Hills gold for half the gold, not a sale, and that only about one-sixth of the Cheyenne (friendly bands and Army scouts) were present and had no authority to sign for the rest.
verbatim_quote: they made a treaty with the commissioners giving the white people the right to mine gold in the Black Hills for half of the gold mined, but they did not sell the Black Hills.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows a cession of the Black Hills; Cheyenne account says it was a mining-share arrangement by an unauthorized minority.
map_implication: Flag the 1877 Black Hills cession as contested by Cheyenne testimony (gold-sharing, not sale; 1/6 present).
notes: Single affidavit, 42 years after the event; interpreted by Robert Burns.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
nations: Northern Cheyenne; Southern Cheyenne; Arapaho; Lakota
place: Black Hills and lands south of the North Platte
instrument: Fort Laramie Treaty of 1851, Article 5
summary: Cheyenne joined to claim the Black Hills; the 1851 treaty assigned Cheyenne-Arapaho lands south of the North Platte but Article 5 preserved claims to other lands and hunting rights. A Black Hills claim was filed in 1926.
verbatim_quote: the aforesaid Indian nations do not hereby abandon or prejudice any rights or claims they may have to other lands
federal_account_contrast: Atlas may show Black Hills as solely Lakota; source asserts a Cheyenne claim too.
map_implication: Indicate Cheyenne claim to Black Hills as overlapping; note 1926 claim filing.
notes: 1926 claim not otherwise identified; verify (possibly Court of Claims petition).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: BIA horse reduction program
summary: From about 1919 the BIA killed up to 100 Cheyenne horses a month, paying $6.50 per hide, to make room for cattle; the herd fell from 15,000 to 3,000 by 1930, and the BIA-run tribal cattle herd failed within five years.
verbatim_quote: As many as 100 horses were killed monthly, and the owner received a measly $6.50 per hide.
map_implication: Context only.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Allotment of Northern Cheyenne Reservation (completed 1932); IRA Constitution 1936
summary: Under heavy BIA pressure the Cheyenne voted to allot; 1,457 members got 160 acres, there was not enough land, and allotment let many non-Indians buy and lease reservation land. The 1936 IRA constitution vote is called suspicious.
verbatim_quote: Under tremendous pressure from the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Cheyenne tribal members voted to allot their reservation lands.
federal_account_contrast: Allotment framed as tribal choice in federal record; source stresses coercion.
map_implication: Note allotment-era land loss within the Northern Cheyenne Reservation.
notes: Category DURESS_MILITARY used loosely for administrative pressure; consider OTHER. Allotment act cite not given (likely Act of June 3, 1926).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Oct 14, 1865 (used as ICC taking date)
summary: Both sides' attorneys stipulated the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty date as the taking date, which lowered value: mining was in a slump and railroads had not yet crossed the land. The author notes the 1865 treaty did not apply to the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho at all.
verbatim_quote: First, the 1865 Treaty did not apply to Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho; second, the 1865 Treaty should never have been ratified
federal_account_contrast: The ICC used a treaty the Northern Cheyenne never signed as the date their land was 'taken'.
map_implication: Note that the ICC valuation date (Oct 14, 1865) rests on a treaty not involving the Northern Cheyenne.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC offsets from 1861, 1865, 1867, 1868 treaties
summary: The ICC allowed offsets from four treaties, so the government 'bought' the tract four times for offset purposes. Consideration for Southern Cheyenne-Arapaho was $1,434,131.38; the government sought $7 million more in gratuitous offsets; boarding schools were counted as offsets.
verbatim_quote: although the land changed hands only once for legal purposes, the government bought the tract four separate times for offset purposes.
federal_account_contrast: Offsets included unwanted expenditures such as boarding schools.
map_implication: Record offset structure in ICC data for the 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho claim.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC no-interest practice
summary: The ICC paid no interest, settling in 1865 dollars; at 5% compounded over 100 years the payment would have been about 130 times larger, over $1.5 billion.
verbatim_quote: the Cheyenne payment would have increased by 130 times the original amount, exceeding $1.5 billion!
sources_cited_by_source: Carlson 1985, in Sutton ed., Irredeemable America, 97-99
federal_account_contrast: Shows 'compensation' was a fraction of value.
map_implication: Display ICC award alongside interest-adjusted value.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC compromise settlement, Northern Cheyenne Indians of the Tongue River Reservation, Docket 329-C (with 348)
summary: Northern Cheyenne interlocutory award was $5,360,886.19 before offsets; the U.S. claimed $3,213,580.46 offsets; the compromise deducted $1,000,000 for a net $4,360,886.19 which also released accounting, rights-of-way, buffalo/timber/grass destruction, and intentional tort claims including wrongful attacks and wrongful removal.
verbatim_quote: a net judgment for the petitioner of $4,360,886.19 was considered somewhat more than the probable value of the Fort Laramie land cession claim alone
sources_cited_by_source: ICC settlement transcript (counsel Charles A. Hobbs, Wilkinson, Cragun & Barker); 13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1
federal_account_contrast: Massacre and removal claims were extinguished as part of a land settlement, never heard.
map_implication: Note that Northern Cheyenne tort claims (wrongful attacks, wrongful removal) were released in the 1963 ICC compromise.
notes: Verification: verify-plains s.8: 13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 not surfaced; 12 Ind. Cl. Comm. 212 (1963) sets Northern Cheyenne share $5,950,200.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Congressional appropriation and distribution of ICC award
summary: After legal fees the Northern Cheyenne got under $4 million for more than 12,500,000 acres, distributed per capita; the BIA released only $100 of each $1,000 share and required business plans for the rest.
verbatim_quote: the Northern Cheyenne received a credit of less than $4 million for more than 12,500,000 acres of land!
sources_cited_by_source: 16 ICC 162, 178; interview with Dennis Limberhand, May 2023; Perkinson 1993
map_implication: Show Northern Cheyenne share as roughly 12.5 million acres for under $4 million (about 32 cents/acre before fees).
notes: Mix of ICC citation and oral interview.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC Docket 348 (Rufus Wallowing, class petition)
summary: The author argues the Northern Cheyenne had inadequate representation: tribal attorneys (BIA-approved) talked clients out of claims filed by Rufus Wallowing in Docket 348 and merged them, saying they had little merit.
verbatim_quote: the attorney representing the Tribes inserted a false claim that the claims requested by Rufus Wallowing had little or no merit.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Vol. 13 No. 1; ICC Act Sec. 2
map_implication: Note conflict-of-interest critique of the ICC Northern Cheyenne settlement.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: ICC Dockets 329/348
summary: The ICC record acknowledged the buffalo's central role but gave no compensation for loss of the buffalo economy, which the author calls an additional treaty violation of 1851 Art. 5 and 1868 Art. 2 hunting rights.
verbatim_quote: Despite being mentioned, there was no consideration for compensation for the economic loss of Buffalo.
sources_cited_by_source: Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5; 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty Art. 2 (Kappler 1012)
map_implication: Note uncompensated hunting rights/buffalo loss on the 1851 polygon.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024

summary: The treaty recited Tabeguache country as running from the 37th parallel at the base of the Sierra Madre north along the Rockies to the 41st parallel, west to the Snowy Range, south via Rabbit Ears to the Grand River, down to the Gunnison and Uncompahgre, then south to the La Plata range and back along the 37th parallel.
verbatim_quote: Beginning on the 37th degree of north latitude, at the eastern base of the Sierra Madre mountains; running thence northerly with the base of the Rocky mountains to the forty-first parallel
federal_account_contrast: This US-written description assigns lands also used by Mouache, Capote, Grand River and Yampa bands to the Tabeguache alone.
map_implication: Use as the 1863 'claimed Tabeguache territory' polygon; flag overlap with other bands.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
nations: Grand River Ute; Uintah Ute; Yampa Ute; Muache Ute; Tabaguache Ute; Capote Ute; Weeminuche Ute
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Senate amendment assent
summary: The 1868 treaty was signed in Washington by ten Ute men, then amended by the Senate. Assent to the amendment was collected band by band: Grand River (7) and Uintah (4) Aug. 15, Yampa (5) Sept. 1, Muache and Tabaguache Sept. 14, Capote (15) Sept. 24, Weeminuche (6) Sept. 25. The Weeminuche and Capote signed only the amendment, not the original.
verbatim_quote: We, the chiefs and headmen of the aforesaid named bands of Ute Indians, duly authorized by our people, do hereby assent and agree to the amendment of the Senate
federal_account_contrast: Consent here was obtained; this is not a no-consent case. But the original March 2 signing had no Capote or Weeminuche named signers.
map_implication: Record band-by-band assent dates for 1868; note the Washington signing lacked Capote and Weeminuche.
notes: PSL lists Ou-ray under 'Muaches' and Ka-ni-ache under 'Tabaguaches', the reverse of their usual band identities (Ouray Tabeguache, Kaniache Mouache). Likely a heading/transcription error in source or AccessGenealogy; verify against 15 Stat. 619. The 'Date of signing' lines appear after each group, so dates may attach to the following group; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Ute (Hunt Treaty / Kit Carson Treaty), Mar. 2, 1868
summary: PSL says officials insisted on making Ouray principal chief of all Utes to ease further cessions, and that the delegation was 'forced to relinquish' large tracts in a hotel room, with some sources citing 'questionable tactics'.
verbatim_quote: finally coming to an agreement in a hotel room on March 2, wherein they were forced to relinquish large tracts of their ancestral homelands. Some sources mention "questionable tactics" being used
sources_cited_by_source: Part II note 32 (not in chunk). 'Some sources' unnamed.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents a negotiated treaty with a single head chief; Ute bands had no single chief (p.407).
map_implication: Flag 1868 cession as contested consent; note imposed head-chief structure.
notes: Nature of the force is not specified; 'questionable tactics' is unattributed.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Ute bands each had their own leaders and councils, and no single chief held power over the whole nation. US officials imposed Ouray as principal chief to simplify cessions, and there were at least five attempts on Ouray's life by Ute warriors after 1868.
verbatim_quote: No single chief held absolute power or made decisions for the entire tribe.
federal_account_contrast: Federal instruments treat Ouray as 'Head Chief of the Ute nation' (e.g., Brunot salary clause, p.361).
map_implication: In signatory metadata, mark Ouray's 'head chief' status as a US designation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
nations: Ute (Tabeguache, Muache, Capote, Weeminuche, Yampa, Grand River, Uintah)
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Art. 2
summary: The 1868 reservation took roughly the western third of Colorado. PSL's narrative gives the bounds as west of the 107th meridian and south of the 40th parallel, but the Supreme Court's recital (Court of Claims findings) says the northern line was fifteen miles north of and parallel to the 40th parallel. The full Article 2 metes-and-bounds text is not quoted in this chunk.
verbatim_quote: The northern boundary of the 15 million acres there ceded was described in the treaty as a line fifteen miles north of, and parallel to the 40th parallel of north latitude.
sources_cited_by_source: Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States, 330 U.S. 169 (1947), via LII.
federal_account_contrast: PSL narrative (p.410) misstates the northern boundary as the 40th parallel; treaty says 15 miles north of it.
map_implication: Draw 1868 reservation with north line 15 mi north of 40N, east line 107W, south line Colorado-New Mexico (37N), west line Colorado-Utah; confirm against 15 Stat. 619 Art. 2.
notes: Also note the court's wording '15 million acres there ceded' appears odd (reserved?). Verification: verify-ute-shoshone s.3: north line is 15 miles NORTH of the 40th parallel; PSL p. 410 'south of the 40th parallel' is wrong.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, Mar. 2, 1868, Art. 2 and three-fourths clause
summary: Article 2 promised that no unauthorized persons would ever be allowed to pass over, settle on, or reside in the reservation. The treaty also barred further cessions without the consent of three-fourths of adult Ute men.
verbatim_quote: no persons, except those herein authorized so to do ... shall ever be permitted to pass over, settle upon, or reside in the Territory described in this article
sources_cited_by_source: Jones v. United States (Fed. Cir. 2017) via NARF (note 72).
federal_account_contrast: Later cessions (Brunot 1873/74; 1880) should be checked against the three-fourths requirement.
map_implication: Attach Art. 2 exclusion promise to 1868 polygon; check Brunot and 1880 for three-fourths compliance.
notes: Quote edited with ellipsis from p.390 text.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Brunot Agreement, Sept. 13, 1873 (approved Apr. 29, 1874)
summary: Miners entered the San Juan Mountains, which the 1868 treaty protected, soon after the treaty. The government planned to use troops to remove squatters but the territorial governor objected and protection never came. Under pressure from the miners, the Utes 'reluctantly' ceded a 60 by 90 mile block in the Brunot Agreement.
verbatim_quote: prospectors and miners were sneaking into the San Juan Mountains, a region specifically protected from white encroachment by the 1868 Treaty, at an alarming pace.
sources_cited_by_source: Rust 2017, Ashley NF Tribal Uses Report, p.9 (notes 12-13); Part II.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the Brunot area as a cession; PSL shows the area was already trespassed in breach of Art. 2 before the cession.
map_implication: Flag Brunot cession polygon as 'ceded after US failed to remove trespassing miners, in breach of 1868 Art. 2'.
notes: Ouray's son captive story is NOT in this chunk (likely later pages). Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-UTE-A-036 (PSL pp. 369-370).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Miller survey (1875) of 1868 northern boundary; Executive Order of Nov. 22, 1875
summary: Surveyor Miller, under instructions, staked the 1868 northern boundary 15 to 18 miles south of the true line, which would have cut out the White River Valley and the agency. Agent Danforth said the error was about 17.5 miles. The President then issued an 1875 executive order adding land up to the first standard parallel north.
verbatim_quote: Miller's instructions, however, required him to stake out a line which he admitted to the local Indian agent and to the Utes themselves to be fifteen to eighteen miles south of the true boundary
sources_cited_by_source: Confederated Bands v. US, 330 U.S. 169; Senate Ex. Doc. No. 29, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., pp. 41-45 (Danforth letter).
federal_account_contrast: Federal survey itself misplaced the treaty boundary.
map_implication: Map the 1875 EO addition (107W north to first standard parallel north, west to Utah line, south to 1868 NW corner, east along 1868 north line) as executive-order land.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States
summary: The Supreme Court held the Utes had no compensable interest in the 1875 executive-order lands north of the true 1868 line, calling them tenants at will, so no compensation was owed when the 1882 order restored them to the public domain. Justices Murphy, Frankfurter and Douglas dissented, saying the 1880 Act's 'present reservation' included those lands.
verbatim_quote: That order made the Indians no more than tenants at the will of the Government on that part of the land outside the true treaty reservation.
federal_account_contrast: EO lands taken without payment; the Court admitted the Indians 'in all probability' thought they owned them.
map_implication: Mark 1875 EO strip as 'taken 1882, never compensated (330 U.S. 169)'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Ute Agreement of 1880; Act of June 15, 1880
summary: After the 1879 Meeker/Milk Creek fighting, Congress used the 1880 Act to punish the Utes and remove them from Colorado, barring payments until the participants surrendered and deducting victims' compensation from land proceeds. The Uncompahgre were removed too though they had no role in the incident.
verbatim_quote: With the massacre in mind, Congress decided to remove the Indians from the Colorado reservation as part of the punishment meted out for this tragedy.
federal_account_contrast: The 1880 'agreement' was a punitive removal; chiefs only promised to 'use their best endeavors' to obtain consent.
map_implication: Flag 1880 cession (Royce) as punitive and obtained under threat; note Uncompahgre uninvolved.
notes: This chunk covers 1880 only via legal excerpts; detailed narrative likely in next chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
nations: Uncompahgre Ute; Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
instrument: EO Jan. 5, 1882; Acts of 1894 (28 Stat. 286, 337-338) and 1897 (30 Stat. 62, 87); ICC Docket 349; Ute Indian Tribe v. Utah (Ute III)
summary: In 1894 Congress declared the Uncompahgre had 'no title' and only temporary occupancy. The 1897 Act opened unallotted lands; only 83 allotments were made. The ICC settled Docket 349 for $300,000 barring further claims, yet the Tenth Circuit holds the reservation boundary intact, and Interior (Jorjani 2018) denied restoring the land.
verbatim_quote: Uncompahgre Indians have no title to any of the lands within the [Uncompahgre] reservation [and] nothing more than the privilege of temporary occupancy.
sources_cited_by_source: Jorjani M-37051; H. Rpt. No. 660, 53rd Cong.; ICC Dkt 349.
federal_account_contrast: Reservation is legally intact as Indian country but tribe has no recognized ownership; payment used as extinguishment.
map_implication: Show Uncompahgre Reservation (Utah) as existing reservation boundary, mostly BLM/SITLA owned; note ICC $300,000 settlement.
notes: This is Utah, not Colorado; outside the Brunot/1868 focus but in chunk. Verification: verify-ute-shoshone s.6: Docket 349 $300,000 confirmed by M-37051; cite volume 12 vs 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 707 unresolved.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
nations: Weber Ute; Paiute; Utah Ute bands
instrument: Utah Indian Treaty of 1865 (Spanish Fork)
summary: The 1865 Spanish Fork treaty relinquished all Ute lands in Utah Territory for a Uinta Basin reservation. Congress never ratified it, but the Army enforced it and removed Utes from the Wasatch Front within a year, which helped spark the Black Hawk War.
verbatim_quote: The treaty was never ratified by Congress, but the U.S. Army implemented the terms of the treaty and removed the Utes from the Wasatch Front within the next year.
federal_account_contrast: Utah land treated as taken without any ratified cession.
map_implication: Mark Utah Wasatch Front Ute lands as taken without ratified treaty (1865 unratified).
notes: Also cites a separate unratified treaty with Weber Utes and Paiute, Sept. 18, 1865.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Conejos Treaty, 1863, Art. 8
summary: The 1863 treaty promised $10,000 in goods and $10,000 in provisions a year for ten years, but the US failed to deliver; in 1866 Gov. Alexander Cummings found the Utes destitute and called the annuity goods worthless and rotten.
verbatim_quote: "disgracefully worthless, rotten, and disgusting, and might reasonably have been made the grounds of revocation of the treaty."
federal_account_contrast: Federal official himself said the breach could justify revocation, yet the 1868 cession followed.
map_implication: Flag 1863 annuities as unperformed; treat 1868 as negotiated amid starvation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Kaniache's son was murdered by white settlers in the mid-1860s, after which Kaniache attacked settlements. Ouray declined to join and warned settlers and Fort Garland, building his standing with whites.
verbatim_quote: In the mid-1860s, Chief Kaniache's son was murdered by white colonizers.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II (no note on this sentence).
federal_account_contrast: Not in federal treaty record.
map_implication: Context only.
notes: Not the 'Ouray's son held captive' story (Ouray's son Cotoan/Paron taken by Arapaho/Sioux), which is not in this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, 1868, Art. 6 ('bad men' clause)
summary: The Harvard Law Review note says the Ute treaty, unlike every other 1867-68 Peace Commission treaty, buried the 'bad men' clause in Article VI, had no preceding peace declaration, and omitted the standard language on regulations and damages review.
verbatim_quote: the Ute treaty buried these clauses in Article VI.
federal_account_contrast: Text differs from template treaties; Ute treaty concluded in Washington not in the field.
map_implication: Note structural difference in 1868 treaty metadata.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
instrument: Agreement with Ute Indians of Colorado (1880); H.R. Rep. No. 1401
summary: Interior Secretary Carl Schurz told Congress that large reservations were untenable because the government could not control Western settlers and Indian tenure would become 'more and more precarious'. PSL frames this as the US declining to honor treaty protections.
verbatim_quote: the government will not always be able in all things to control the action of our Western people
sources_cited_by_source: H.R. Rep. No. 1401 via OU Digital Commons (note 73).
federal_account_contrast: A federal admission that encroachment, not consent, drove the 1880 cession.
map_implication: Quote in 1880 cession panel.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Kit Carson enlisted Ute warriors against the Navajo in 1863 (leading to the Long Walk) and Ute and Jicarilla scouts against Kiowa and Comanche in 1864. PSL calls this a divide-and-conquer strategy.
verbatim_quote: In this way, Indian nations were turned against each other, further dividing and conquering them
map_implication: Context for intertribal relations layer.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
summary: Spaniards from Taos mined gold in the San Juans in the mid-1700s until Utes killed almost all of the expedition. Rumors drew Charles Baker's 1860 prospecting party, starting the San Juan rush.
verbatim_quote: a group of Spaniards from the Taos area discovered a rich vein of gold in the San Juan Mountains.
federal_account_contrast: Only Spanish-era item in this chunk; no Spanish/Mexican land grants named.
map_implication: Context only.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: San Juan Mountains; Animas River; Baker's Park
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, March 2, 1868
summary: Prospectors, probably sanctioned by Territorial Governor McCook, trespassed into the 1868 reservation in 1870 and found rich mineral deposits; by 1871 a stamp mill and scores of mining claims existed on Ute land in direct violation of the treaty.
verbatim_quote: Scores of individuals filed claims on Indian land
sources_cited_by_source: McCook quotes from Annual Report of the Dept. of the Interior 1869 p.711 (n33) and Manypenny, Our Indian Wards (1880) p.404 (n34)
federal_account_contrast: Royce frames 566 as a cession by agreement; this shows the mining takeover preceded and forced the cession.
map_implication: Annotate Royce 566 as occupied by illegal trespass (1870-1873) before any cession; add timeline layer of trespass before treaty.
notes: PSL says McCook 'probably' sanctioned the trespass; that inference is the authors'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1872 San Juan cession negotiation (failed)
summary: Federal commissioners admitted trespassers were violating the 1868 treaty but said nothing could be done and the Utes should cede the mines to avoid bloodshed. Ouray refused to sell and demanded removal of intruders; the council ended without a cession.
verbatim_quote: it would be to the Utes' advantage to give up the mining districts so that they could avoid conflicts and avert possible bloodshed
federal_account_contrast: Shows the US openly conceded treaty breach and offered cession as the remedy for its own non-enforcement.
map_implication: Note on Royce 566: Ute refusal of 1872, and conceded US non-enforcement of 1868 treaty.
notes: Interested parties present included Otto Mears and McCook's brother-in-law J.B. Thompson; interpreter Curtis previously accused of selling Ute rations to Mears.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Los Pinos; Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory; Washington DC
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: 18 Stat. 36 (1874) (cited via US v. Southern Ute, 402 U.S. 159)
summary: Commissioner Felix Brunot used Ouray's captive son (taken by Lakota, traded to Arapaho) as a bargaining tool, promising recovery in return for Ouray urging the San Juan cession. The boy was never delivered; the youth produced in Washington was disowned by Ouray.
verbatim_quote: Brunot was content to exploit this belief without even knowing whether the boy was alive or dead.
sources_cited_by_source: Hafen, Efforts to Recover the Stolen Son of Chief Ouray, Colorado Magazine XVI(2) 1939 p.60 (n41)
federal_account_contrast: Official report states no inducements were used; PSL documents a captive child used as leverage.
map_implication: Flag Royce 566 cession as obtained with leverage over a captive child of the lead signatory.
notes: Brunot's 1901 account that the youth was Ouray's son is uncorroborated per PSL.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 43d Cong., 1st Sess. (1873) pp.453-467
summary: The Utes would cede only existing mines and mountain land, not farming valleys; Brunot refused a mines-only sale. Ouray's letter of Sept 13 says they would sell 'mountainland' but not valleys. Utes understood they retained hunting rights and had sold only mining areas.
verbatim_quote: We are perfectly willing to sell our mountainland, and hope the miners will find heaps of gold and silver
sources_cited_by_source: Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1873, H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 43d Cong. 1st Sess. pp.454, 467 (n35-37)
federal_account_contrast: Royce draws a clean 60x100 mile cession; Ute understanding was a narrower mines-only sale with retained hunting rights.
map_implication: Show Ute-understood scope (mining districts only) vs. drawn Royce 566; mark retained hunting rights over 566.
notes: Approx. 4 million acres per PSL narrative; 3.7 million per Supreme Court in 402 U.S. 159.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Uncompahgre Park; Gunnison and San Miguel rivers; south end of reservation
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 43d Cong., 1st Sess. p.454
summary: Brunot's own report says the cession took mineral country of over 60 by 100 miles, while Uncompahgre Park, the Gunnison and San Miguel Rivers and the agricultural and grazing lands on the south end were reserved to the Indians. Utes were to receive $25,000 per year in perpetuity.
verbatim_quote: The Uncompagre Park, the Gunnison and San Miguel Rivers, and the agricultural and grazing lands on the south end of the present reservation are reserved to the Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: Brunot report, H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 43d Cong. 1st Sess. (n38)
federal_account_contrast: Adds the reserved areas inside/adjacent to 566 that were later taken anyway.
map_implication: Draw Uncompahgre Park and the southern agricultural lands as land expressly reserved in 1873.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: Brunot stated no presents or extra promises were made, yet Article 6 gave Ouray a $1,000 annual salary for ten years while he remained at peace and 'head chief of the Utes'.
verbatim_quote: No presents were given to influence them, and no promises were made other than those mentioned in this report
sources_cited_by_source: H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 43d Cong. 1st Sess. p.453 (n39)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents the salary as a routine clause; PSL frames it as an inducement to the key signatory.
map_implication: Note on Royce 566: payment to principal signatory written into the agreement.
notes: A separate claim (Sidney Jocknick) that Mears arranged the signing is flagged by PSL as uncorroborated. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-UTE-A-030 (PSL pp. 361).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: After signing, the Indian Bureau told the Utes the $25,000 annuity would not go to them but would be spent at agents' discretion; a request to buy horses was answered that they needed a schoolhouse.
verbatim_quote: was to go into the hands of government agents and be dispersed according to the discretion of such agents
sources_cited_by_source: Rocky Mountain News, Nov 1, 1873 (quoted in text)
federal_account_contrast: Changes the meaning of the consideration after signature.
map_implication: Note that the 1873 consideration was controlled by agents, not paid to the nation.
notes: Newspaper report; 'supposedly' in PSL.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Little Annie mine, San Juan country
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: Per an 1873 Colorado newspaper, Ute Agent Charles Adams, while in Washington with the Ute delegation, sold two-thirds of the Little Annie gold mine (on trespassed Ute land) for half a million dollars.
verbatim_quote: has made a sale of two-thirds of the Little Annie gold mine in the San Juan country
federal_account_contrast: The agent charged with protecting Ute interests profited from trespass during the cession negotiation.
map_implication: Conflict-of-interest note on Royce 566 negotiation.
notes: Single newspaper source, unnamed; needs verification.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Treaty with the Ute, 1868
summary: Investigator found Agent Jabez Trask held $25,000 of Ute appropriations locked in a Denver bank while refusing to issue food.
verbatim_quote: Trask had $25,000 of Ute appropriations money locked up in a Denver bank
federal_account_contrast: Annuity withholding not reflected in treaty text.
map_implication: Add to annuity non-performance record for 1868 treaty.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1873 Brunot Agreement (signed Los Pinos Sept 1873; approved by Act of April 29, 1874)
summary: The greatest portion of the San Juan cession came from southern band territory; the southern bands felt they had been tricked into signing, refused to come to Los Pinos even for rations, and rejected the first-year Brunot payments, accusing the Tabeguache of manipulating them.
verbatim_quote: The southern Utes felt they had been tricked into signing the compact
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats 566 as ceded by the confederated Utes; the bands whose land it mostly was rejected it.
map_implication: Flag Royce 566 as contested by the southern bands whose territory it mainly was.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: Brunot Agreement 1873; Executive order 1876; Act of May 14, 1884
summary: Uncompahgre Park was expressly reserved in 1873, but a government surveyor (Miller) contracted the boundaries and included it in the cession; settlers moved in. Grant's 1876 executive order restored about sixteen square miles but the military could not enforce it. After the Utes were removed, the Act of May 14, 1884 returned the park to public domain.
verbatim_quote: In 1876, President Grant had issued a special order restoring sixteen square miles of the Uncompahgre Park to the Utes
sources_cited_by_source: Smith, ARCIA 1876 p.19 (n42); ICC Docket 327 findings
federal_account_contrast: Not a treaty cession at all: taken by survey error and statute after removal.
map_implication: Map Uncompahgre Park (10,240 acres) separately as reserved land taken by statute 1884, never ceded; do not color as part of Royce 566 cession.
notes: PSL p.455 says the surveyor 'deliberately' included it; p.420 calls it an 'error'. Internal inconsistency.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
place: Los Pinos; White River Agency; Rawlins depot
instrument: Treaty 1868; Brunot Agreement 1873
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 1, 45th Cong., 2d Sess. (1877) p.442
summary: By 1877 the US was about $90,000 behind on Ute annuities. Agent Danforth reported White River supplies were under half of need, with no clothing, blankets or tools for nearly two years and flour sitting at Rawlins.
verbatim_quote: The annuities and supplies furnished these Indians amount to not over one-half that required for their support.
sources_cited_by_source: ARCIA 1877, H.R. Exec. Doc. 1, 45th Cong. 2d Sess. p.442 (n43)
federal_account_contrast: Documents non-performance of treaty consideration.
map_implication: Annuity default layer for 1868/1873 obligations.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
instrument: 1878 congressional authorization to negotiate consolidation at White River (act not named by PSL); 1878 Ute Commission
instrument_cite: H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 84, 45th Cong., 3d Sess. (1879) pp.1-2

federal_account_contrast: Shows pre-Meeker federal intent to diminish the reservation.
map_implication: Context note; no boundary change.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: PSL argues Nathan Meeker was placed at White River through Pitkin, Teller, Evans and Byers, men with mining and railroad interests in removing the Utes. Meeker withheld rations from Utes who would not farm on his terms.
verbatim_quote: Meeker began to withhold rations from those who would not work according to his instructions
federal_account_contrast: Federal record frames Meeker as a civilizing agent; PSL frames appointment as a setup.
map_implication: Context note for 1880 removal.
notes: The 'setup' thesis is the authors' interpretation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: Governor Pitkin telegraphed that White River Utes had burned 'millions of dollars of timber' and urged removal to Indian Territory; Major Thornburgh investigated and found no such activity, and settlers gave statements that the Utes had set no fires.
verbatim_quote: so far as I can learn no one attributes the burning of timber to these Indians
sources_cited_by_source: Colorado Daily Chieftain July 8, 1879; Thornburgh report to Crook July 27, 1879 (no endnote)
federal_account_contrast: State fabrication used to build a removal case.
map_implication: Note: state-generated false accusations preceded 1879-1881 removal.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
nations: White River Utes; Canalla (Johnson); Nicaagat (Captain Jack)
instrument_cite: H.R. Exec. Doc. No. 83, 46th Cong., 2d Sess. (White River Ute Commission)
summary: Meeker plowed Ute horse pasture, then telegraphed a false claim of assault by Canalla; troops were sent. Thornburgh agreed to halt, then crossed Milk Creek, the reservation's northern boundary, with his whole column on Sept 29, 1879, triggering the battle.
verbatim_quote: The Indians seem to consider the advance of troops as a declaration of real war.
sources_cited_by_source: White River Ute Commission evidence, H.R. Exec. Doc. 83 pp.7, 37-38, 55 (n50-53)
federal_account_contrast: Federal and popular narrative calls it the 'Meeker Massacre' and an 'outbreak'; record shows troops entered the reservation contrary to agreement.
map_implication: Mark Milk Creek battle site (Sept 29, 1879) as US military entry onto the 1868 reservation.
notes: Who fired first is unresolved per PSL; Jack said soldiers did.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Ute Tribes chapter
summary: After news of Milk Creek reached the agency, Ute warriors killed Meeker and the male employees and took three women and two children captive. PSL notes 12 soldiers killed and 43 wounded at Milk Creek.

verbatim_quote: Even though under the provisions of various later treaties the Cheyenne and Arapaho ceded their land in the Pikes Peak region, this did not give title to the town companies.
map_implication: Pin Colorado City as pre-cession townsite.
notes: Weak sourcing (tourism website).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: Bent's New Fort; Upper Arkansas Agency
instrument: Upper Arkansas Agency administration
summary: Agent William Bent (1859-60) kept trading while agent and stayed mostly in Westport, Missouri; 1859 annuity goods were found undistributed in 1860 by F.B. Culver, Commissioner Greenwood's personal physician, who was left in charge of annuities.
verbatim_quote: When Culver arrived at Bent’s Fort, he found that the 1859 annuity goods had not yet been distributed.
sources_cited_by_source: H.R. Rep. No. 228 (1878), Culver claim; King n.d., Colorado Encyclopedia
federal_account_contrast: Conflict of interest of trader-agent not in federal treaty record.
notes: TREC says it is 'likely' goods arrived while Bent was away: inference.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: In 1858 Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal governments passed laws to accept farming; Left Hand traveled to Council Bluffs, worked on farms and concluded ranching suited the Arapaho better. Government ignored both; Greeley in 1859 dismissed Left Hand's view as a 'savage' defect.
verbatim_quote: In 1858, the Cheyenne and Arapaho passed laws within their tribal governments to accept farming as a new way of life. They were ignored by the government.
federal_account_contrast: Counters federal narrative of Native refusal to adapt.
map_implication: Story card: Native-initiated land-use policy ignored.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Governor William Gilpin wrote that the 1834 Act did not apply to the Great Plains and that enforcement would lead to war. TREC says this was legally wrong.
verbatim_quote: enforcement of existing laws “leads point blank to expensive and bloody wars, to the destruction of property, to the massacre of the innocent and the escape of the guilty.”
federal_account_contrast: Shows territorial executive deliberately declining to enforce federal Indian Country law.
notes: Gilpin became governor 1861; TREC places him during treaty attempts.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: Fort Wise (Bent's New Fort), Arkansas River
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18, 1861
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 1163; Kappler II 807 [not given by source]
summary: Senate in executive session deleted Article XI (land to Denver and nearby communities at $1.25/acre), likely because the 1834 Act barred tribe-to-private land deals. The amendment was 'allegedly' re-signed Oct 29, 1861; TREC says the X marks are bold crosses in a rare uniform hand, suggesting forgery. Many chiefs did not sign; some signers repudiated it.
verbatim_quote: If one studies the manner of the signatures, specifically the “X” markings, they are done as crosses in a bold hand, which is a rare manner of marking.
sources_cited_by_source: Prucha 1994, 212 (adjacent claim); signature analysis appears to be TREC's own document inspection, uncited
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats Fort Wise as a ratified, assented cession.
map_implication: Flag Royce 426 cession as: Senate-amended; amendment assent signatures possibly forged (TREC claim, unverified).
notes: Forgery is implied, not stated outright. Needs check of NARA RIT 315 original. Article XI content: Denver land at $1.25/acre is notable evidence that townsite speculators sought treaty validation. Verification: verify-plains s.2: forgery inference untested by handwriting exam; assent paper exists.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country') | PSL TREC 2024 (quoting Unrau)

place: Colorado north of South Platte; 1851 territory

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18, 1861, Article VI (assent of absent bands within one year)
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 1163; Kappler II 807 [not given by source]
summary: Article VI required non-signatory Upper Arkansas bands to come in within a year (deadline Dec 6, 1862). The required chiefs never signed; Commissioner Dole wrote Evans in 1863 that more signatures were needed; no signatures exist after 1861. Evans ignored the deadline.

notes: Archival correspondence cited but not quoted. Verification: verify-plains s.2 OVERRIDES: some Northern marks were collected (1863 Upper Platte agreement, annuity-conditioned, never sent to the Senate).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: North of the South Platte: Fort Collins, Greeley, Julesburg, Boulder, parts of Denver
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18, 1861
instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 1163; Kappler II 807 [not given by source]
summary: US District Attorney S.E. Browne told Dole the treaty failed to define ceded boundaries; federal courts found no basis for a cession north of the South Platte; Dole, reviewing Interior and GLO maps, concluded only lands south of the South Platte were ceded. TREC: this land is still unceded today.

map_implication: HIGH PRIORITY: draw land north of South Platte in Colorado as 'not ceded by Fort Wise per 1863 Commissioner Dole and US Attorney Browne'; check later 1868 Fort Laramie (Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho) and 1876 agreements before calling it never ceded.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: Upper Arkansas Agency, Fort Lyon; Denver
instrument: Fort Wise annuities
summary: Agent Samuel Colley, cousin of Commissioner Dole, diverted annuity goods to his son Dexter Colley and partner John Smith ('Lying John'), who sold them to the Indians or hauled them to Denver. Dexter reportedly made $25,000-$35,000. Rocky Mountain News (Byers, an Evans ally) reported the pilfering.
verbatim_quote: Dexter and Smith then traded the annuity goods to the Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: Kelsey 1968, Background to Sand Creek, Colorado Magazine XLV(4), 280-286
federal_account_contrast: Federal record lists annuities as paid; this shows diversion.
map_implication: Annuity ledger flag: Upper Arkansas 1862-64 annuities diverted by agent.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Upper Platte agent John Loree appointed friends as traders, refused renewals to established traders, withheld hunting ammunition, absent from agency while drawing salary (per Eugene Ware).
verbatim_quote: Loree was also withholding hunting ammunition, and there was a shortage of annuities.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Spotted Wolf's band of 12 lodges stranded starving near Denver because annuities were distributed at Fort Larned, Kansas instead of the Arkansas. Evans appointed John Smith interpreter despite Arapaho (Neva) objections; Surgeon John J. Saville reported mistreatment at Fort Wise.
verbatim_quote: they would not believe anything Smith said and refused to have him as their interpreter.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Survey of Fort Wise reservation (1862)
summary: Interior Secretary John P. Usher appointed his friend Judge John W. Wright, with no surveying credentials, to survey the reserve; the survey was so poor it had to be redone. Wright later got $4,000 plus $5/day as Caddo special agent; Caddos (400+) remained destitute, he built three unusable houses.
verbatim_quote: Wright had no credentials as a surveyor and had to hire a subcontractor to perform the survey.
federal_account_contrast: Explains why reservation boundaries in federal surveys may be unreliable.
map_implication: Treat 1862 reservation survey lines as low-confidence.
notes: Caddo story includes the only non-Plains nation in this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')

verbatim_quote: This proposal’s aim was to extinguish land claims of the Utes, Comanche, Kiowa, and Plains Apache.
federal_account_contrast: Territorial attempt to extinguish title, which only Congress could do.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862
summary: The Act provided for extinguishing Indian title, a 200-foot right-of-way and 6,400 acres (ten sections) per mile of track. TREC ties Evans's refusal to accept Dole's South Platte ruling to his railroad interests; he attended a Pacific Railroad company meeting in New York, Nov 1863.
verbatim_quote: The government also promised 6,400 acres of land adjacent to the track for each mile of track laid.
sources_cited_by_source: Roberts 2016, Massacre at Sand Creek, 93; Roberts 1984, 208
federal_account_contrast: Federal land-grant maps show railroad land as federal grant; TREC links grant to unceded Native title and a conflicted governor.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Reports of Indian raids on the Platte in July 1862 proved false after investigation; fabricated by settlers hoping to get Indians removed from land they had taken.
verbatim_quote: They had been fabricated by settlers who hoped their stories would lead to the removal of Indians from land which the settlers had stolen.
federal_account_contrast: Federal depredation narratives partly fabricated.
notes: Pattern repeated: Irwin-Jackman cattle 1864, Chivington's Nov 24 1864 report, Hancock 1867, stage-line and freighters' rumors.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb 18, 1861 (1863 adherence agreement with agent Loree)
summary: Friday, Roman Nose, Black Bear, Spotted Horse and Shield signed an adherence agreement with Loree; annuities were issued only after signing. Other chiefs threatened to kill Spotted Horse and Shield because the Council of 44 had not approved. Other bands called Fort Wise a swindle.
verbatim_quote: Annuities were not issued until after the document was signed.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record may cite these signatures as Northern assent; TREC shows annuity leverage and lack of council authority.
map_implication: Flag 1863 Upper Platte adherence as annuity-conditioned and unauthorized.
notes: 'Friday' is an Arapaho chief; source lists him with Cheyenne. The document stated no gifts were given, yet annuities followed signing.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: 1863 was 'the year of hunger'; no buffalo within 200 miles of the reservation. Major Scott Anthony said starvation 'would probably be the easier way of disposing of them'. Colley's diversion partly caused starvation.
verbatim_quote: starvation “would probably be the easier way of disposing of them.”
sources_cited_by_source: Grinnell 1915, 125-128; Trenholm 1970, 170-171; Hoig 1961, 35; Jackson 1994 (Century of Dishonor), 86

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
nations: Arapaho; Cheyenne; Kiowa; Comanche; Plains Apache
place: Washington DC delegation from Fort Lyon
instrument: Washington delegation 1863
summary: Colley took a delegation of minor chiefs to Washington, leaving before Left Hand (fluent English speaker) arrived; Little Raven refused to go in protest. TREC suggests Left Hand was excluded to ease trickery and avoid exposure of Colley-Smith swindles.
verbatim_quote: It may have been that Left Hand was not wanted in the delegation because he spoke fluent English, and trickery would have been made more difficult with him there.
notes: Motive is inferred.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Proposed Cache la Poudre reservation talks (Ute agent Simeon Whitely)
summary: Friendly Arapaho asked for a reservation along the Cache la Poudre in exchange for peace; it would have displaced 16 white squatter families on unceded land. Talks led by incompetent agent Simeon Whitely failed.
verbatim_quote: The Arapaho wanted a reservation along the Cache la Poudre in exchange for peace.
federal_account_contrast: A Native land request absent from the federal map.
map_implication: Draw 'requested Arapaho reserve, Cache la Poudre 1864' as point/area of a Native proposal (boundaries not given).
notes: Also: Whitely lived in a Denver hotel at public expense.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Delegate H.P. Bennet told Dole troops occupied the 1861 reservation; Arapaho chiefs agreed to move if troops were removed; troops stayed; after three years nothing had been provided.
verbatim_quote: Arapaho chiefs agreed to move to the reservation if the military was removed from the reservation. The troops were not removed.
map_implication: Annotate Royce 477: military occupation of reserve.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Cheyenne received about 25% of robe value; ~200 robes traded for watered whiskey worth $0.25 each; trader Beggs passed eleven $1 bills as $10 bills.
verbatim_quote: Approximately 200 robes had been traded for whiskey.
sources_cited_by_source: Hyde 1968, 252 (Special Agent H.T. Ketchum report, April 4, 1864)

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Major Jacob Downing captured Spotted Horse, a Fort Wise adherent, threatened to burn him on a pyre to force him to lead troops, then attacked his sleeping village: 26 killed, 30 wounded, lodges burned, horses given to troops, over one stolen horse.
verbatim_quote: Downing surrounded a sleeping Cheyenne village and killed 26 people, wounded 30, and burned lodges
map_implication: Add massacre point (Cedar Canyon/Fremont's Orchard area is likely; source gives no place, verify).
notes: Likely the Cedar Canyon fight, May 3, 1864; place not named by source.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: Camp Weld (Denver); Fort Lyon; Sand Creek
instrument: Camp Weld Agreement, Sept 28, 1864
summary: At Camp Weld the chiefs' bands became prisoners of war and surrendered at Fort Lyon on Chivington's orders. Evans declined peace so as not to embarrass military operations. Anthony cut rations and moved them to Sand Creek; Chivington, knowing they were prisoners, attacked Nov 29 under white and US flags. Chivington's Nov 24 depredation report was fabricated.
verbatim_quote: Chivington then said, “They won’t be prisoners after we get there.”
sources_cited_by_source: Hoig 1961, 139-154; S. Rep. No. 142 (1865), 195-241; Kansas State Historical Society; Hyde 1968, 149
federal_account_contrast: Sand Creek lies within the Fort Wise reserve (Royce 477) the US had promised.
map_implication: Tie Sand Creek massacre point to Royce 477 and to Little Arkansas cession that followed 11 months later.
notes: Cost to government $30 million (unsourced figure). Silas Soule murdered April 23, 1865; killers never tried.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
summary: Delegate Allen A. Bradford charged Evans with pursuit of private interests and countenancing massacre; Committee on Conduct of the War called for his resignation; Seward requested it July 18, 1865. Chivington never prosecuted.
verbatim_quote: He has given countenance and encouragement to massacre of peaceable Indians and destroyed their faith and confidence in the sincerity and obligation of Government Treaties.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
nations: Southern Cheyenne; Southern Arapaho; Plains Apache
place: Little Arkansas River, Kansas; reservation in Indian Territory/Kansas; Arkansas-Platte territory
instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct 14, 1865
instrument_cite: 14 Stat. 703; Kappler II 887 [not given by source]
summary: Art. II reservation included land the US did not hold title to; Art. III allowed residence between Arkansas and Platte except white-occupied land; 640 acres to mixed-blood relatives vs 160 acres to Sand Creek survivors; Art. VII $20/$40 per capita. TREC says never ratified, promised land never given; only one sixth of Cheyenne present; Dog Soldiers refused; Little Raven limited it to signers.

federal_account_contrast: Atlas (TLA-T-341) lists it ratified, 14 Stat. 703 with reparations clause. Ratified with Senate amendments the Cheyenne say they refused.
map_implication: Flag Royce 477 (and remaining 426) cession as obtained 11 months after Sand Creek with minority attendance; mark Art. VI Sand Creek reparation lands as never delivered.
notes: TREC 'never ratified' conflicts with standard record (proclaimed 1867 with amendments). Likely TREC means amendments not assented/reservation never established. Verify. Verification: verify-plains s.5 OVERRIDES the UNRATIFIED tag: Little Arkansas was ratified with amendments May 22, 1866, amendments accepted Nov. 10 and 19, 1866, proclaimed Feb. 2, 1867.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')

instrument_cite: Flute et al. v. United States (filed 2013; 10th Cir. affirmed; cert. denied 2016)

map_implication: Add court-outcome node: Flute v. US (808 F.3d 1234, 10th Cir. 2015) [cite from memory, verify].

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Treaty of the Little Arkansas (Kiowa and Comanche), Oct 18, 1865
summary: Art. II reservation in Indian Territory; Art. III roaming south of Arkansas; $15 per capita after removal; agent's written permission needed to leave. Dole ordered 'the valley of the Platte River and all the country south must be entirely abandoned'.
verbatim_quote: “the valley of the Platte River and all the country south must be entirely abandoned by the Indians with whom you treat.”

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: Pawnee Fork village near Fort Larned, Kansas
summary: Hancock, without treaty authority, advanced on a Cheyenne-Lakota village to intimidate; residents fled fearing another Sand Creek; Hancock burned 110 Cheyenne and 140 Sioux lodges (property at least $100,000 per Stanley), kept 40 lodges for scouts. Acted on false depredation reports.
verbatim_quote: Henry M. Stanley, a journalist embedded with Hancock’s troops, estimated that the total value of the property destroyed was at least $100,000.
sources_cited_by_source: Grinnell 1915, 238-243; ARCIA 1868, 310-314; Jones 1966; Hyde 1968, 262; Peace Commission Proceedings 1868, 35-39

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')

summary: Annuity goods were inferior (Captain Bogey, W.R. Irwin, William Bent); no promised hardware. Sand Creek indemnity and 1865 guaranteed land never received.
verbatim_quote: considered them all of inferior quality, “more so that [sic] any goods I ever saw delivered to the Indians.”

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct 28, 1867
summary: Big Head refused to sign unless children taken at Sand Creek were returned; investigator Jeff Campbell estimates up to 30 children taken. Commissioner John B. Sanborn moved that captured children be detained until a later meeting that apparently never occurred.
verbatim_quote: Big Head, who described himself as half chief and half Dog Soldier, said he would not sign anything unless the children who had been taken at Sand Creek were returned.
sources_cited_by_source: RIT 364 docs; Roberts 2016, 137; J. Campbell personal communication 2022; Indian Peace Commission 1868, 67
federal_account_contrast: Captive children used in treaty context; absent from federal treaty summary.
map_implication: Flag Medicine Lodge as negotiated while Sand Creek captive children were held.
notes: 30-children figure is single-source personal communication.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
place: Medicine Lodge Creek; Arkansas-South Platte hunting range; Smoky Hill; Big Bend
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct 28, 1867
summary: Talks stalled until Sen. John Henderson took Buffalo Chief aside privately; treaty then signed. Henderson's oral promises (hunting between Arkansas and South Platte if 10 miles from settlements; possibly no whites south of Arkansas) were never written into the treaty, later leading to Cheyenne-Arapaho being declared hostile.
verbatim_quote: Even though this provision for hunting between the Arkansas and South Platte Rivers was in Henderson’s summary, it was not included in the final treaty documents.
federal_account_contrast: Written treaty omits oral terms the Native signers relied upon.
map_implication: Draw 'orally promised hunting range 1867: Arkansas to South Platte' as promised-but-unwritten land.
notes: Sherman himself told subordinates the hunting right existed (Jones 182).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')

instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct 28, 1867; Executive Order reservation 1869
summary: Medicine Lodge reservation included Cherokee Outlet land the US did not own; water bitter in gypsum belt; Little Raven believed the reserve included land from Bent's Fort to the Rockies. Hazen declared them hostile in Sept 1868 for not being on a reservation; reserve only came by Grant's 1869 executive order.
verbatim_quote: The land given to the Cheyenne and Arapaho included land that belonged to the Cherokee and not to the government.
map_implication: Note Little Raven's understanding of reserve (Bent's Fort to Rockies) as divergent account.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct 28, 1867

verbatim_quote: This is an important amendment, although other sources do not mention it.
sources_cited_by_source: Brill 1938, Conquest of the Southern Plains, 95
notes: Single uncited source; TREC flags its own uncertainty.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct 28, 1867, Article VIII
summary: Farming aid capped at $100 first year and $25 for three years, when a pair of mules cost $120, a wagon $75, a yoke of oxen $80.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
nations: Cheyenne; Arapaho; Kiowa; Comanche; Sioux; all bison-reliant nations
place: Southern and northern plains; Colorado (Logan County, Lost Park)
instrument: Pocket veto of 1874 buffalo protection bill (Grant, on Delano's advice)
summary: Military and railroads aided buffalo slaughter: ammunition, excursions, driving herds to hunters. 1872-74: whites killed 3,158,730 vs 1,215,000 by tribes (Dodge). Bills of 1871, 1872 failed; 1874 bill pocket-vetoed; Sheridan lobbied Texas against protection. Bison-reliant nations still ~$3,100 lower per capita income (2010$).
