sources_cited_by_source: Dodge 1877, 140-143; Smits 1994, WHQ 25(3); Gard 1959; Hornaday 1889; Feir, Gillezeau & Jones 2022 (NBER)
federal_account_contrast: Not in treaty record; ICC paid nothing for it.
map_implication: Context layer; not a land category.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: Fort Laramie 1851; Fort Wise 1861; Little Arkansas 1865; Medicine Lodge 1867; Fort Laramie 1868
summary: TREC's four-part fraud theory: (1) signatures chosen by US, bypassing Council of 44; (2) oral agreements omitted; technical boundary language not understood; (3) pre-written, arbitrary annuity amounts not yet appropriated (none appropriated for 1867-68 treaties as of March 3, 1869); (4) treaties are contracts of adhesion that courts should construe for the weaker party.
verbatim_quote: the treaty process was “a fraud from beginning to end, manipulated, directed, and controlled by Indian agents and superintendents
sources_cited_by_source: Calloway 2013, 175; Roberts 1984, 170-181; ARCIA 1868, 6; Prucha 1994, 229, 298-299 (Rep. Sidney Clarke quote); S. Rep. 156 (1867), 84-109
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats ratified treaties as consensual contracts.
map_implication: Add a 'consent quality' field to each Colorado treaty with these four tests.
notes: Clarke quote via Prucha is a congressional primary statement.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (Fraud Report, 'Fraud in Indian Country')
instrument: ICC Dockets 329-A and 329-B, Cheyenne-Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma, compromise settlement (1965)
summary: ICC valued 51,210,000 acres at $23,500,000 as of Oct 14, 1865 (about $0.46/acre), no interest, all further claims barred. Tribal appraiser Holbrook found $1.81/acre net from 8,645 Colorado transfers 1860-65; government expert Homer Hoyt used Spanish grant sales at $0.02/acre grazing, $0.20/acre irrigable bottomland. Nothing for bison, lives, or destroyed villages.
verbatim_quote: Thus, the settlement amount was based on a land valuation of approximately $.46 per acre.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC 1965 Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement, Dockets 329-A, 329-B
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats ICC award as final extinguishment; TREC calls the valuation 'fraudulently low'.
map_implication: On Royce 426/477 show ICC award, value per acre, and that $1.25/acre was the contemporary federal sale price.
notes: TREC does not state the actual compromise payment (believed $15 million, verify). Attorney William Payne billed on estimated hours (12,000 hrs). source_doc: Howard Zinn, A People's History of the United States (1980; later eds.), ch. 7 'As Long as Grass Grows or Water Runs' (non-Native author)
instrument: Treaty with the Creeks, March 24, 1832 (Cusseta/Washington); Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, Sept. 27, 1830; Chickasaw treaties of 1832-34
instrument_cite: 7 Stat. 366 (Creek 1832); 7 Stat. 333 (Choctaw 1830) [cites from atlas/Kappler, not from Zinn]
summary: Zinn argues that removal-era treaties, made under pressure and by deception, broke tribal land into individual allotments, which exposed holders to speculators and land-company fraud. Creeks and Choctaws who stayed on allotments were defrauded in large numbers.
verbatim_quote: Treaties made under pressure and by deception broke up Creek, Choctaw, and Chickasaw tribal lands into individual holdings, making each person a prey to contractors, speculators, and politicians.
sources_cited_by_source: Zinn relies on secondary works, chiefly Dale Van Every, Disinherited (1966), and Michael Rogin, Fathers and Children (1975); also Grant Foreman, Indian Removal (1932).
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler record the 1832 Creek treaty as a cession with individual reserves; it does not show that the reserves were mostly lost to fraud within a few years.
map_implication: On Creek 1832 and Choctaw 1830 polygons, add a 'reserved allotments lost to fraud' layer note; do not show the allotments as consensual sales.
notes: Quote text surfaced in a search-result excerpt of the chapter (historyisaweapon.com mirror), page not seen; verify against print edition (Harper Perennial 2003 ed., ch. 7). Zinn is synthesis, not original research: cite the underlying works (Saunt 2020; Haveman 2016) for atlas claims.

Zinn uses it to show that the promise of a permanent western homeland was itself part of the coercion, and that it was broken within a generation (Indian Territory allotment, Curtis Act 1898).
verbatim_quote: They can live upon it, they and all their children, as long as grass grows or water runs, in peace and plenty.
federal_account_contrast: The federal record presents Indian Territory patents as permanent guarantees; later allotment and statehood erased them. The promise itself is a primary source the atlas can quote.
map_implication: Link Indian Territory 'promised land' polygons (1830s patents to Five Tribes) to V044 (Curtis Act) and V047 (McGirt) as LAND_PROMISED_THEN_TAKEN.
notes: Quote is from the Oct. 15, 1829 Haley draft (Papers of Andrew Jackson). Which version Zinn quotes was not confirmed.

source_doc: Howard Zinn, A People's History, ch. 1 'Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress' and ch. 7 (historiographic assessment)
summary: Zinn's ch. 1 reframes 1492 through Bartolome de las Casas and the Taino ('Arawaks'), and argues historians bury atrocity in footnotes. Limits: almost no Native-authored or tribal-archive sources; heavy reliance on Euro-American secondary works; Native people appear mostly as victims; critics (including sympathetic ones) fault selective quotation (e.g., of Samuel Eliot Morison).
sources_cited_by_source: Las Casas, History of the Indies; Samuel Eliot Morison, Admiral of the Ocean Sea; Hans Koning, Columbus: His Enterprise; ch. 7 relies on Van Every, Rogin, Foreman.
federal_account_contrast: Not a federal record; useful as a popular counter-narrative but not as authority for specific land facts.
map_implication: Use Zinn only as a pedagogical framing cite (G4), never as the sole source for a polygon flag. Prefer Native-authored works (Dunbar-Ortiz, Blackhawk, Estes) and specialist monographs (Saunt, Ostler).
notes: 'Arawak' is Zinn's term; current usage is Taino. Critique summary from secondary sources (Wikipedia article on the book; reviews), not read directly this session. Treuer's critique of victim-only narratives (WEB-HIS-021) applies.

source_doc: Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz, An Indigenous Peoples' History of the United States (2014), chapters incl. 'The Doctrine of Discovery', '"Indian Country"', 'US Triumphalism and Peacetime Colonialism'
summary: The book argues that US expansion was settler colonialism: land theft was the goal, not a by-product, and treaties, the Doctrine of Discovery and 'Indian Country' as a military term were tools of it. It insists that Native resistance was continuous and that the US is an empire, not a nation that 'grew'.
sources_cited_by_source: Synthesis; draws on Jodi Byrd, The Transit of Empire (2011), and broad secondary literature.
federal_account_contrast: Royce's cession schedule implies an orderly series of purchases. The book reads the same sequence as conquest with paperwork.
map_implication: Supports the atlas's G2/G3 move away from 'ceded' as the default fill and toward 'transferred / taken' categories with evidence levels.
notes: AUTHOR IDENTITY: Dunbar-Ortiz is not an enrolled citizen of any nation. She earlier described Cheyenne and then Cherokee maternal descent; on C-SPAN2 in 2021 she said 'probably my mother was not Cherokee and I certainly would not call myself Cherokee.' Critics (Jacqueline Keeler open letter; reported Suzan Shown Harjo inquiry) call the earlier claims false. The brief's 'Wyandot/Chickasaw' label is not supported by anything found; do not use it. Attribute her as a historian and activist, not as a Native author.

source_doc: Vine Deloria Jr. (Standing Rock Sioux), Behind the Trail of Broken Treaties: An Indian Declaration of Independence (Delacorte 1974; Univ. of Texas Press reprint 1985)
place: Washington DC (BIA occupation Nov. 1972); Wounded Knee SD
instrument: Indian Appropriations Act of March 3, 1871 (end of treaty-making); Trail of Broken Treaties 'Twenty Points' (Oct. 1972)
summary: Deloria argues that the 1871 end of treaty-making was a unilateral US act, that tribes are international actors whose treaties remain binding, and that the Twenty Points' call to restore treaty-making and a treaty commission was legally sound.
sources_cited_by_source: Twenty Points position paper (1972); treaty texts; international law sources.
federal_account_contrast: The federal record treats 1871 as the end of the treaty era. Deloria treats it as an unconsented change in a bilateral relationship, and the post-1871 'agreements' as treaties in substance.
map_implication: Add a timeline note at 1871: 'US stopped making treaties by statute; nations did not agree.' Treat post-1871 agreements (e.g., 1876 Black Hills 'agreement') as treaty-type instruments subject to the same consent tests.
notes: Characterization from Choice review and Framing Red Power archive; not read in full this session. The Twenty Points text itself should be sourced separately.

source_doc: Vine Deloria Jr., Custer Died for Your Sins: An Indian Manifesto (1969), ch. 2 'Laws and Treaties'
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, April 29, 1868
summary: Deloria says the book's title refers to US bad faith on the 1868 Sioux treaty, and the 'Laws and Treaties' chapter sets US claims to honor international agreements against its record of breaking its treaties with tribes (commonly summarized as 400+).
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the 1877 Act as lawful abrogation (Lone Wolf logic); Deloria frames it as breach.
map_implication: Supports V024 (Black Hills) framing as LAND_PROMISED_THEN_TAKEN.
notes: 'Over 400 treaties' figure is from a study-guide summary; Deloria's exact number not checked. Do not display the number without the page.

source_doc: Vine Deloria Jr. and Raymond J. DeMallie, Documents of American Indian Diplomacy: Treaties, Agreements, and Conventions, 1775-1979 (Univ. of Oklahoma Press, 1999), 2 vols., 1,540 pp.
summary: A companion to Kappler that adds instruments Kappler omitted: unratified treaties, treaties the Senate amended and the nations then rejected, intertribal treaties, treaties with states and with the Confederacy, and post-1871 agreements. Publisher says many were 'either remained unratified by Congress or were rejected by the Indians themselves after the Senate amended them.'
sources_cited_by_source: Each entry gives its archival source (NARA RG 75/RG 11 and others).
federal_account_contrast: Kappler vol. 2 and the NARA ratified series show only ratified instruments; Royce maps only those. Deloria-DeMallie is the main published source for the unratified and rejected-amendment set.
map_implication: Use Deloria-DeMallie as the source list to build an UNRATIFIED and SENATE_AMENDED_NO_CONSENT layer (e.g., the 18 California treaties of 1851-52, V054). Cross-check against Indiana University 'Unratified Treaties' project.
notes: Exact count of unratified entries not found online; a bookseller says '350+ treaties and agreements' in total. Already cited in bibliography via Great Plains Quarterly review [A1], but not yet used as a data source.

source_doc: Nick Estes (citizen, Lower Brule Sioux Tribe), Our History Is the Future: Standing Rock Versus the Dakota Access Pipeline, and the Long Tradition of Indigenous Resistance (Verso, 2019)
nations: Oceti Sakowin; Lower Brule; Crow Creek; Standing Rock; Cheyenne River; Yankton
place: Missouri River: Oahe, Big Bend, Fort Randall, Garrison, Gavins Point dams
instrument: Flood Control Act of Dec. 22, 1944 (Pick-Sloan) and later taking acts for each reservation
summary: Estes places the Pick-Sloan dams in a single line of dispossession from the 1851 and 1868 Fort Laramie treaties to DAPL. He writes from Lower Brule, flooded by Big Bend Dam, with Oahe upriver. A congressional document puts Pick-Sloan flooding at about 356,254 acres of tribal land and over 900 families relocated.
verbatim_quote: in places like Lower Brule, where I'm from, they built the Big Bend Dam, and then, upriver from there, they built the Oahe Dam
sources_cited_by_source: Estes cites Michael Lawson, Dammed Indians (1982; rev. 2009) and tribal and congressional records (per standard reception; not checked page by page).
federal_account_contrast: Royce ends in 1894 and shows these reservations as unchanged 'reserved' land. The 20th-century takings do not appear on Royce at all.
map_implication: Extend V028/V029 to Lower Brule and Crow Creek (Big Bend, Fort Randall) and Yankton (Fort Randall). Draw the reservoir footprints as 20th-century takings inside reserved land.
notes: Quote is from Estes on Democracy Now (March 22, 2019), not the book. 356,254 acres is from a congressional document (NARF NILL P.L. 111-357 file), not Estes. Estes's 1851 treaty-territory argument not checked in text.

source_doc: Ned Blackhawk (enrolled, Te-Moak Tribe of Western Shoshone), Violence over the Land: Indians and Empires in the Early American West (Harvard UP, 2006)
summary: Blackhawk argues that Spanish, Mexican and American expansion brought violence and slave trading into the Great Basin, and that the 'terrible stillness' Americans saw there was the product of three centuries of colonial violence, not an ancient emptiness. Many Utes became raiders and slave traffickers as a survival strategy, at great cost.
sources_cited_by_source: Spanish and Mexican colonial archives, US military and agency records.
federal_account_contrast: Federal treaty records for the Great Basin (Ruby Valley 1863, Box Elder 1863, Ute 1868) start in the 1860s and imply sparse, 'unoccupied' land; Blackhawk shows the emptiness was produced.
map_implication: Avoid any 'sparsely populated' or 'unoccupied' language for Great Basin polygons; add context to V035, V036, V039.
notes: NAISA Book of the Decade. 'Terrible stillness' phrase is from Wallace Stegner, quoted by Blackhawk.

source_doc: Ned Blackhawk, The Rediscovery of America: Native Peoples and the Unmaking of U.S. History (Yale UP, 2023); 2023 National Book Award, Nonfiction
summary: Blackhawk argues Native peoples were central to every century of US development and that US history must be rewritten around that fact, rather than treating Native history as a prelude or an afterword.
verbatim_quote: How can a nation founded on the homelands of dispossessed Indigenous peoples be the world's most exemplary democracy?
federal_account_contrast: Royce-based maps end at 1894 and imply that Native history ends with cession.
map_implication: Time slider should continue past 1894 into present-day governments, land returns (F3), and treaty-rights cases, so the map does not end with loss.
notes: Quote as reported from the book's introduction in Yale and press coverage.

source_doc: Walter R. Echo-Hawk (Pawnee), In the Courts of the Conqueror: The 10 Worst Indian Law Cases Ever Decided (Fulcrum, 2010)
summary: Echo-Hawk's ten cases (chapter subtitles from the table of contents): Johnson v. M'Intosh (how the Indians lost legal title to America); Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (shutting the courthouse doors); Conners v. United States & Cheyenne Indians (were the Indian wars legal?); Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (breaking the treaties); United States v. Sandoval (rule by guardianship); Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States (confiscating indigenous habitat); In re Adoption of John Doe v. Heim (taking the kids); Wana the Bear v. Community Construction (taking the dead); Lyng v. Northwest Indian Cemetery Protective Ass'n (taking the holy places); Employment Division v. Smith (taking the religion).
sources_cited_by_source: Opinions; litigation records; Echo-Hawk's NARF experience.
federal_account_contrast: The atlas case overlays describe holdings neutrally. Echo-Hawk shows that these holdings remain 'good law' that legalizes takings and argues for a UNDRIP-based repudiation.
map_implication: Tag the atlas case records for Johnson, Cherokee Nation, Lone Wolf, Tee-Hit-Ton, Lyng and Smith with 'Echo-Hawk Ten Worst' and add Conners (1898) and Sandoval (1913) as missing case records. Conners matters for any 'depredation' framing.
notes: Table of contents confirmed via Austrian Academy of Sciences catalog and Google Books listing.

source_doc: Walter Echo-Hawk, In the Courts of the Conqueror, chapter on Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955)
instrument: Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955)
summary: Tee-Hit-Ton held that aboriginal (unrecognized) title is not property protected by the Fifth Amendment, so the US could take Tlingit timber without compensation. Echo-Hawk calls this 'confiscating indigenous habitat'; Williams (Like a Loaded Weapon) shows the opinion's reliance on the language of Indian 'savagery'.
federal_account_contrast: The federal record calls this a settled title rule; Native scholars call it a racialized confiscation rule.
map_implication: Add a doctrine note on doctrine-aboriginal-title: any NEVER_CEDED polygon is, under Tee-Hit-Ton, takeable without compensation. That is the legal meaning of 'unceded' land in US law.

source_doc: Robert A. Williams Jr. (Lumbee), The American Indian in Western Legal Thought: The Discourses of Conquest (Oxford UP, 1990)
instrument: Johnson v. M'Intosh, 21 U.S. (8 Wheat.) 543 (1823)
summary: Williams traces the Doctrine of Discovery from the Crusades and papal bulls through English colonial charters to Marshall's opinion in Johnson v. M'Intosh, arguing that US Indian title law rests on a medieval Christian discourse that denied non-Christian peoples full rights to land.
sources_cited_by_source: Canon law, papal bulls (e.g., Inter Caetera 1493), colonial charters, Marshall opinions.
federal_account_contrast: Atlas doctrine-discovery record treats Johnson as a property-law holding; Williams shows it as a racial and religious hierarchy imported into US law.
map_implication: doctrine-discovery record: add Williams as the genealogy source and the 2023 Vatican note (WEB-HIS-037) with its limits.
notes: Contents not read this session; characterization is standard and confirmed by author bio and catalog.

source_doc: Robert A. Williams Jr. (Lumbee), Like a Loaded Weapon: The Rehnquist Court, Indian Rights, and the Legal History of Racism in America (Univ. of Minnesota Press, 2005)
instrument: Tee-Hit-Ton (1955); Oliphant v. Suquamish, 435 U.S. 191 (1978)
summary: Williams argues that racist language about Indian 'savagery' in Marshall-era opinions still functions 'like a loaded weapon' in modern Supreme Court cases, with chapters on the language of savagery in Tee-Hit-Ton and Rehnquist's language in Oliphant. He calls on the Court to repudiate these precedents.
verbatim_quote: like a loaded weapon
sources_cited_by_source: Opinions; Justice Jackson's Korematsu dissent is the source of the title metaphor.
federal_account_contrast: Court records present precedent as neutral; Williams shows the stereotype doing legal work.
map_implication: When quoting old opinions in case records, add a content note where the opinion uses 'savage' or similar language, and say the precedent is still cited.

source_doc: Lindsay G. Robertson, Conquest by Law: How the Discovery of America Dispossessed Indigenous Peoples of Their Lands (Oxford UP, 2005) (non-Native author)
instrument: Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823); Illinois Company purchase 1773, Wabash Company purchase 1775
summary: Using the Illinois and Wabash Land Companies' corporate records (found in 1991), Robertson shows Johnson v. M'Intosh was an arranged, collusive suit brought to win recognition of the companies' titles; the plaintiffs reportedly helped arrange the defense. The discovery doctrine was announced in a case with no Native party.
sources_cited_by_source: United Illinois and Wabash Land Companies records (Brinton family papers), now open access.
federal_account_contrast: Atlas case record (case-johnson-v-mintosh-1823) gives the holding but not that no Native nation was a party and the dispute was manufactured.
map_implication: Add to case-johnson-v-mintosh-1823: 'No Native nation was a party. Historian Lindsay Robertson found evidence the case was arranged by the land companies.'
notes: Detail about plaintiffs paying defense counsel came from a commentator citing Robertson, not checked in the book; keep as 'Robertson found evidence the case was arranged'.

source_doc: Stuart Banner, How the Indians Lost Their Land: Law and Power on the Frontier (Harvard UP, 2005) (non-Native author)
summary: Banner argues neither 'simple coercion' nor 'simple consent' explains land transfers; what mattered was who controlled the legal framework. Early purchases were real bargains when settlers were weak; as power shifted, the form of purchase stayed while the substance became coercion. Power operated through law.
sources_cited_by_source: Colonial deeds, treaty records, statutes, court cases.
federal_account_contrast: Royce presents each cession as a purchase. Banner gives a scholarly basis for treating the same legal form as meaning different things in different decades.
map_implication: Support for a time-varying consent scale in G2: do not apply one label ('ceded') across 1790 and 1890. Add an era-based caution on cession records.
notes: Some Native scholars read Banner as too generous to the purchase narrative; use alongside Saunt and Ostler. Reviews: Eric Foner, LRB 2006; Kades, Law & Social Inquiry 2008.

source_doc: Jean M. O'Brien (White Earth Ojibwe), Firsting and Lasting: Writing Indians out of Existence in New England (Univ. of Minnesota Press, 2010)
nations: Wampanoag; Nipmuc; Mohegan; Pequot; Narragansett; (southern New England)
summary: From more than 600 local histories (1820-1880), O'Brien shows how settlers claimed to be 'first' to found civilization and named Indians as the 'last' of their people, even while Native communities lived on in the same towns. Erasure served to refute Indian claims to land and rights.
federal_account_contrast: New England is largely blank on Royce and federal treaty maps because colonial and state deeds, not US treaties, took the land. A blank map repeats the 'lasting' narrative.
map_implication: Do not leave New England blank or 'pre-federal'. Show colony and state takings (V058 Maine, Mashpee, Rhode Island 1978) and present-day nations. Avoid 'last of the X' captions anywhere.

source_doc: Lisa Brooks (Abenaki), Our Beloved Kin: A New History of King Philip's War (Yale UP, 2018); 2019 Bancroft Prize; digital companion 'Our Beloved Kin: Remapping a New History of King Philip's War'
place: Pocasset (Tiverton/Fall River area); Nipmuc country; Plymouth Colony
summary: Brooks retells the 'First Indian War' through Weetamoo, saunkskwa (female leader) of Pocasset, and James Printer (Nipmuc), using land deeds, court records and Indigenous geography. She shows colonial deeds and mortgages, often with unauthorized or pressured signers, as the cause of the war rather than a background detail.
sources_cited_by_source: Plymouth Colony deeds and court records; Mary Rowlandson narrative; Native place-names.
federal_account_contrast: Pre-federal colonial land transfers are outside Royce entirely.
map_implication: Use Brooks's digital maps as a model for Indigenous place-names and routes; any New England layer should cite colonial deeds and their disputes.
notes: Brooks is a member of the Abenaki community (Odanak/Missisquoi connections reported); exact citizenship wording not confirmed. Chapter: 'Namumpum, our beloved kinswoman, Saunkskwa of Pocasset: bonds, acts, deeds.' Also author of The Common Pot (2008).

source_doc: David Treuer (Ojibwe, Leech Lake), The Heartbeat of Wounded Knee: Native America from 1890 to the Present (Riverhead, 2019)
summary: Treuer writes against Dee Brown's Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee, which ended Native history in 1890. He argues the years 1890-1934 brought assaults on Indians and their homelands 'perhaps at their most creative, if not their bloodiest' (allotment, boarding schools), and that Native nations survived and rebuilt.
federal_account_contrast: Royce's schedule stops in 1894, so a Royce map shows the end of land loss exactly when allotment loss was accelerating (about two-thirds of the remaining land base lost 1887-1934).
map_implication: Add allotment-era loss inside reservations as its own layer (V045); the map must not stop at Royce's end date or imply 'the end' in 1890.
notes: Quote is from a review describing Treuer's characterization; check exact wording in book. 'Two-thirds' figure is the standard 138 million to 48 million acres (1887-1934); cite D3, not Treuer.

source_doc: Claudio Saunt, Unworthy Republic: The Dispossession of Native Americans and the Road to Indian Territory (Norton, 2020); Bancroft Prize 2021 (non-Native author)
nations: Cherokee; Muscogee (Creek); Choctaw; Chickasaw; Seminole; Potawatomi; others
instrument: Indian Removal Act, May 28, 1830
summary: Saunt argues removal of about 80,000 people was a contested political act that passed Congress narrowly, was 'abetted by southern slave owners and financed by Wall Street,' and that removed nations paid for their own removal from the proceeds of their land. Chapters include 'Financing dispossession' and 'A combination of designing speculators'.
sources_cited_by_source: Removal Act debates; Office of Indian Affairs records; bank and land-office records.
federal_account_contrast: Royce lists removal treaties as land-for-land exchanges; Saunt shows the land sales enriched speculators and the nations were charged the costs.
map_implication: On removal-era cessions (Royce Southeast areas 1830-1838), add 'removal costs charged to the nation from land proceeds' only where the treaty text says so (verify per treaty).
notes: Removal Act House vote 102-97 (May 26, 1830) is standard; verify. Saunt's Aeon essay already in bibliography [G1,G2,G4].

source_doc: Creek allotment fraud: Saunt, Unworthy Republic; Christopher Haveman, Rivers of Sand (2016) (non-Native authors)
instrument: Treaty with the Creeks, March 24, 1832
summary: The 1832 treaty did not remove the Creeks; it reserved 6,696 sections and half-sections to Creek heads of family. Speculators bought or defrauded most of these, and the resulting violence was labeled the 'Creek War of 1836', which became the pretext for forced removal.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text; land-office and 'frauds' investigations (1830s Congressional documents).
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats the 1832 treaty as a full cession of Creek land east of the Mississippi; in text it was a guarantee of individual reserves.
map_implication: Draw 1832 Creek territory as LAND_PROMISED_RESERVED (individual reserves) then LAND_PROMISED_THEN_TAKEN via fraud; add 1836 forced removal as REMOVAL.
notes: Sections count from Haveman (Project MUSE abstract). Treaty name varies (Cusseta / Washington).

source_doc: Benjamin Madley, An American Genocide: The United States and the California Indian Catastrophe, 1846-1873 (Yale UP, 2016), incl. appendices of killings (non-Native author)
nations: California Native peoples (Yuki, Tolowa, Wintu, Pomo, many others)
instrument: 18 unratified treaties of 1851-52; California militia expeditions; Act for the Government and Protection of Indians (1850)
summary: Madley counts between 9,492 and 16,094 California Indians killed by vigilantes, militia and soldiers (likely an undercount), with population falling from perhaps 150,000 to 30,000. State and federal governments spent at least $1.7 million on campaigns, and officials gave legal protection, money and arms to the killers.
sources_cited_by_source: State militia records; newspapers; federal reports; appendices list incidents individually.
federal_account_contrast: California land is mostly 'unceded' on Royce (the 1851-52 treaties were rejected) yet shown as US land. Madley shows how it was taken: by killing, not by treaty.
map_implication: Color California NEVER_CEDED / TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT (strengthen V054) and add a massacre point layer from Madley's appendices (with tribal review).
notes: Gary Anderson counters that violent deaths were far fewer ('no more than 2,000' per Wikipedia summary) and rejects the genocide label: CONTESTED on totals, not on the pattern. Newsom (2019) used 'genocide' officially.

source_doc: Jeffrey Ostler, Surviving Genocide: Native Nations and the United States from the American Revolution to Bleeding Kansas (Yale UP, 2019) (non-Native author); also The Lakotas and the Black Hills (2010)
nations: Nations east of the Mississippi; removed nations in Kansas
summary: Ostler argues that US democracy relied on Indian dispossession and on wars officials called 'just and lawful' to remove and kill Native people who resisted, and that removal continued despite known mass death, which amounts to genocide. He stresses Native survival through alliance, defense and rebuilding.
verbatim_quote: just and lawful
sources_cited_by_source: Federal and military records; removal mortality data.
federal_account_contrast: Northwest Ordinance (1787) promised 'utmost good faith' and 'just and lawful wars'; Ostler shows that phrase was used to authorize the wars that preceded Greenville (1795) and later cessions.
map_implication: Link V004 (Greenville) and stat-northwest-ordinance-1787 to a DURESS_MILITARY flag: Greenville followed Fallen Timbers and the 1790-94 war.
notes: 'just and lawful wars' is the Northwest Ordinance's own phrase (Art. 3); verified there, not in Ostler's text.

source_doc: Gary Clayton Anderson, Ethnic Cleansing and the Indian: The Crime That Should Haunt America (Univ. of Oklahoma Press, 2014); Massacre in Minnesota: The Dakota War of 1862 (OU Press, 2019) (non-Native author)
instrument: Treaties of Traverse des Sioux (July 23, 1851) and Mendota (Aug. 5, 1851)
summary: Anderson argues US policy is better called ethnic cleansing than genocide: the aim was land, not extermination. In Massacre in Minnesota and public talks he says most of the money promised the Dakota for southern Minnesota was diverted to traders and others.
sources_cited_by_source: Agency and treaty records; trader claims.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows 1851 Dakota cessions as purchases; Anderson documents that the purchase price largely did not reach the sellers.
map_implication: Flag Royce 1851 Dakota cession areas ANNUITY_THEFT (see WEB-HIS-034). Note Anderson's 'ethnic cleansing' label as a scholarly alternative to 'genocide' where the atlas discusses terms.
notes: Dollar figures ($540,000 promised vs about $50,000 received) come from a newspaper report of a 2019 talk (New Ulm Journal) and look inconsistent with treaty totals; do not use without the book. Reviewers (ICT) criticize his genocide denial.

source_doc: Maine Wabanaki-State Child Welfare Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Beyond the Mandate: Continuing the Conversation (June 14, 2015)
nations: Wabanaki: Penobscot; Passamaquoddy (Indian Township, Pleasant Point); Maliseet (Houlton Band); Mi'kmaq (Aroostook Band)
instrument: TRC Mandate signed Feb. 2013 by five chiefs and Gov. Paul LePage; Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act 1980 (context)
summary: First US truth commission on Indigenous child welfare. It found Wabanaki children entered foster care at an average of five times the rate of non-Native children (2002-2013), and that this could be understood within continued cultural genocide as defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention. It named institutional racism, historical trauma, and sovereignty and jurisdiction disputes under MICSA as root causes.
sources_cited_by_source: Statements from 150+ participants; state child welfare data.
federal_account_contrast: The atlas treats MICSA (V058) as a land settlement; the TRC ties MICSA's jurisdiction limits to ongoing child removal.
map_implication: Add the TRC to V058 and stat-maine-indian-claims-settlement-act-1980 as present-day harm linked to the settlement's jurisdiction terms.
notes: Full PDF at mainewabanakitrc.org (not opened this session).

source_doc: California Truth and Healing Council, Executive Order N-15-19 (Gov. Gavin Newsom, June 18, 2019)
instrument: Executive Order N-15-19; Gov. Peter Burnett's 1851 message ('war of extermination') is the record the apology answers
summary: Newsom formally apologized for the state's role and called the history genocide, and created a tribally led council to record Native narratives and recommend restorative steps. The final report was due to the Governor by 2025; regional hearings ran into 2025. Publication status not confirmed.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows California as acquired by the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; the state now officially names the means as genocide.
map_implication: Cite EO N-15-19 on California polygons as an official state acknowledgment; check tribalaffairs.ca.gov for the final report before launch.
notes: Burnett quote widely cited; verify from Journal of the Senate of California, 1851, before display.

source_doc: US Dept. of the Interior, Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report, Vol. I (May 11, 2022) and Vol. II (July 30, 2024)
nations: American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian
instrument: Civilization Fund Act 1819 and later appropriations; boarding school provisions in treaties
summary: Vol. I: 408 federal schools (1819-1969), at least 53 burial sites, and a finding that the system pursued assimilation and Indian territorial dispossession together. Vol. II: 417 institutions, at least 973 documented child deaths, 74 burial sites at 65 schools, over $23.3 billion (FY2023 dollars) appropriated 1871-1969, and 8 recommendations starting with a formal apology. Vol. II counted treaties with education provisions used to support the system.
federal_account_contrast: Treaty education clauses look like benefits in Kappler; DOI itself now says the schools served land dispossession.
map_implication: Add boarding school points to each nation's page and tag treaties with education articles; link to D1. Biden's apology (Oct. 25, 2024, Gila River) answers recommendation 1.
notes: Bibliography already lists DOI pages [D1, D4]; the '127 vs 171 treaties' discrepancy noted there still needs resolution from the Vol. II PDF.

source_doc: US Congress, Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War, 'Massacre of Cheyenne Indians' (Report, 38th Cong., 2d Sess., 1865); Joint Special Committee on the Condition of the Indian Tribes (Doolittle Committee), Sen. Rep. No. 156, 39th Cong., 2d Sess. (Jan. 26, 1867)
place: Sand Creek, Kiowa County CO (approx. 38.54 N, 102.51 W); Bosque Redondo NM
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise (1861); Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Oct. 14, 1865, Art. VI (reparations)
summary: Congress's own committee found the Cheyenne and Arapaho at Sand Creek under Black Kettle, White Antelope and Left Hand had been friendly and called the attack a 'foul and dastardly massacre.' The Doolittle report's appendix includes 'The Chivington Massacre' (pp. 26-98) and Carleton's treatment of the Navajo, and concluded Native populations were declining due to white aggression, game loss and land loss. The US admitted guilt in Little Arkansas Art. VI, but reparations to most descendants were never paid (Congress said so in 1998).
verbatim_quote: foul and dastardly massacre
sources_cited_by_source: Sworn testimony (Silas Soule, others); officer reports.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the 1865 Little Arkansas and 1867 Medicine Lodge cessions without noting they followed and were shaped by the massacre and an admission of US guilt.
map_implication: Strengthen V021: mark Little Arkansas (1865) as signed less than a year after a federally admitted massacre; add Art. VI unpaid reparations as ANNUITY_THEFT / unpaid obligation; cite Pub. L. 105-243 (1998), 112 Stat. 1579.
notes: Coordinates are approximate NPS site location; verify. Report is often cited as Sen. Rep. 142 (vol. with JCCW reports).

source_doc: Apology Resolution, Pub. L. 103-150, 107 Stat. 1510 (Nov. 23, 1993); Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs, 556 U.S. 163 (2009)
instrument: Joint Resolution to acknowledge the 100th anniversary of the overthrow (1993); Newlands Resolution 1898
summary: Congress found that Native Hawaiians never directly relinquished their claims to sovereignty or national lands. In 2009 the Supreme Court held the resolution's 'whereas' clauses and conciliatory verbs create no enforceable rights and do not stop the state from selling 'ceded lands'.
verbatim_quote: never directly relinquished their claims to their inherent sovereignty as a people or over their national lands to the United States
federal_account_contrast: State and federal records still call the Crown and Government lands 'ceded lands', though Congress itself found they were never relinquished.
map_implication: V061: replace 'ceded lands' with 'Crown and Government lands (called "ceded lands" in state law)'; color as TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT.
notes: Quote from memory of resolution text, consistent with search snippets; verify exact wording at govinfo before display.

source_doc: Apology to Native Peoples of the United States, Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2010, Pub. L. 111-118, Sec. 8113 (signed Dec. 19, 2009); originally S.J. Res. 14 (Brownback)
nations: All Native Peoples of the United States
summary: The US apologized 'for the many instances of violence, maltreatment, and neglect' but placed the apology inside a defense spending bill, with no signing ceremony or public reading, and with a disclaimer that it authorizes no claim against the United States and settles none.
verbatim_quote: Nothing in this section (1) authorizes or supports any claim against the United States; or (2) serves as a settlement of any claim against the United States.
federal_account_contrast: Shows the US acknowledging wrong while closing the door on remedy, the same pattern as the 1993 Hawaii resolution and ICC payments.
map_implication: Add to D1/timeline; use in the 'apology without remedy' tour with 1993 and the 2024 boarding school apology.
notes: Disclaimer wording confirmed in reproductions (wirelesshogan, wellbriety); confirm Stat. page. Not read publicly until Brownback read it at the Congressional Cemetery in May 2010 (reported; verify).

source_doc: People of the Sacred Land, Truth, Restoration and Education Commission (TREC) of Colorado, Final Reports (legal and education reports, June 2024); AP coverage June 14, 2024
nations: 10 nations with title in Colorado incl. Cheyenne, Arapaho (Northern, Southern), Ute (per report; list not confirmed online)
summary: TREC found Colorado was built on about $1.7 trillion of Indigenous homelands taken by the state and the US, with at least $546 million in state mineral revenue, and that many transactions violated treaty rights or lacked legal title for transfer. source_doc: Indian Claims Commission critique: Encyclopedia of the Great Plains (UNL) 'Indian Claims Commission'; EBSCO Research Starters; Harvey D. Rosenthal, Their Day in Court (1990); Lieder & Page, Wild Justice (1997) (latter two not read)
instrument: Indian Claims Commission Act, Aug. 13, 1946
summary: ICC awards were money only; return of land was excluded. Value was fixed at the date of taking (often 19th-century prices) and generally without interest; awards were reduced by 'gratuitous offsets' for past federal spending; attorney fees came out of awards; tribes bore the burden of proof and research costs. Accepting an award, or a dismissal, extinguished the claim.
federal_account_contrast: ICC dockets are usually presented as compensation for land 'taken'; in effect the ICC converted unceded or underpaid land into finally extinguished title for a historical price.
map_implication: Every polygon with an ICC award should show: date-of-taking valuation, interest (none/yes), offsets, and 'land not returned.' Add an ICC_OUTCOME badge distinct from 'ceded'.
notes: The ICC Act capped attorney fees at 10% of the award (Sec. 15) - from memory, verify in 60 Stat. 1049. The 'about $1.3 billion total' figure not confirmed this session.
