place: Boa Ogoi (Bear River at Beaver Creek), near Preston, Franklin Co ID; approx 42.10,-111.91 (APPROXIMATE; NHL boundary)
instrument: Treaty of Box Elder (Northwestern Shoshone) 1863-07-30; Fort Bridger 1863-07-02 (Eastern Shoshone); Ruby Valley 1863-10-01 (Western Shoshone); Tooele Valley 1863-10-12 (Goshute)
summary: Col. Patrick Edward Connor's California Volunteers attacked the winter camp at Boa Ogoi at dawn, killing 250 to 500 people, many women and children. Within nine months federal commissioners concluded the 1863 Shoshone and Goshute 'peace and friendship' treaties across the region.
verbatim_quote: No formal purchase of the territorial claim of these tribes or bands was made, but the U. S. took possession of the same
sources_cited_by_source: Royce 1899 Schedule remark on Ruby Valley (Royce 444), as transcribed in atlas
federal_account_contrast: Army called it the 'Battle of Bear River' and promoted Connor; the 1863 treaties appear as voluntary.
map_implication: Use 'Bear River Massacre' / Boa Ogoi / Wuda Ogwa naming; flag 1863 Shoshone treaties as signed after massacre; Royce 444 as no purchase.
notes: Deaths 250-500 (Smithsonian), up to 350 (TPL), 400+ (Deseret), about 500 (tribal official per BLM). NHL 1990. Tribe acquired 19 acres (2003, TPL) and about 550-650 acres (2017-18). Site name in Shoshone appears as Boa Ogoi and Wuda Ogwa in different sources; ask the Band which to use. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-SHO-A-011 (PSL pp. 105-106).

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Moses A. McLaughlin'; militarymuseum.org Owens Valley and Camp Independence; NPS Manzanar 'Owens Valley Paiute'; HistoryNet
nations: Owens Valley Paiute (Nuumu); Big Pine, Bishop, Lone Pine, Fort Independence Paiute descendants
date: 1862-03 (Alabama Hills raid); 1863 (killings under Capt. McLaughlin); 1863-07-10 forced march
place: Owens Valley, Inyo Co CA; Camp Independence approx 36.82,-118.19; Owens Lake approx 36.40,-117.95 (APPROXIMATE)
instrument: None. Forced march from Camp Independence to Fort Tejon (Sebastian Reserve), July 1863
summary: During the Owens Valley war of 1862-63 settlers and California Volunteers killed Paiute in several attacks, including a massacre of about 35 attributed to Capt. Moses McLaughlin. Over 1,000 Paiute were then marched about 200 miles to Fort Tejon in July 1863; by Jan 1864 only 380 remained there, many having fled home.
federal_account_contrast: No cession; the valley's land passed to the public domain with no instrument at all.
map_implication: Mark Owens Valley NEVER_CEDED; add removal route line Camp Independence to Fort Tejon.
notes: The specific 'Owens Lake massacre, March 1863, 35 killed' could not be confirmed; McLaughlin is linked to a massacre of 35 and to the 1863 Keyesville massacre. Needs a primary or Madley cite before mapping a point.

source_doc: NPS Sand Creek Massacre NHS place page and stories page; atlas violations-seed.csv V021; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 426, 477
nations: Southern Cheyenne; Arapaho (Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes; Northern Cheyenne; Northern Arapaho)
place: Big Sandy Creek, Kiowa Co CO; approx 38.54,-102.51 (Sand Creek Massacre NHS)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise 1861-02-18 (before); Treaty of the Little Arkansas 1865-10-14 (after)
summary: About 675 men of the 1st and 3rd Colorado Cavalry under Col. John Chivington attacked Black Kettle's and White Antelope's camp, which flew a US flag, killing more than 230. Eleven months later the survivors ceded the Fort Wise reserve and their Colorado claims at the Little Arkansas, in a treaty that itself acknowledged the 'gross and wanton outrages'.
verbatim_quote: killed more than 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho over the course of seven hours
federal_account_contrast: Royce 477 shows the Fort Wise reserve 'Ceded by treaty of Oct. 14, 1865' with no mention of the massacre.
map_implication: Flag Royce 426 and 477 as ceded after massacre; already in atlas V021, add explicit massacre point and edge.
notes: Other counts: 'over 200' (NPS stories), 163 (eyewitness via Lonely Planet), about 150 (AP 2007); atlas V021 says 70 to over 600. NHS authorized 2000, established 2007.

source_doc: NPS Washita (Stop Six page; soldier online book); Plains Humanities Encyclopedia; ICT News; HMdb marker; atlas treaties-seed TLA-T-366 | PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes) | Researcher knowledge: NPS Washita Battlefield NHS interpretation; Hazen correspondence (Nov. 1868)
nations: Southern Cheyenne (Black Kettle's band); Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes
place: Washita River near Cheyenne, Roger Mills Co OK; approx 35.62,-99.69 (Washita Battlefield NHS)
instrument: Medicine Lodge Treaty (Cheyenne and Arapaho) 1867-10-28
summary: Lt. Col. George Custer's 7th Cavalry attacked Black Kettle's winter village in Sheridan's campaign to force Cheyenne bands onto the Medicine Lodge reservation, killing Black Kettle and his wife among others, and taking 53 women and children captive who were held to compel surrender.
federal_account_contrast: Custer claimed 103 warriors; Cheyenne counts are much lower and mostly noncombatants. Federal framing is treaty enforcement.
map_implication: Link point to Medicine Lodge Cheyenne-Arapaho reserve; flag subsequent compliance as obtained by force and hostage-holding.
notes: Deaths 13 to 150: Cheyenne count 13 men, 16 women, 9 children (marker); tribe 50-60 (ICT); NPS page 60 Cheyenne; Custer 103. 53 captives consistent. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): PSL-KCA-A-032 (PSL pp. 42), PSL-SCA-019 (PSL pp. 217), WEB-DUR-056.

source_doc: Montana Historical Society IEFA (Henderson, Montana Magazine 2018); Bozeman Daily Chronicle; Indianz 2012; EJI calendar; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 565, 692
nations: Piikani (Piegan / Blackfeet), Heavy Runner's band; Blackfeet Nation
place: Big Bend of the Marias River, MT; approx 48.4,-111.1 (APPROXIMATE, LOW confidence location; exact site not verified)
instrument: Executive order 1873-07-05 and Act of Apr 15, 1874 reducing Blackfeet reserve; Agreement 1888-05-01 (ratified 1888)
instrument_cite: 18 Stat. 28 [from memory, verify]; 25 Stat. 113 [from memory, verify]
summary: Maj. Eugene Baker's 2nd Cavalry attacked Heavy Runner's camp, which held papers of peace and was not the band sought; the Army counted 173 dead, mostly women, children and elders, and later accounts give 217 or more. Within four years the Blackfeet reservation was cut by executive order and statute without a treaty.
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the 1873-74 reductions as administrative; the land cut came without consent shortly after the massacre.
map_implication: Flag Royce 565 reductions as TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT, add massacre point once location verified.
notes: Causal link massacre -> 1873/74 reductions is temporal and contextual; do not state that one caused the other without a cite. Survivor breakdown 90 women, 50 children, 15 men (EJI).

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Camp Grant massacre'; U. Arizona Press, Jacoby 'Shadows at Dawn' / Colwell-Chanthaphonh 'Massacre at Camp Grant'; HistoryNet; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 541
nations: Aravaipa and Pinal Apache (San Carlos Apache Tribe descendants)
place: Aravaipa Creek near old Camp Grant, Pinal Co AZ; approx 32.85,-110.70 (APPROXIMATE)
instrument: Camp Grant reservation EO 1871-11-09; restored to public domain by EO 1872-12-14; San Carlos EO 1872-12-14
summary: A party of Tucson Anglo-Americans (William Oury), Mexican Americans (Jesus Maria Elias) and Tohono O'odham (Francisco Galerita) attacked Apache families living under Army protection, killing about 85 to 144, mostly women and children, and taking 27 to 30 or more children who were kept or sold. The Camp Grant reserve created afterwards was abolished in 1872.
sources_cited_by_source: Royce remark: Camp Grant Apache reservation approved 1871 and restored to public domain by EO 1872
federal_account_contrast: Perpetrators were tried in 1871 and acquitted; the reserve's revocation appears in Royce only as an executive act.
map_implication: Link to Royce 541 'retroceded' polygon: flag TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT. Note intertribal participation carefully and in consultation with Tohono O'odham Nation and San Carlos Apache.
notes: 144 widely cited but not firm. Children captured: 27, 29, or 30+.

source_doc: NPS Big Hole National Battlefield (nps.gov/biho); NPS 1992 brochure; Wallowa Nez Perce; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 441, 442
nations: Nimiipuu (Nez Perce), non-treaty bands (Joseph, Looking Glass, White Bird, Toohoolhoolzote)
place: Big Hole Valley near Wisdom, Beaverhead Co MT; approx 45.65,-113.65 (Big Hole NB)
instrument: Nez Perce Treaty 1863-06-09 ('Thief Treaty', not signed by non-treaty bands)
summary: Col. John Gibbon's 7th Infantry and volunteers attacked the sleeping Nimiipuu camp at dawn, killing 60 to 90, of whom only about 30 were warriors. The bands were fleeing forced removal onto the reduced 1863 reservation, which their leaders had never signed.
federal_account_contrast: Royce 441 records the 1855 reserve as ceded in 1863 by the whole tribe; the bands at Big Hole did not sign.
map_implication: Flag Royce 441 SIGNATORY_ILLEGITIMATE for Wallowa and Salmon River bands; add point; link the 1877 flight and 1878 exile to Indian Territory.
notes: US losses 29-31 dead. Treaty-band split detail drawn from general record (search on that point returned nothing).

source_doc: House Rpt 118-197 (resolution text); Senate Rpt 119-72; Spokesman-Review; New World Encyclopedia; atlas royce-entry-roles.csv Royce 699-705
nations: Mniconjou and Hunkpapa Lakota (Big Foot / Spotted Elk's band); Oglala Sioux Tribe, Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe descendants
place: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation SD; approx 43.14,-102.37
instrument: Act of Mar 2, 1889 (Sioux Agreement) dividing the Great Sioux Reservation; Act of Feb 28, 1877 (Black Hills)
summary: The 7th Cavalry killed about 250 to 375 Lakota, mostly women, children and elders, while disarming Spotted Elk's band. It came 21 months after the 1889 act broke up the Great Sioux Reservation and amid ration cuts.
federal_account_contrast: The Army awarded about 20 Medals of Honor; Royce shows the 1889 division as a reservation reorganization.
map_implication: Link to Royce 699 (1889 retrocession) and 1877 Black Hills; add point. Site is on Pine Ridge; follow Oglala Sioux Tribe on display.
notes: Deaths: 153 killed + 150 missing (Army-style table), about 300 (Spokesman), 350-375 (congressional resolution). Medal of Honor count from memory.

source_doc: General knowledge (Lott killings 1854; Spirit Lake 1857); NOT verified this pass
place: Spirit Lake/Okoboji, Dickinson Co IA (approx 43.42,-95.12, APPROXIMATE); Lott killings near Humboldt Co IA
instrument: Context only
summary: Spirit Lake (1857) was a killing of about 35 to 40 settlers by Inkpaduta's band, not a massacre of Native people; it followed the unpunished 1854 murder of Inkpaduta's brother Sintominaduta and family by Henry Lott. It was later invoked against all Dakota.
federal_account_contrast: Settler-victim event; included to prevent it being miscoded.
map_implication: Do NOT include in the Native-victim massacre layer; optionally include the 1854 Lott killings as a small-scale killing if sourced.
notes: Brief listed 'Spirit Lake?'; answer: excluded from this layer.

source_doc: Search found no documentation (Porter Rockwell / Skull Valley searches returned only Aiken massacre of Californians, 1857)
nations: Goshute (Skull Valley Band of Goshute; Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation)
place: Skull Valley, Tooele Co UT; approx 40.4,-112.75 (region only)
instrument: Treaty of Tooele Valley (Goshute) 1863-10-12
summary: No specific massacre of Goshute people in Skull Valley could be verified in this pass. California Volunteers from Camp Douglas and Fort Ruby did kill Goshute in 1863 in western Utah/eastern Nevada before the Tooele Valley treaty, but specific sites were not confirmed.
map_implication: Do not map until a Goshute-authored or scholarly source is found.
notes: Open question. Check Goshute tribal histories and Utah Division of State History.

source_doc: California Native American Heritage Commission Digital Atlas, 'Genocide' map service (gis.cnra.ca.gov/arcgis/rest/services/NAHC/Genocide/MapServer)
summary: State-hosted ArcGIS layer of recorded incidents of the California genocide, 1846-1873, sourced from Madley's An American Genocide, with a note that location precision varies. NAHC also publishes regional genocide timelines (Sacramento Valley, Humboldt, Mendocino, etc.).
map_implication: Best candidate to ingest as a California layer; request permission from NAHC and attribute Madley. Service was not reachable from this environment (DNS blocked).
notes: License: NOT determined. Being a California state service suggests it is public, but Madley's underlying data is copyrighted (Yale UP). Ask NAHC.

source_doc: Bales and Annerfalk, 'Introducing the Euro-Invasion Conflict Database 1513-1901', Western Historical Quarterly 55(2):127 (2024), doi:10.1093/whq/whae002
summary: Database of 1,375 conflicts between Indigenous peoples and colonizers/US forces, coded on up to 30 variables including coordinates and casualties, flagging 'genocidal massacres' using Madley's criteria. First compiled by Michael L. Nunnally, developed by the Rights Lab, University of Nottingham.
map_implication: Strongest national-scale candidate; contact Rights Lab for data and terms.
notes: No public download or license statement found.

source_doc: Northwestern California Genocide Project (nwgenocide.omeka.net), Cal Poly Humboldt students
nations: Tolowa; Wiyot; Yurok; Hupa; Wailaki and others
summary: Omeka document archive with exhibits on specific massacres (e.g., Yontocket 1853), not a geodataset.
map_implication: Use for citations and narrative, not as geometry.
notes: License not checked.

source_doc: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia 1788-1930 (University of Newcastle, Lyndall Ryan et al.; c21ch.newcastle.edu.au/colonialmassacres; TLCMap layer 1336)
nations: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples (Australia; analog only)
summary: Methodological analog: a massacre defined as 6 or more undefended people killed in one operation, each site scored for evidence, coordinates deliberately offset/generalized. Licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 with a data use agreement and a request that reuse be respectful to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
map_implication: Adopt its definition, evidence scoring and location generalization as the atlas method; do not use its data (wrong country).
notes: Some lecture media are CC BY-NC-ND. Location-blurring practice is from memory of the project's method; confirm on terms page.

source_doc: NPS units and landmarks: Sand Creek Massacre NHS; Washita Battlefield NHS; Big Hole NB; Horseshoe Bend NMP; Bear River Massacre Site NHL (1990); Wounded Knee NHL; ABPP-funded Battlefields of the Pequot War (Mashantucket Pequot Museum, pequotwar.org)
summary: Federally documented massacre sites with NPS boundary data and NRHP/NHL nominations (npgallery.nps.gov). NPS boundary GIS is generally US government public domain; tribal co-management statements should govern interpretation.
map_implication: Use NPS unit boundaries for precise site geometry where they exist; otherwise generalize.
notes: Public-domain status of NPS GIS is general practice, not checked per dataset. Digital Paxton (digitalpaxton.org) is a parallel archive for the Conestoga massacre.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
instrument: USFS Royce polygon legal_type field
summary: By the dataset's legal_type field, 474 polygons (1,472M polygon-acres, 73.5%) are treaty_or_agreement, 76 statute (224M, 11.2%), 113 executive_order (198M, 9.9%) and 54 unknown (108M, 5.4%). Polygon acres overlap (sum 2,002M vs about 1,597M acres of union coverage on the repo's 0.1-degree grid), so these are shares of mapped polygon area, not of land.
federal_account_contrast: The map colors all 717 polygons the same way, implying a treaty basis for all; 26.5% of mapped polygon area has no treaty link at all in the source data.
map_implication: Expose legal_type as a visible style dimension (hatch or outline) and legend it; never present the Royce layer as 'land ceded by treaty'.
notes: Acreage computed by this project from polygon geometry (spherical-excess formula), not from Royce's own acreage column. legal_type is the USFS dataset's inference from which links exist (Kappler, statute, EO), not a legal finding.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
nations: Western Shoshone; Goshute; Eastern and Western Apache; Paiute; Uintah Ute; Pima; Maricopa; Tohono O'odham (Papago); Yuma (Quechan); Walapai; Mohave; Hopi (Moki); Cocopah; Washoe; Methow; Okanagan; Chehalis; Chinook; Cowlitz
place: Great Basin, Southwest, interior Pacific Northwest
instrument: None (Royce records no cession instrument)
summary: Sixteen Royce areas totalling about 330M polygon-acres are, in Royce's own remarks, land the United States took possession of or 'assumed title' to with no treaty, purchase or relinquishment. The largest are 688 eastern Apache (86.0M), 444 Western Shoshone (75.7M), 689 western Apache (55.9M), 432 Uintah Ute (24.9M), 558 and 562 Paiute (23.8M, 23.4M) and 687 Pima-Maricopa-Papago (10.2M).
verbatim_quote: No treaty of purchase was ever made with this tribe. The U. S. assumed title to their country
sources_cited_by_source: Royce 1899 Schedule pp. 824-922 remarks column, as quoted in royce-entry-roles.csv
federal_account_contrast: Royce himself (a federal source) says no cession happened here, yet the map shows these as cession polygons, and the dataset's legal_type labels them statute (8), executive_order (4), treaty_or_agreement (2) or unknown (2).
map_implication: Create a class 'taken with no instrument' for these 16 areas; this is the single largest correction (about 330M polygon-acres).
notes: Quote from Royce remark on 683/685 (Walapai, Yuma). 432 quote: 'taken possession of by U. S. without formal purchase'. Royce number assignment for 558 is flagged low-confidence in the crosswalk (garbled OCR).

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
nations: Apache; Walapai; Yuma; Mohave; Hopi; Cocopah; Pima; Maricopa; Papago
instrument: (dataset artifact) 'statute' legal_type with 1886-10-01 date
summary: The eight Southwest 'country claimed at beginning of their relations with the U.S.' areas all carry the date 1886-10-01 and legal_type 'statute' only because a federal statute link is present in the USFS data; Royce describes no statute that ceded them. Together they are about 162M polygon-acres.
verbatim_quote: Country claimed by them at beginning of their relations with the U. S.
federal_account_contrast: A user reading 'statute, 1886' would infer a congressional cession that did not occur.
map_implication: Override legal_type for 682-689 to 'no_instrument'; do not show 1886 as a cession date in the timeline.
notes: Why the USFS record has 1886-10-01 is not established here; possibly the date of a report or map compilation. Verify against USFS attribute documentation.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
instrument: 18 California treaties of 1851-52 (unratified)
instrument_cite: Royce Schedule pp. 780-784; atlas instrument ids TLA-U-CA-*
summary: Royce maps California almost entirely through the 18 unratified 1851-52 treaties: 35 polygons (about 88M polygon-acres) split into 'reserve' and 'cession of all other claims' plates. All 35 carry legal_type 'unknown'. No legal cession took place under these instruments.
verbatim_quote: Cede all claim to territory outside of reserved tract
federal_account_contrast: Royce's plates show California as if ceded by these treaties; the Senate rejected them in 1852.
map_implication: Render 273-310 as 'unratified-treaty area' and mark the 'reserve' polygons as promised-then-never-set-aside land.
notes: Crosswalk note already says 'no legal cession took place'; number assignment within each treaty is by row order (OCR scrambled).

source_doc: NARA Prologue 2013 (archives.gov/publications/prologue/2013/fall-winter/treaties.pdf); Wikipedia 'California Indian Reservations and Cessions'
instrument: Senate rejection of the 18 California treaties in executive session
summary: The Senate refused to ratify the 18 treaties on July 8, 1852 and filed them under an injunction of secrecy lifted January 18, 1905. NARA's Prologue attributes the rejection to objections from white Californians and commissioner irregularities. Reported reserve acreage varies by source (7.4M to 8.5M acres).
federal_account_contrast: Promised reserves of several million acres were never set apart; the land became public domain anyway.
map_implication: Add the promised 1851-52 reserves (Royce 'reserve' polygons) as a 'promised, never delivered' layer.
notes: One source gives June 28, 1852 for the rejection; one gives 1909 for the end of secrecy. 1852/1905 are the majority readings.

source_doc: Barker v. Harvey, 181 U.S. 481 (1901) (law.resource.org); United States v. Title Insurance & Trust Co., 265 U.S. 472 (1924)
instrument: California Land Claims Act, Act of Mar. 3, 1851
summary: The 1851 Act required private land claims in California to be presented to a commission within two years or be treated as abandoned. In Barker v. Harvey the Court held Mission Indians' occupancy rights forfeited because no claim was filed for them; in 1924 the Court refused to overrule Barker as a 'rule of property'.
federal_account_contrast: Indian title in California was lost by a filing deadline under a land-title statute, not by any cession.
map_implication: Tag California areas with 'title treated as abandoned under 1851 Land Claims Act'; link Barker and Title Insurance cases.
notes: Critics (ICT) note the Indians were likely never told to file; that is advocacy commentary.

source_doc: BIA press releases 1965 and 1969 (bia.gov/node/10035; bia.gov/as-ia/opa/online-press-release/doi-recommends-bill-disposition-291-m-award-ca-indians); NPS 'Five Views'
nations: Indians of California; Mission Indians; Pit River
instrument: ICC award to the Indians of California
instrument_cite: ICC Dockets 31 and 37 (consolidated; docket numbers not confirmed by fetched sources)
summary: The ICC awarded $29.1 million (appropriated 1964) for California land; Interior described it as compensation for land 'taken by the United States March 3, 1853'. Secondary sources compute about 47 cents per acre. Pit River and other groups opposed it, and many refused checks in 1972.
verbatim_quote: land taken by the United States March 3, 1853
federal_account_contrast: Federal law treats California aboriginal title as extinguished by taking (1853) plus later payment, not by cession.
map_implication: Date of taking 1853-03-03 should be shown instead of 1851-52 treaty dates; class 'taken, compensated by ICC money award'.
notes: Separate $5M 1944 Court of Claims K-344 award under 1928 Jurisdictional Act was for unfulfilled treaty benefits, not title. Offset amounts ($17M gross / $12M offsets) are unverified.

source_doc: ICT News, 'The Court of Claims ruling in California Indians K-344'; 25 U.S.C. 661
instrument: California Indians Jurisdictional Act of May 18, 1928; Indians of California v. U.S., 102 Ct. Cl. 837
summary: Under the 1928 Act the Court of Claims compensated the unfulfilled benefits of the 18 treaties (about $5M net, 1944) and expressly said it was not paying for land cession or for a taking.
federal_account_contrast: Even the federal court refused to treat the treaties as cessions.
map_implication: Cite as evidence that 273-310 are not cessions.
notes: Gross award and offset figures unverified.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes); Statutes at Large 18 Stat. 689 (dheller.org transcription)
place: Ruby Valley, Nevada; Western Shoshone country NV/CA/ID/UT/OR
instrument: Treaty of Ruby Valley, Oct. 1, 1863 (ratified with amendment 1866; proclaimed Oct. 21, 1869)
summary: The treaty defined Western Shoshone boundaries and granted passage, telegraph, stage, railroad and mining rights, but contains no land cession. Royce maps the area (444, about 75.7M polygon-acres) and says the U.S. 'took possession' without purchase. The dataset types it treaty_or_agreement because it links to Kappler.
verbatim_quote: No formal purchase of the territorial claim of these tribes or bands was made, but the U. S. took possession of the same
federal_account_contrast: The map's color implies cession; the treaty is a peace and right-of-way treaty.
map_implication: Reclassify Royce 444 (and Goshute 447) as 'never ceded, still contested'; show Ruby Valley boundary as treaty-recognized territory.

source_doc: CIDH/IACHR Report 75/02 procedural history (cidh.oas.org/annualrep/2002eng/USA.11140b.htm); DOJ OSG briefs
instrument: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, ICC Docket 326-K
summary: The ICC found Western Shoshone title to about 24.4M acres; it held California title ended in 1853 and Nevada title was lost over time by 'gradual encroachment by whites'. A stipulated valuation date of July 1, 1872 was used and about $26M was awarded (final award 1979).
verbatim_quote: gradual encroachment by whites
federal_account_contrast: The 'taking' is a legal fiction fixed by stipulation for valuation, not a dated instrument; Western Shoshone groups say they never agreed to it.
map_implication: Store taking_date=1872-07-01 (stipulated) with basis 'ICC finding of gradual encroachment'; style as 'taken, no instrument'.
notes: Acreage reported as 24.4M (CA+NV) in one source and 24,396,403 acres in Nevada in another; check the opinion.

source_doc: United States v. Dann, 470 U.S. 39 (1985) syllabus (chanrobles.com/usa/us_supremecourt/470/39) | Ned Blackhawk (on Western Shoshone; context for Dann) plus United States v. Dann, 470 U.S. 39 (1985)
instrument: Indian Claims Commission Act s.22(a)
summary: The Court held that 'payment' occurred when the $26M award was certified and deposited in a Treasury trust account, barring the tribal-title defense, even though the Western Shoshone had not accepted the money. The Court relied on the government being both judgment debtor and trustee.
verbatim_quote: this certification automatically appropriated the amount of the award and deposited it for the Tribe in an interest-bearing trust account
federal_account_contrast: Extinguishment by unilateral deposit, not by consent or cession.
map_implication: Add class marker 'title extinguished by ICC payment (unaccepted)' for 444.
notes: Merged duplicate rows (same fact): WEB-HIS-012.

source_doc: UN CERD Decision 1(68), CERD/C/USA/DEC/1 (digitallibrary.un.org/record/573142)
instrument: CERD early warning and urgent action decision
summary: CERD, at its 68th session (Feb-Mar 2006), acted on Western Shoshone requests, expressed concern that their land rights were being denied and that US measures could cause irreparable harm, and noted the US had not responded. The Western Shoshone Claims Distribution Act of 2004 authorized distribution of the award (reported as about $145-160M with interest), which many councils refuse.
federal_account_contrast: International body treats the title as live; US treats it as extinguished.
map_implication: Note the CERD decision and IACHR Report 75/02 (Dann) on 444's info panel.
notes: Operative paragraphs not retrieved; read the PDF before quoting. Also IACHR Mary and Carrie Dann, Report No. 75/02, Case 11.140 (2002).

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes); United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980) (law.justia.com; law.resource.org) | United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980); Encyclopedia of the Great Plains (egp.law.050); NARF bulletin Different Horse v. Salazar | United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980) and Lakota refusal
instrument: Agreement of Sept. 26, 1876, enacted by Act of Feb. 28, 1877
summary: Royce shows 598 (7.2M polygon-acres, Black Hills portion of the 1868 Great Sioux Reservation) and 597 (21.2M, art. 16 unceded territory) as cessions. In 1980 the Supreme Court affirmed that the 1877 Act was a taking under eminent domain, with interest on $17.1M from 1877 (about $106M in 1980). The Sioux refused payment; the fund is reported at over $1B.
federal_account_contrast: The atlas crosswalk labels 598 'ceded' (status=ceded); the Supreme Court characterized it as a taking.
map_implication: Reclassify 597/598 from 'ceded by agreement' to 'taken by statute (judicially found a taking); payment refused'.
notes: The phrase 'ripe and rank case of dishonorable dealings' (from the Court of Claims, quoted in the opinion) was not confirmed in fetched excerpts; verify before quoting. Fund size figures vary ($757M 2010; $1.3B 2011 per PBS). Merged duplicate rows (same fact): WEB-PRM-012, WEB-HIS-036.

source_doc: City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, 544 U.S. 197 (2005) (law.resource.org; Cornell LII)
place: Central New York (Oneida reservation of about 300,000 acres)
instrument: 1788 Treaty of Fort Schuyler (with New York); Trade and Intercourse Act 1790; later state purchases
instrument_cite: 544 U.S. 197; County of Oneida v. Oneida Indian Nation, 470 U.S. 226 (1985)
summary: Oneida II (1985) held the Oneidas had a federal common-law claim for state purchases made without federal approval. Sherrill (2005) then barred the Nation from asserting sovereignty over reacquired land on equitable grounds (laches, acquiescence, impossibility) because two centuries had passed.
federal_account_contrast: The illegality of the state purchases was accepted; relief was denied on equity, not because the land was validly ceded.
map_implication: Class 'taken by state purchase in violation of Nonintercourse Act; claim barred by laches'. Royce does not map these state purchases as federal cessions; check gap.

source_doc: Cayuga Indian Nation v. Pataki, 413 F.3d 266 (2d Cir. 2005) (secondary summaries; NARF petition appendix)
instrument: New York state treaties of 1795 and 1807
summary: New York took 64,012 acres in 1795 and 3 more in 1807 under state treaties never ratified by the federal government. The district court awarded $247,911,999.42 (damages plus interest); the Second Circuit, applying Sherrill, held laches barred the possessory claim and entered judgment for defendants.
federal_account_contrast: Federal law required federal consent; none was given; land still lost.
map_implication: Add Cayuga 1795/1807 state takings as 'taken without federal instrument'.

source_doc: CS Monitor 1980-04-17; Wikipedia 'Indian Land Claims Settlements'; Maine: An Encyclopedia
nations: Passamaquoddy; Penobscot; Houlton Band of Maliseet
place: Maine (claim about 12.5M acres, two-thirds of state)
instrument: Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Oct. 10, 1980
instrument_cite: Pub. L. 96-420; Joint Tribal Council of Passamaquoddy v. Morton, 528 F.2d 370 (1st Cir. 1975)
summary: The tribes claimed about 12.5M acres sold by Massachusetts and Maine without federal approval under the 1790 Act. Congress settled for $81.5M (trust funds and land acquisition) and ratified the prior transfers.
federal_account_contrast: Title was extinguished by a 1980 federal statute ratifying unlawful state transactions, not by any 18th or 19th century cession.
map_implication: Maine is a Royce gap; draw the claim area with class 'taken by state, extinguished by 1980 settlement act'.
notes: Public Law and F.2d cites from memory; verify.

source_doc: Mashpee Tribe v. New Seabury Corp., 592 F.2d 575 (1st Cir. 1979); 447 F.Supp. 940 (D. Mass. 1978)
instrument: Trade and Intercourse Act claim
summary: The first Nonintercourse Act case tried to a jury: the jury found the Mashpee were not a tribe at key dates (including 1870 and 1976), so the claim failed. The tribe was federally recognized in 2007.
federal_account_contrast: Land loss upheld by finding the plaintiffs not a 'tribe', not by any cession.
map_implication: Massachusetts is a Royce gap; note Mashpee as 'taken by town/state action, claim defeated on tribal-status grounds'.
notes: Sources differ on exact jury findings by year. 2007 recognition from memory.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Indian Land Claims Settlements' table
instrument: Rhode Island Indian Claims Settlement Act, Sept. 30, 1978
summary: Narragansett aboriginal-title claim settled in 1978 with $3.5M listed compensation and a land base (commonly given as about 1,800 acres, unverified here); Carcieri v. Salazar (2009) later blocked trust acquisition.
federal_account_contrast: Claim area was taken by colonial and state detribalization (1880 RI 'sale'), not by federal treaty.
map_implication: Rhode Island is a Royce gap; mark 'taken by state action; 1978 settlement'.
notes: 1,800 acres, 1880 detribalization and Carcieri details are from memory, not verified this session.

source_doc: Oregon Encyclopedia 'Willamette Valley Treaty Commission' and 'Willamette Valley Treaties'; ndnhistoryresearch.com (David G. Lewis, Santiam Kalapuya/Grand Ronde)
nations: Kalapuya (Santiam, Tualatin, Yamhill etc.); Molalla; Clackamas
instrument: Six Willamette Valley Treaty Commission treaties (Champoeg, 1851)
summary: Commissioners Gaines, Skinner and Allen concluded six treaties in spring 1851 reserving parts of the valley. Settlers had already claimed the land under the Donation Land Claim Act, so Dart advised against them and the Senate let them die; sources say they were 'effectively rejected through neglect'. Bands got a ratified treaty only in 1855.
verbatim_quote: effectively rejected through neglect
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the Willamette as ceded in 1855 (Kalapuya treaty); settlement and title-taking had already happened from 1850.
map_implication: Show 1850-55 Willamette as 'settled under federal statute before any cession'; add the unratified 1851 reserves as promised land.
notes: Western Oregon totals vary: 24 unratified treaties (Lewis) or 18 sent by Dart.

source_doc: Oregon Encyclopedia 'Oregon Donation Land Act'; Oregon History Project 'A New Legal Landscape'; ODE 'The Demise of Indian Land'
instrument: Donation Land Claim Act, Sept. 27, 1850; Oregon Organic Act, Aug. 14, 1848
summary: The 1848 Organic Act protected Indian rights to land so long as they remained unextinguished by treaty. The 1850 Donation Act nonetheless granted free land to white settlers before any ratified cession in western Oregon; Delegate Thurston had called extinguishment of Native title the 'first prerequisite step'.
verbatim_quote: so long as such rights shall remain unextinguished by treaty between the United States and such Indians
federal_account_contrast: Federal statute disposed of land before any cession, contrary to the Organic Act savings clause.
map_implication: Overlay 1850-1855 Donation claims as 'disposed of before cession' over the later Royce cession polygons.
notes: Exact Organic Act wording to be checked against 9 Stat. 323 s.1.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes); Chinook Indian Nation site (chinooknation.org); chinookstory.org; ndnhistoryresearch.com
nations: Chinook; Clatsop; Waukikum; Chehalis; Cowlitz; Klikitat
place: Tansey Point, Clatsop Plains, OR; lower Columbia, WA
instrument: Tansey Point treaties of Aug. 1851 (Anson Dart), unratified
summary: Dart's 1851 Tansey Point treaties with the Clatsop and Chinook bands were never ratified. Royce 458 (4.9M polygon-acres, WA) is recorded as Chehalis, Chinook, Cowlitz-area country taken without any treaty; the dataset types it executive_order (date of a later reserve order).
federal_account_contrast: Executive-order coloring implies a legal transfer; Royce describes none.
map_implication: Reclassify 458 as 'taken with no instrument'; draw 1851 Tansey Point reserves as unratified-treaty promised land. Chinook Indian Nation is not federally recognized.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes) | Oregon Encyclopedia 'Coast Indian Reservation'; Wikipedia 'Alsea' (via search); Lewis, 'Redressing Payments for Clatsop and Tillamook Peoples' Landclaims'
instrument: Coast treaty of Aug. 11, 1855 (unratified)
summary: Royce 397 (3.9M polygon-acres) is the unratified 1855 Oregon coast treaty area; Royce says the U.S. treated the cession as binding anyway, and the Coast (Siletz) reservation was set apart inside it by executive order of Nov. 9, 1855.
verbatim_quote: The treaties were not ratified, but the U. S. authorities assumed that the cession was binding
federal_account_contrast: Royce openly records a cession that never legally occurred.
map_implication: Class 'unratified-treaty area treated as ceded'.
notes: Merged duplicate rows (same fact): WEB-UR-011.

source_doc: Texas State Library and Archives annexation pages (tsl.texas.gov); Texas Historical Commission marker 'Brazos Indian Reservation'; treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
nations: Comanche; Caddo; Anadahko; Waco; Tonkawa; Lipan Apache; Wichita and others
instrument: Joint Resolution for annexation of Texas, Mar. 1, 1845
summary: Texas kept its public lands at annexation, so the federal government never held a public domain there to acquire by cession. Texas set aside 12 leagues (53,136 acres) in 1854 for the Brazos and Clear Fork reserves, emptied them in 1859 by removal to Indian Territory, and the land reverted to the state. Only 5 Royce polygons touch Texas; on the repo grid central Texas (94-103W, 28-33N) is about 45% covered, mostly by Apache 688 (a no-instrument area).
federal_account_contrast: No federal cession framework applies to most of Texas; title passed by state action and removal.
map_implication: Render Texas as 'taken by state action, no instrument' rather than blank or ceded.
notes: 5 Stat. 797 cite from memory.

source_doc: CRS R46997 (everycrsreport.com); BLM ANCSA at 50 infographic; Tee-Hit-Ton v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955) (govinfo)
instrument: Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Dec. 18, 1971
summary: No treaties were made with Alaska Natives. Tee-Hit-Ton held unrecognized aboriginal title could be taken without Fifth Amendment compensation. ANCSA extinguished aboriginal claims over more than 360M acres for about 44-45M acres and $962.5M to Native corporations.
federal_account_contrast: Royce and the atlas show nothing for Alaska; title was extinguished by a 1971 statute, not by cession.
map_implication: Add Alaska as 'extinguished by statute (ANCSA 1971), no treaty'.
notes: 1867 Treaty of Cession art. III 'uncivilized tribes' clause not verified this session.

source_doc: Apology Resolution, Pub. L. 103-150, 107 Stat. 1510 (congress.gov); UH Richardson Native Hawaiian Law Center column (M. MacKenzie)
instrument: Newlands Joint Resolution, July 7, 1898; Apology Resolution, Nov. 23, 1993
summary: After the 1893 overthrow, the Republic of Hawaii ceded about 1.8M acres of crown, government and public lands to the US by the 1898 Newlands Resolution, without Native Hawaiian consent or compensation. Congress in 1993 found Native Hawaiians never directly relinquished their claims.
verbatim_quote: never directly relinquished their claims to their inherent sovereignty as a people or over their national lands to the United States
federal_account_contrast: The only 'cession' was by the post-overthrow Republic, which Congress itself has called illegal.
map_implication: Add Hawaii as 'never ceded, still contested' (ceded lands about 1.8M acres; state controls about 1.4M).
notes: Hawaii v. OHA, 556 U.S. 163 (2009) held the Apology Resolution created no substantive rights (from memory; not verified this session).

source_doc: United States v. Sandoval, 231 U.S. 28 (1913); Mountain States Tel. v. Pueblo of Santa Ana, 472 U.S. 237 (1985) (law.resource.org)
instrument: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo 1848; Pueblo Lands Act of June 7, 1924
summary: Pueblo land is held under Spanish grants recognized after 1848, not acquired by cession. About 3,000 non-Indian claimants (12,000 people) were inside Pueblo grant boundaries by 1924; the Pueblo Lands Act set up a board to adjudicate them, with Congress acknowledging a 'moral, if not legal, obligation' for its failure to protect the lands.
verbatim_quote: moral, if not legal, obligation to make reasonable restitution
federal_account_contrast: Losses inside Pueblo grants came by encroachment and a 1924 quiet-title process, not by treaty.
map_implication: Royce has no polygons for Pueblo grants (repo grid shows the Rio Grande box fully covered by other areas, e.g. Apache 688); overlay Pueblo grants as 'never ceded; partly lost to encroachment confirmed by 1924 Act'.
notes: Quote is from the 1924 Senate committee report as quoted in 472 U.S. 237.

source_doc: (not verified this session; general knowledge)
instrument: Gadsden Purchase treaty, Dec. 30, 1853
summary: The Gadsden boundary split O'odham country without O'odham consent; the US made no treaty with them, and Royce 687 records Papago country as taken with no purchase. An ICC award for O'odham aboriginal land followed in the 1970s.
federal_account_contrast: Purchase from Mexico is not a cession by the O'odham.
map_implication: Class 'taken with no instrument' for 687; note the international boundary.
notes: Search budget exhausted before verifying ICC docket (believed Docket 345) and award amount. Verify before use.

source_doc: Royce 1899 schedule scope (LOC catalog: 'from the organization of the Federal Government to and including 1894'); treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
nations: Wampanoag; Narragansett; Pequot; Mohegan; Lenape; Powhatan; Piscataway; Catawba; Abenaki and others
place: New England, Mid-Atlantic, Tidewater and Piedmont
instrument: (none in federal record) colonial deeds, conquest, colonial and state statutes
summary: Royce covers federal-era cessions only. On the repo's 0.1-degree grid, test boxes over New England (69-73.5W, 41.5-45N), Maryland-Delaware-New Jersey and the Virginia Piedmont have 0% Royce coverage. Overall, Royce union coverage is about 1,597M acres against about 1,894M acres of contiguous-US land, so roughly 300M acres (about 16%) of the lower 48 has no Royce polygon at all, before adding Alaska and Hawaii.
federal_account_contrast: Blank areas read as either 'no Native land' or 'already settled'; in fact title passed by colonial or state means outside the federal treaty system.
map_implication: Fill Royce gaps with a 'pre-federal colonial or state taking (no federal instrument)' class rather than leaving them blank.
notes: Coverage figures computed by this project from cession-cells.json (cells may include some water); CONUS land area 1,894M acres is a standard Census figure from memory.

source_doc: USGS pubs 70114965; LOC item 80695449; ArcGIS FeatureServer 'Indian_Land_Areas_Judicially_Established_1978' (services1.arcgis.com/fBc8EJBxQRMcHlei); ICC Final Report 1978 (nill.narf.org/documents/icc_final_report.pdf)
instrument: Map 'Indian Land Areas Judicially Established' (USGS for ICC), 1:4,000,000, Albers
summary: The 1978 ICC map shows each area where a tribe proved original occupancy before the ICC or Court of Claims. A public ArcGIS FeatureServer exists with a polygon layer (layer 5) 'Indian Land Areas Judicially Established 1978' with fields including CATNUM and Affiliatio; this contradicts the repo's G2 note that no vector dataset exists. The ICC completed 546 dockets and awarded about $818.2M; it could only award money at land value at the 'time of taking'.
federal_account_contrast: Provides a federal, judicially based alternative to Royce: where title was proven and then 'taken', often with no cession.
map_implication: Evaluate the FeatureServer for a 'judicially established aboriginal title' layer (check license, CATNUM-to-docket crosswalk); join ICC docket, taking date and award per polygon.
notes: Service could not be fetched from this sandbox (proxy 403); field list partial. Fort Lewis finding aid gives about $1.3B total; difference unexplained.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
instrument: Executive orders and acts restoring reservation land to the public domain
summary: The crosswalk marks 16 Royce areas (about 12M polygon-acres) status=taken, e.g. 699 (8.3M, remainder of Great Sioux Reservation restored by Act of Mar. 2, 1889), 717 (1.4M, north half of Colville restored by Act of July 1, 1892) and repeated White Mountain Apache restorations by executive order 1873-1893.
federal_account_contrast: Royce sometimes calls these 'ceded portions'; they were restored to public domain unilaterally.
map_implication: Use the crosswalk's existing status=taken as a separate class 'taken by statute or EO'.
notes: Colville 1892 restoration was done without tribal consent (Royce calls it 'the ceded portion'); 699 took effect with the Sioux agreement proclaimed Feb. 10, 1890, so it is mixed.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: data/derived/cessions.json + cession-events.json + crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv (Royce 1899 Schedule OCR quotes)
nations: Sac and Fox; Choctaw; Chickasaw; Wichita; Crow; Ute; Jicarilla Apache
instrument: Unratified agreements underlying executive-order reserves
summary: Several reserves were set apart by executive order under agreements Congress never ratified: 557 Judith Basin (Crow, 1874), 563 Jicarilla (1874), 609 San Juan (Southern Ute, 1878 agreement), 540a Wichita (1872 agreement). Royce 368 (7.1M) was a lease, not a cession, until 1866.
federal_account_contrast: These promised reserves were later revoked or reduced without ratified instruments.
map_implication: Show these as 'promised under unratified agreement' rather than as reservations.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
instrument: Royce 1899 Schedule (as crosswalked)
summary: The crosswalk has 1,172 role rows over 724 Royce area ids. Distinct areas per role: reserved 469, confirmed 51, described_or_recognized 36, retroceded 57, us_reserved 4, ceded 402, ceded_part 16, other 62. 498 areas carry at least one promise role (reserved/confirmed/described_or_recognized).
federal_account_contrast: Royce already records promised land; the atlas's 'ceded' framing hides that two-thirds of polygons began as land reserved or recognized to a nation.
map_implication: Add a 'promised' layer filter built from roles reserved/confirmed/described_or_recognized; no new geometry needed for 491 of 498 areas.
notes: Counts are distinct area ids; one area can hold several roles. Role labels are the crosswalk's, assigned by an earlier pipeline from Royce remarks.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
instrument: Royce 1899 Schedule (as crosswalked)
summary: Of 498 promised areas: 259 ended ceded or taken by Royce's last date (256 with geometry, about 370 million acres summed), 227 were still 'kept' (226 with geometry, about 359 million acres summed), 12 unclear (about 23 million acres). Seven areas have no geometry (Royce 47, 65, 128, 129, 130, 543, 690); 690 (Meskwaki, Tama County) is a promise-role area without geometry.
federal_account_contrast: Acre sums overlap (Royce polygons stack, e.g. 1851 territories under later reserves), so they show scale, not a land balance.
map_implication: Show 'promised then lost' (status ceded/taken with a promise role) as its own class distinct from plain cessions; never sum overlapping acres in UI copy.
notes: Areas computed by spherical-excess formula on the repo GeoJSON; overlapping polygons double-count. 'Kept' means kept as of Royce's input dates (to 1894), not today.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent); src/lib/land.ts ROLE_KIND
instrument: General Allotment Act Feb. 8, 1887 and surplus-land acts
summary: Royce ends in 1894, so 'kept' freezes reservations before most allotment and surplus-land openings. Indian landholding fell from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million (1934). Royce 700-705 (Sioux), 715 (Crow), 374 (Flathead), 540 (Wind River) are all shown kept but were opened after 1900.
sources_cited_by_source: FEMA EMI IS-650b allotment page; Encyclopedia of the Great Plains
federal_account_contrast: The map's 'kept' green overstates what nations held in the 20th century; diminishment came by statute, not treaty.
map_implication: Rename 'kept' to 'still reserved in 1894' and add a post-1894 overlay (opening acts) before claiming land is still Native-held.
notes: 138M/48M figures repeated by many secondary sources; some cite ~100M lost. Use 'about 90 million acres'.

source_doc: Kappler vol. 2 pp. 594-596 (treaty text, as reprinted at indianlaw.mt.gov and littlebighorn.info); treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
nations: Sioux (Dakota/Lakota); Cheyenne; Arapaho; Crow; Assiniboine; Gros Ventre (Hidatsa); Mandan; Arikara
place: Fort Laramie / Horse Creek, Nebraska Territory (approx. 41.95N, -103.95W treaty ground at Horse Creek)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851
summary: Article 5 defines by metes and bounds the territory of each nation; the nations did not abandon claims to other lands. The repo maps these as 'described_or_recognized' but only in fragments: there is no single polygon per nation, and area 300 is labelled 'several nations' at only 6.3 million acres.
verbatim_quote: the aforesaid Indian nations do not hereby abandon or prejudice any rights or claims they may have to other lands
federal_account_contrast: The treaty recognized (did not grant) Native title; it was not a cession at all.
map_implication: Digitize all seven Art. 5 territories as named 'recognized 1851' polygons (descriptions in web-promised.md) and draw them as promised land beneath later cessions.
notes: Quote taken from widely reprinted Kappler text; verify exact wording against Kappler page image. Stat. cite uncertain because the treaty was never proclaimed.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
nations: Blackfeet (Blackfoot Confederacy: Piegan, Blood, Siksika); Gros Ventre (A'aninin)
instrument: Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5 (Blackfoot territory) and Lame Bull Treaty Oct. 17, 1855
summary: Fort Laramie 1851 assigned a 'Blackfoot' territory though the Blackfeet did not attend or sign. The 1855 treaty then recognized it as Blackfeet land and created a common hunting ground (399). The 1873-74 executive orders and act and the 1888 agreement cut it to the present reservation (695).
federal_account_contrast: Royce draws a non-party nation's land by another treaty's description.
map_implication: Label Royce 398 as 'described in a treaty the Blackfeet did not sign; recognized 1855'.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
instrument: Fort Laramie 1851; Crow Treaty May 7, 1868; agreement June 12, 1880 (act Apr. 11, 1882); act Mar. 3, 1891
summary: Crow country recognized in 1851 (30.1 million acres in repo polygon 517) was relinquished outside an 1868 reservation, which was then cut in 1880-82 (619) and 1891 (714), leaving 715.
verbatim_quote: This relinquishment comprises that portion of the country assigned them by unratified Fort Laramie treaty of Sept. 17, 1851
federal_account_contrast: Royce calls the 1851 treaty 'unratified'; the Crow alone did not assent to the Senate amendment.
map_implication: Animate Crow sequence 517 -> 619 -> 714 as one 'promised then reduced' story.
notes: Quote is Royce's own wording as recorded in the repo note column.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
instrument: Fort Laramie 1851; EO Apr. 12, 1870; EO July 13, 1880; act Mar. 3, 1891
summary: The 1851 territory of the Three Affiliated Tribes outside the 1870 executive-order Fort Berthold reserve was 'considered as ceded' with no cession instrument (529). The 1880 order removed more (620).
verbatim_quote: the remainder of that tract being considered as ceded
federal_account_contrast: 'Considered as ceded' is not a cession; the repo status 'ceded' for 529 flattens a taking by executive order.
map_implication: Re-status Royce 529 and 620 as 'taken by executive order' (TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT), not ceded.

source_doc: Fort Laramie Treaty 1868 text (Kappler 2:998); treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Dakota Territory west of the Missouri
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Apr. 29, 1868, Art. 2
summary: Art. 2 'set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation' of the Sioux all land from the 46th parallel south to the Nebraska line and from the Missouri's east bank west to the 104th meridian (the Great Sioux Reservation).
verbatim_quote: set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named
map_implication: Draw the Art. 2 rectangle explicitly (46N; Nebraska north line ~43N; Missouri east bank; 104W) as the promised Great Sioux Reservation.
notes: Quote from widely reprinted treaty text; verify against Kappler.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent) (area calc by research agent)
instrument: Fort Laramie 1868
summary: Repo maps the Great Sioux Reservation as Royce 516 (status kept), but polygon 516 covers only about 4.3 million acres and its own note doubts the match. The union of 598 (Black Hills cession) + 699 (1889 restored remainder) + 700-705 (six 1889 reservations) is about 27.7 million acres, which fits the Art. 2 area.
verbatim_quote: Number column OCR is garbled. 516 could instead be the companion relinquishment
federal_account_contrast: Likely misidentification in the atlas, not in Royce.
map_implication: Do not show 516 as the Great Sioux Reservation; build the 1868 promise from 598+699+700-705 (or digitize Art. 2) and re-check 516 against Royce map plates for Dakota.
notes: Verify against Royce Dakota plates (LOC).

source_doc: Fort Laramie Treaty 1868 Art. 11, 16; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: north of North Platte, east of Big Horn summits (Wyoming, Montana, Nebraska)
instrument: Fort Laramie 1868 Art. 16; Sioux agreement June 23, 1875; agreement Sept. 26, 1876 / act Feb. 28, 1877
summary: Art. 16 kept the country north of the North Platte and east of the Big Horn summits as 'unceded Indian territory' closed to whites; Art. 11 kept hunting on the Republican Fork. These were extinguished by the 1875 agreement (584) and the 1876-77 Black Hills agreement/act (597).
verbatim_quote: shall be held and considered to be unceded Indian territory
federal_account_contrast: Repo shows 597 'ceded' by the 1876 agreement, though that agreement lacked the Art. 12 three-fourths signatures.
map_implication: Mark 597 as 'unceded territory taken by 1877 act without Art. 12 consent'.
notes: Statute cite 19 Stat. 254 from general knowledge; verify.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent); Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903); Kansapedia; Supreme Court Historical Society
instrument: Little Arkansas treaty Oct. 18, 1865; Medicine Lodge Oct. 21, 1867 Art. 2, 12; Jerome Agreement 1892 ratified act June 6, 1900
summary: The 1865 reserve (511, about 43 million acres in repo polygon, incl. Texas Panhandle) was cut in 1867 to the Medicine Lodge reservation between the Washita and Red rivers. Art. 12 required three-fourths of adult men to sign any cession. The 1892 Jerome Agreement lacked that; Congress ratified it in 1900, taking about 2.99 million acres, and Lone Wolf upheld Congress's power to abrogate.
verbatim_quote: signed by at least three-fourths of all the adult male Indians occupying the same
sources_cited_by_source: Medicine Lodge Art. 12 (quoted in 187 U.S. 553 syllabus)
federal_account_contrast: Royce's last date for 478 'kept' predates the 1900-01 opening; the map shows it intact.
map_implication: Add 1901 opening of KCA surplus lands as a post-Royce taking over Royce 478.
notes: Signatures alleged counterfeit (SCHS); treat as contested.

source_doc: Medicine Lodge Treaty with Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867; accessgenealogy 'History of Arapaho and Cheyenne Treaties'; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Indian Territory between south Kansas line and Cimarron (in Cherokee Outlet)
instrument: Medicine Lodge (Cheyenne-Arapaho) Oct. 28, 1867; EO Aug. 10, 1869; act Mar. 3, 1891
royce_areas: 525 (1869 reserve); 1867 treaty reserve not found as its own repo area
summary: The 1867 treaty reservation lay in the Cherokee Outlet; the nations never settled there and an 1869 executive order substituted a reserve on the North Canadian and Washita (525, 4.3 million acres), which was ceded subject to allotment in 1891.
federal_account_contrast: The treaty-promised reserve vanishes from the map because Royce folds it into Cherokee Outlet area 489.
map_implication: Digitize the 1867 Art. 2 reserve as promised-never-delivered, overlapping 489.
notes: Royce number for the 1867 reserve not confirmed in repo; check Royce Indian Territory plate.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent); accessgenealogy; military-history wiki (Little Arkansas)
place: Arkansas River and Sand Creek, southeastern Colorado (Sand Creek massacre site approx. 38.54N, -102.51W)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise Feb. 18, 1861; Treaty of Little Arkansas Oct. 14, 1865
summary: Fort Wise ceded most of the 1851 territory (426, about 47 million acres in repo polygon) and reserved a tract on the Arkansas and Sand Creek (477, 3.7 million acres). The Sand Creek massacre happened in that area in 1864; the 1865 treaty then ceded the reserve and promised a new one partly in Kansas, which was never set up.
verbatim_quote: no part of which should be within the state of Kansas
federal_account_contrast: Repo shows 477 as 'ceded' in 1865, just 11 months after the massacre on that land.
map_implication: Flag 477 'reserve where the Sand Creek massacre occurred, ceded 1865'; show 1865 Art. 2 reserve as promised, never established.
notes: Quote is a paraphrase-quote in a secondary source, not the treaty text; verify. Sand Creek NHS coords approximate.

source_doc: Ute Treaty Mar. 2, 1868 (Kappler 2:990); treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent); Univ. of Utah collections (act June 15, 1880); Aspen Journalism
nations: Ute (Tabeguache/Uncompahgre, Muache, Capote, Weeminuche, Yampa, Grand River, Uintah bands)
instrument: Ute Treaty 1868 Art. 2; Brunot Agreement 1873 (act Apr. 29, 1874); act June 15, 1880
summary: Art. 2 reserved Colorado west of the 107th meridian and south of a line 15 miles north of the 40th parallel (566+616+617, about 16 million acres in repo polygons). Brunot (1873) took the San Juan strip (566); after the 1879 Meeker events the 1880 act removed White River and Uncompahgre Utes, leaving the Southern Ute strip (617).
federal_account_contrast: Repo notes it is unsure which of 616/617 is ceded vs retained.
map_implication: Draw the 1868 Art. 2 rectangle as one promised polygon; resolve 616/617 from Royce Colorado plate.
notes: Stat. cites for 1874/1880 from general knowledge; verify.

source_doc: WyoHistory.org 'Coming to Wind River'; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent); Wyoming v. EPA, 875 F.3d 505 (10th Cir. 2017), cert. denied 138 S. Ct. 2677 (2018)
instrument: Fort Bridger 1863; Fort Bridger July 3, 1868 Art. 2; Brunot/Lander cession 1872 (act 1874); act Mar. 3, 1905
summary: The 1863 treaty recognized about 44 million acres of Shoshone country; the 1868 treaty reserved about 3 million (539+540 = 3.2 million acres in repo). The southern part was ceded in 1872 (539). The 1905 act opened land north of the Big Wind River; in 2017 the Tenth Circuit held that act diminished the reservation (Riverton outside).
verbatim_quote: Congress evinced a clear intent to diminish the Reservation
federal_account_contrast: Repo status for 540 is 'unclear' and stops in 1894; 20th-century diminishment absent.
map_implication: Add Wyoming v. EPA as a diminishment overlay on 540; contrast with McGirt.
notes: 1863 Stat. cite and 1905 cite from general knowledge; verify. Quote from search-result summary of the opinion.

source_doc: Andrew Jackson, Letter to the Creek Indians, Mar. 23, 1829 (American Presidency Project); Papers of Andrew Jackson (UTK), Jackson to David W. Haley, Oct. 15, 1829
instrument: Presidential talk (not a treaty)
summary: Jackson told the Creeks the western land would be theirs 'as long as the grass grows or the water runs'. This is a presidential promise, not treaty text; the binding guarantees are in the Removal Act sec. 3 and the removal treaties.
verbatim_quote: as long as the grass grows or the water runs, in peace and plenty
federal_account_contrast: Often misattributed to a treaty; the map should cite it as a talk.
map_implication: Use in narrative captions for Indian Territory, attributed to Jackson's 1829 letter, not to a treaty.
notes: Wording varies slightly between the March letter and the Oct. draft.

source_doc: McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. 894 (2020) slip op.; 221 U.S. 286; 1890 CIA report via accessgenealogy; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Indian Territory between the Arkansas and Canadian rivers
instrument: Creek Treaty Mar. 24, 1832 Art. XIV; Creek Treaty Feb. 14, 1833; Creek patent Aug. 11, 1852; Creek Treaty 1866; Creek agreement 1889
summary: The 1832 and 1833 treaties promised the Creeks a 'permanent home' with a fee patent (issued 1852). The 1866 treaty took the western half (486/698); allotment followed. McGirt held the 1866 reservation was never disestablished.
verbatim_quote: permanent home to the whole Creek Nation of Indians
federal_account_contrast: The repo marks the Creek eastern domain via Royce as reserved and the today layer (Census) shows only 'Creek OTSA (statistical)'.
map_implication: Show the Muscogee Reservation (1866 boundaries) as a legal reservation today, citing McGirt, and relabel the Census OTSA.
notes: Sources disagree whether fee promise is in 1833 or 1834 instrument.

source_doc: 1890 Commissioner of Indian Affairs report via accessgenealogy; Treaty of New Echota 1835 Art. 5; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Cherokee Nation, Indian Territory; Cherokee Outlet; Cherokee Neutral Land (Kansas)
instrument: Cherokee Treaty 1828; 1833; New Echota 1835 Art. 2, 5; patent Dec. 31, 1838; 1866 treaty; Cherokee Outlet agreement (act Mar. 3, 1893)
summary: New Echota (signed by the minority Ridge faction) confirmed 7 million acres plus a 'perpetual outlet' west and promised no state jurisdiction without consent. The Neutral Land (490) was put in trust for sale in 1866; the Outlet (489, about 8 million acres in repo) was sold in 1893; the remaining Cherokee Nation (492) was allotted and absorbed into Oklahoma in 1907.
verbatim_quote: the lands hereby granted shall revert to the United States if the said Cherokees become extinct or abandon the same
sources_cited_by_source: 1838 patent text quoted in 1890 CIA report
federal_account_contrast: Repo status for 492 is 'kept' (Royce era); allotment and statehood, which broke the 'no state' clause, are absent.
map_implication: Mark 492 kept-in-1894 then allotted; flag 489 and 490 as promised then sold; post-McGirt state court ruling (Hogner 2021) says the reservation persists.
notes: Hogner v. State (Okla. Crim. App. 2021) from general knowledge; verify. Stat. cites for 1893 act unverified.

source_doc: 1890 CIA report via accessgenealogy; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Indian Territory south of the Canadian
instrument: Dancing Rabbit Creek 1830; Choctaw patent Mar. 23, 1842; Choctaw-Chickasaw treaty 1855; treaty 1866 (Leased District)
summary: The 1842 patent gave the Choctaw (with Chickasaw lands) a fee title. The 1855 treaty 'leased' the land west of 98 degrees; the 1866 treaty ceded that Leased District (485) for $300,000, which went largely to the Kiowa-Comanche and Wichita reservations.
verbatim_quote: in fee simple to them and their descendants
federal_account_contrast: Repo marks 368 status unclear; Royce dates the cession to 1866.
map_implication: Show 367 as patented promised land; 485 'leased then ceded'.
notes: Choctaw and Chickasaw reservation persistence affirmed by Okla. Crim. App. in 2021 (Sizemore; Bosse) per general knowledge; verify.

source_doc: Treaty of Greenville Aug. 3, 1795 (Kappler 2:39); treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
nations: Wyandot; Delaware; Shawnee; Ottawa; Chippewa; Potawatomi; Miami; Eel River; Wea; Kickapoo; Piankashaw; Kaskaskia
place: Ohio/Indiana; line from Cuyahoga River via Fort Laurens and Loramie's to Fort Recovery and the Ohio opposite the Kentucky River
instrument: Treaty of Greenville, Art. 3-5
summary: Art. 4 relinquished US claims to Indian lands north and west of the Greenville line, and Art. 5 says the tribes 'are quietly to enjoy them'. That promised zone has no polygon of its own in the repo; it appears only as later cessions (1803-1840s).
verbatim_quote: the Indian tribes who have a right to those lands, are quietly to enjoy them
federal_account_contrast: The map shows only ceded land south/east of the line, not the guaranteed land beyond it.
map_implication: Draw the Greenville line as a 'promised boundary' and shade land beyond it 1795-1805 as guaranteed Native land.
notes: Quote from widely reprinted Art. 5 text; verify.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Hellgate Treaty'; Montana Historical Society Charlo biography; Char-Koosta News; treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Bitterroot Valley and Jocko (Flathead) Valley, Montana
instrument: Hellgate Treaty July 16, 1855 Art. 2, 11; EO Nov. 14, 1871; Garfield agreement 1872; Flathead Allotment Act Apr. 23, 1904
summary: Art. 11 promised a survey of the Bitterroot Valley before deciding the Salish reservation; the survey was not done before an 1871 order directed removal. Charlo's mark on the 1872 Garfield agreement is described by the Montana Historical Society as not signed by him. Troops moved the band in 1891. The Jocko reservation (374, 1.46 million acres in repo) was opened by the 1904 act.
verbatim_quote: Charlo never signed the document
federal_account_contrast: Repo has 374 'kept' and no polygon for the conditional Bitterroot reserve.
map_implication: Draw Bitterroot Valley above Lolo Fork as 'conditionally promised 1855, taken 1871-91'; add 1904/1910 opening over 374.
notes: Quote is search-summary paraphrase; get exact MHS wording. 1904 cite from general knowledge.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
instrument: Nez Perce Treaty 1855; Treaty 1863; agreement 1893 (act Aug. 15, 1894)
summary: The 1855 reserve (441, about 6.6 million acres in repo) was cut in 1863 to about 770,000 acres (442), signed by bands whose own lands lay inside the reduced reserve; non-treaty bands (Joseph's Wallowa) never signed. Unallotted 442 land was ceded in 1893.
federal_account_contrast: Royce records a cession by 'the Nez Perce' as one body.
map_implication: Flag 441 cession 'by treaty bands only; non-treaty bands did not consent'.
notes: Signatory claim from standard histories, not fetched this pass.

source_doc: Navajo Treaty June 1, 1868 Art. 2 (Kappler 2:1015); treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
place: Arizona/New Mexico; Bosque Redondo (Fort Sumner, NM) signing
instrument: Treaty of Bosque Redondo, June 1, 1868
summary: Signed while the Dine were held at Bosque Redondo after the Long Walk. Art. 2 reserved land bounded by 37N, a line through old Fort Defiance, a meridian through Bear Spring, and about 109 30'W (518, 3.3 million acres in repo). One of few promised reservations later enlarged (608, 615 and many 20th-century additions).
federal_account_contrast: Royce 519 'relinquishment' was signed in confinement.
map_implication: Show 518 as the 1868 promise and later additions as growth; tag 519 DURESS.
notes: Boundary paraphrased from treaty; verify.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent); Heizer 1972 (via search); Wikipedia 'California Indian Reservations and Cessions'; Mechoopda tribal site
instrument: 18 unratified California treaties (Barbour, McKee, Wozencraft)
summary: The repo has 19 reserve polygons from the 18 treaties, summing to about 8.5 million acres (sources give 7.4-8.5 million). All are status 'kept', but the Senate rejected the treaties and filed them under secrecy until 1905, so the reserves never existed in law.
verbatim_quote: Reservation set apart by the unratified treaty of Apr. 29, 1851, not a cession.
federal_account_contrast: 'Kept' wrongly implies Native nations held these lands; in fact they were promised and never delivered, and the matching 'ceded' areas (274, 279 etc.) were never ceded either.
map_implication: New status 'promised, never delivered' for the 19 CA reserves; status 'taken without ratified cession' for their paired cession areas.
notes: Acreage is repo-polygon sum and overlaps nothing else in CA as far as checked.

source_doc: treaty-land-atlas repo: crosswalks/royce-entry-roles.csv + data/derived/cessions.json (computed by research agent)
nations: Delaware; Shawnee; Potawatomi; Sauk and Fox; Kickapoo; Chippewa and Munsee; Ottawa; Miami; Wyandot; Kaw; Iowa
instrument: Removal-era treaties 1825-1846; Kansas reductions 1854-1867
summary: Nations removed to Kansas were promised permanent homes there, then the 1854 Kansas-Nebraska opening led to a chain of reductions, trust sales and railroad sales (e.g. Delaware remainder sold to a railroad, 488) and a second removal to Indian Territory by 1867-1873.
verbatim_quote: the remainder sold to the Missouri River Railroad Company
federal_account_contrast: Royce codes most as 'ceded' or 'sold in trust', hiding that they were the promised permanent homes of removal.
map_implication: Tag Kansas reserves as 'second promise' (post-removal) and link each to its removal treaty.
notes: Stat. cites from general knowledge.

source_doc: McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) via teachingamericanhistory.org, Indianz, Osage News
place: eastern Oklahoma (about 3 million acres incl. most of Tulsa)
instrument: McGirt v. Oklahoma
summary: 5-4, Gorsuch: only Congress can disestablish a reservation, and it must say so clearly; allotment, statehood and loss of tribal government did not do it. The Creek reservation remains Indian country for federal criminal law.
verbatim_quote: Because Congress has not said otherwise, we hold the government to its word.
federal_account_contrast: Shows a treaty promise can survive allotment in law, so 'promised' is not only history.
map_implication: Model McGirt as the template for 'promised and still legally reservation'; label Census OTSA layer accordingly.
notes: Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022) later allowed state jurisdiction over non-Indian defendants; mention in caption.

source_doc: Solem v. Bartlett 465 U.S. 463 (1984); Nebraska v. Parker 577 U.S. 481 (2016); South Dakota v. Yankton Sioux 522 U.S. 329 (1998); Hagen v. Utah 510 U.S. 399 (1994); Rosebud Sioux v. Kneip 430 U.S. 584 (1977)
nations: Cheyenne River Sioux; Omaha; Yankton Sioux; Ute (Uintah); Rosebud Sioux
instrument: Surplus-land acts 1892-1910
summary: Courts split on whether surplus-land acts shrank reservations: not diminished (Solem, Cheyenne River 1908 act; Parker, Omaha 1882 act); diminished (Rosebud 1904-1910 acts; Yankton 1894 act; Hagen, Uintah 1902-05 acts; Wind River 1905 per 10th Cir.).
federal_account_contrast: Royce cannot show any of this; boundaries today depend on case law, not on the 1894 map.
map_implication: Build a 'diminishment status' attribute per reservation (not diminished / diminished / disputed) with the controlling case.
notes: Case holdings from general legal knowledge, not fetched this pass; verify each before publishing.

source_doc: Heizer 1972 (digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/83366); NARA Prologue 2013 'treaties.pdf'; Mechoopda and Pechanga tribal history pages (via web search)
nations: More than 100 California bands (Miwok, Yokuts, Mono, Maidu, Nisenan, Wintun, Pomo, Yurok, Hupa, Karuk, Shasta, Luiseno, Cahuilla, Kumeyaay and others)
instrument: Eighteen treaties negotiated by commissioners McKee, Barbour and Wozencraft
instrument_cite: none (rejected); Senate Executive Journal 1852; injunction of secrecy removed 1905-01-18
summary: The 18 treaties reserved roughly 7.4 to 7.5 million acres (sources range from about 5 to over 8.5 million). The Senate rejected all 18 in secret executive session in 1852 under pressure from the California legislature and governor, and ordered them filed under an injunction of secrecy that was lifted only on 1905-01-18.
sources_cited_by_source: Heizer 1972 citing Senate Executive Journal; NARA RG 46 and RG 75
federal_account_contrast: Royce lists the cession areas as if ceded. The nations never received the reserves, yet the land was treated as open public domain.
map_implication: Already in atlas. Add a reserve-acreage field per treaty, and show the cession polygons as 'cession never agreed (treaty rejected)', not 'ceded'.
notes: The rejection date is disputed: 1852-07-08 (Heizer, via Mechoopda) vs 1852-07-02 (NARA Prologue) vs 1852-06-28 (one web source). Later remedies: 1928 California Indians Jurisdictional Act and Court of Claims K-344 judgment (1944) with large offsets [from-memory, not verified this session]. Atlas already has these 18 rows.

source_doc: Oregon Encyclopedia, 'Willamette Valley Treaties' and 'Willamette Valley Treaty Commission'; David G. Lewis, ndnhistoryresearch.com (Tualatin 1851 post)
instrument: Treaty with the Santiam band of Kalapuya (Champoeg), Willamette Valley Treaty Commission (Gaines, Skinner, Allen)
instrument_cite: none (laid on the table in the Senate, 1852)
summary: Signed at Champoeg in spring 1851. The bands ceded most land but kept small reservations inside the Willamette Valley because they refused removal east of the Cascades. Interior Secretary Stuart opposed the treaties for not removing the Indians, and the Senate tabled them in 1852; settlers had already filed Donation Land Claims on the reserved land.
federal_account_contrast: The federal record skips straight to the ratified 1855 Kalapuya Treaty (10 Stat. 1143); the 1851 reserves inside the valley, which the bands actually agreed to, disappear.
map_implication: Add as unratified instrument; mark the 1851 proposed valley reserves as 'promised in unratified treaty, overrun by Donation Land Claims'.
notes: Sources disagree on number and dates of the Champoeg treaties (five or six) and exact signing days. Some secondary accounts say Dart recommended against ratification because the reserves were already claimed; that is partly the blogger's interpretation. Atlas lacks these.

instrument: Sturges (Sturgis) Treaty / first Drum Creek Treaty, 1868
summary: Would have sold the whole Osage Diminished Reserve, about 8 million acres, to the Leavenworth, Lawrence and Galveston Railroad for about 20 cents an acre ($1.6 million). Railroad president William Sturges controlled the negotiation. Osage signers objected and Kansas settlers and Rep. Sidney Clarke fought it, and it was withdrawn in 1869.
federal_account_contrast: A near-miss sale of an entire reservation to a private corporation by treaty.
map_implication: Add as unratified; annotate the Osage Diminished Reserve polygon.
notes: Date conflict (May 27 vs June 1868). Successor: Act of July 15, 1870 removal to Indian Territory. Atlas lacks.

verbatim_quote: there is not in our files any acknowledgment by him of their receipt
