source_doc: Legends of America 'Cherokee War and the Battle of the Neches'; East Texas Family Records vol. 6 no. 3 (1982), via Portal to Texas History; Texas Escapes 'Tragedy of Chief Bowles'
nations: Texas Cherokee under Duwali (Chief Bowles) and associated bands (Shawnee, Delaware, Kickapoo, Caddo and others)
place: Bowles's village, East Texas (between the Angelina, Neches and Sabine rivers)
instrument: Treaty of Bowles Village (Sam Houston and John Forbes for the provisional government of Texas)
instrument_cite: none; rejected by Texas Senate Dec. 1837
summary: Gave the Cherokee and allies fee-simple title to land bounded by the San Antonio road, the Angelina, a line north to the Sabine, and the Sabine. The Texas Senate declared it null in December 1837. President Lamar ordered the Cherokee out and Texas troops killed Bowles at the Battle of the Neches in July 1839.
federal_account_contrast: Outside the US federal record entirely (Republic of Texas). Texas kept its public lands at annexation, so no federal cession exists for most of Texas.
map_implication: Draw the 1836 Bowles grant (roughly present Cherokee and Smith counties and parts of Rusk, Van Zandt, Gregg) as 'promised by Texas treaty, rejected, taken by force 1839'.
notes: Rejection date conflict 1837-12-16 vs 1837-12-26. Acreage conflict (about 150 sq mi vs 1.5 million acres). Atlas lacks.

source_doc: Charles D. Bernholz, 'CSA Indian Treaties', UNL Treaties Portal (treatiesportal.unl.edu/csaindiantreaties); Encyclopedia of Arkansas 'Fort Smith Conference (1865)'; History.com
nations: Creek; Choctaw; Chickasaw; Seminole; Cherokee; Wichita, Caddo and affiliated bands; Comanche bands; Osage; Quapaw; Seneca; Shawnee
place: Indian Territory (North Fork Town, Wichita Agency, Park Hill, etc.)
instrument: Confederate States treaties negotiated by Albert Pike, 1861 (nine treaties)
instrument_cite: Ratified by the CSA Congress, 1861; Deloria and DeMallie print them
summary: Pike concluded about nine treaties with Indian Territory nations between July and October 1861. The United States later used them as grounds to declare prior treaties forfeited and to force the 1866 Reconstruction Treaties, which took the western half of Creek and Seminole land and the Choctaw-Chickasaw Leased District.
federal_account_contrast: Many signers were factions (for example the Cherokee split after Ross signed under pressure on 1861-10-07; the 1863 Cherokee council repudiated it). The US treated the whole nation as liable.
map_implication: Annotate 1866 Reconstruction cession polygons with 'justified by Confederate treaties signed by factions under wartime pressure'.
notes: Party lists vary between sources. Not US unratified treaties but a related non-US instrument class. Atlas lacks.

nations: Lakota; Cheyenne; Arapaho; Crow; Assiniboine; Mandan; Hidatsa (Gros Ventre); Arikara
place: Horse Creek near Fort Laramie (approx. 41.9 N, 104.0 W)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), 1851-09-17
summary: The Senate cut the $50,000 annuity from fifty years to ten, with up to five more at the President's discretion (paid through about 1866-67). Assent was sought tribe by tribe; government records say the Crow assented last on 1854-09-18, while Wikipedia and an 1851 newspaper say the Crow never accepted. The ratification was never certified to the State Department, so for decades officials and tribes doubted the treaty was in force.
federal_account_contrast: The atlas says '50 to 10 years' but not that assent was piecemeal and contested, or that the publication gap left the treaty's status unclear.
map_implication: Keep partial; add 'Crow assent disputed' and 'not published until 1904 Kappler' notes to TLA-T-FL1851.
notes: No source confirmed Arikara assent specifically. Atlas has the row. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): WEB-NC-023, WEB-PRM-005. Verification: verify-plains s.1: Senate ratified with amendment May 24, 1852; never proclaimed; Crow assent disputed (Kappler footnote vs littlebighorn.info). Royce 'never ratified' is inaccurate.

source_doc: MNHS 'What's in a Treaty?' (usdakotawar.org); 10 Stat. 949 (govinfo STATUTE-10-Pg949); Wikipedia 'Treaty with the Sioux, 1858'
nations: Sisseton and Wahpeton (Traverse des Sioux); Mdewakanton and Wahpekute (Mendota)
place: Traverse des Sioux and Mendota, Minnesota Territory
instrument: Treaties of Traverse des Sioux (1851-07-23) and Mendota (1851-08-05)
summary: The Senate struck Article 3 of each treaty, which defined the 20-mile-wide Minnesota River reservations, and substituted payment plus a tract to be chosen by the President. Congress withheld cash and goods until the Dakota agreed, so assent was obtained from people who had no bargaining power. Fillmore then let them live on the struck reserve only until wanted for settlement; the 1858 treaties took the north half.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler shows the treaties as ratified; the 'reservation' existed only at presidential sufferance after the amendment.
map_implication: Mark Mendota (TLA-T-259) as partial like Traverse des Sioux; draw the 1851 river reservation as 'promised, struck by Senate, held at sufferance'.
notes: The 'traders' paper' signed at Traverse des Sioux diverted funds to traders (MNHS entry not read). Atlas Mendota row is not marked partial.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Second Treaty of Buffalo Creek'; President Van Buren message Jan. 1839 (Serial Set 355); United States v. New York, 173 U.S. 464 (1899); Seneca memorial Dec. 1839
nations: Seneca; Tonawanda Seneca; other Six Nations in New York
instrument: Treaty of Buffalo Creek, 1838
summary: The Senate amended the treaty and required each tribe to assent in council. For the Seneca, only 42 of 81 chiefs assented, and Van Buren asked the Senate to decide whether that sufficed; it ratified anyway in 1840. Seneca chiefs said the Senate's condition was never met and that fraud, bribery and forgery were used.
verbatim_quote: the assent of forty-two out of eighty-one chiefs has been obtained
sources_cited_by_source: Van Buren message; Fellows v. Blacksmith
federal_account_contrast: Treated as valid; the 1842 compromise treaty restored Allegany and Cattaraugus but not Buffalo Creek or Tonawanda.
map_implication: Flag Buffalo Creek cession as 'Senate consent condition not met'. Atlas violation V012 covers it; add the 42/81 figure.

nations: Lakota bands of the Great Sioux Reservation; Northern Arapaho; Northern Cheyenne
place: Great Sioux Reservation agencies; Black Hills (Paha Sapa)
instrument: Manypenny Agreement 1876 and Act of Feb. 28, 1877
instrument_cite: 19 Stat. 254 (1877 act); 19 Stat. 176, 192 (1876 rider) [from-memory, not verified this session]; United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980)
summary: The 1876 appropriations rider cut off subsistence until the Sioux gave up the Black Hills and hunting rights. The Manypenny commission then gathered signatures from about 10% of adult men, far below Fort Laramie 1868 Art. 12's three-fourths, and Congress enacted the cession in 1877.
federal_account_contrast: The 1980 Court found a taking requiring compensation but the Lakota refused payment; the atlas should not show the Black Hills as ceded.
map_implication: Render the 1877 Black Hills area as 'taken by statute; Art. 12 consent not obtained; compensation refused'.
notes: 10% figure from secondary sources (marker, advocacy). Atlas V024 covers this. Merged duplicate rows (same fact): WEB-DUR-014, WEB-DUR-015.

source_doc: Pres. Benjamin Harrison message on the Great Sioux Reservation, 1890 (presidency.ucsb.edu); Minot State 'A History of the Sioux Agreement' PDF; Newberry Library blog 'Standing Tall at Standing Rock'
nations: Lakota (Sicangu, Oglala, Hunkpapa, Minneconjou, Itazipco, Sihasapa, Oohenunpa); Yanktonai
instrument: Sioux Act of March 2, 1889 and Crook Commission signatures
instrument_cite: 25 Stat. 888 [from-memory, not verified this session] (one source cites 25 Stat. 1002 for the commission provision)
summary: The act broke up the Great Sioux Reservation into six reservations and opened about 9 million acres [from-memory, not verified this session], subject to three-fourths consent. Crook's commission got signatures through promises and threats, including a written promise that rations would not be cut; rations were cut soon after. Harrison certified that more than three-fourths consented.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the Art. 12 threshold as met; Lakota accounts and historians describe coercion and broken promises leading to the 1890 crisis.
map_implication: Annotate 1889 cession polygons 'consent obtained under coercion; promise on rations broken'.
notes: Atlas V025 covers 1889 act.
